product.title: The timer stops in the background and when the screen is off
product.minus: The app's core job — counting time — breaks: the timer shuts off in the background, freezes mid-session and won't run with the screen off, even when background is allowed in settings.

product.title: Distraction-free minimalism — a lifesaver for the ADHD mind
product.plus: Loved for a clean interface without useless animations or clutter: exactly what you need and nothing more. People specifically value the no-ads, no-bloat feel that doesn't keep you in the app longer than needed.

product.title: Indispensable for students: tracks study hours and holds focus
product.plus: The core audience is students building discipline for exams. The app helps visualize study hours, beat procrastination and actually get things finished.

product.title: Groups, leaderboards and Forest gamify study through competition
product.plus: Study groups show who's working now and how many hours they've racked up, while the ranking and the Forest tree motivate those who work better under pressure and like to outpace others.

product.title: Seamless sync across phone, PC and the Chrome extension
product.plus: For those who paid, cross-platform is a big plus: phone, desktop, iPad and the Chrome extension sync almost instantly, and the PC version is free if you have Pro.

product.title: Watch support flops: install fails and constant phone tethering
product.minus: People who picked the app specifically for the watch are let down: install fails on Galaxy Watch, and on Pixel Watch the timer constantly demands a phone connection and throws warnings every few seconds.

product.title: Logged hours vanish or get counted wrong
product.minus: The data is unreliable: updates wipe out groups and months of logged hours, and groups show 20–29 hours instead of the real 4–5, getting people accused of being bots.

product.title: Paid — but premium doesn't activate, and support stays silent
product.minus: A serious trust problem: payments aren't recognized, feature access doesn't unlock, and support emails go unanswered — even for people who've written for years.

product.title: Forest's nice touch stumbles: suns must be tapped one by one
product.minus: The Forest gamification is liked, but a small thing grates: to make the tree grow you have to tap every sun individually — people are begging for a 'collect all' button.

product.title: The loud ticking in fullscreen mode can't be turned off
product.minus: An irritating detail: fullscreen mode defaults to a ticking countdown, and the timer's clicking sound can't be switched off — you can only drop the volume to zero.

product.title: Too complex for newcomers and no way to export your data
product.minus: Some find the app overcomplicated — 'almost a course' just to time things. Plus it's a closed system: data can't be downloaded or exported, which is a red flag for many.

product.title: The headline feature, photo logging, is locked behind a paywall after one shot
product.minus: People install it specifically for the AI food photo from the ads, then get one or two free shots before the paywall. It reads as a bait-and-switch: advertised one thing, delivered another.

product.title: An endless onboarding survey: 10-20 minutes of questions before you can log a thing
product.minus: Before you can use it there's a 10-20 minute questionnaire, and a paywall waiting at the end. People who just want a tracker bail mid-way, feeling interrogated purely to reel them in.

product.title: Dark patterns: a discount fortune-wheel and countdown pressure you before you've even tried it
product.minus: Fake calculation animations, a Temu-style fortune wheel you always 'win', and a '10-minute special offer' timer — a manipulative funnel that repels even people who were willing to pay.

product.title: AI recognition systematically lowballs calories by hundreds — undercutting its whole premise
product.minus: Photos and descriptions return calories well below reality (by 100-300+), and corrections barely help. For an app whose USP is AI accuracy, this undermines the entire point of the product.

product.title: Stacked paywalls: you pay for premium, then workouts and meal plans demand more money
product.minus: Premium is sold as access to workouts and meal plans, but after paying those sections demand even more — a 'super premium'. People feel falsely advertised to and lose all trust.

product.title: Surprise billing: quoted monthly, charged yearly; the 'free trial' takes money unprompted
product.minus: A recurring pattern: a monthly price is shown but the yearly amount is charged; the 'trial' bills you on day one. Refunds are nearly impossible — support stays silent and Google points back to the developer.

product.title: Gamification (the growing 'seed', streaks, animations) flipped from charm to nuisance
product.minus: After updates, every log drowns in unskippable animations, streaks and a 'seed' pet. For people who just want to record a meal it stretches the routine, and there's no way to turn it off.

product.title: Color-coded food 'ratings' and a judgy tone are dangerous for people with eating disorders
product.minus: The app asks about eating disorders, then color-codes food as 'good/bad' and sends sad faces over a donut — even healthy items get warnings. It revives shame and guilt with no safeguards.

product.title: Health Connect sync is one-way: it reads your data but won't write calories or nutrition
product.minus: The integration imports weight and activity but won't export calories and macros to Google/Samsung Health. For paying users it's a half-broken feature: data stays trapped and isn't part of their wider health setup.

product.title: Thin food database and painful manual entry: common foods missing, fixes sit for weeks
product.minus: The database lacks vegetables, restaurant and non-Western foods; adding your own is a chore, and corrections can't be made instantly — only 'reported' and left waiting. Search returns junk instead of the obvious item.

product.title: When the features click, photo/barcode/voice make logging fast and genuinely drive weight loss
product.plus: The loyal core loves it: log food by photo, barcode or voice in seconds, the basic scanner is free, and macro plus fiber tracking genuinely helps. Dozens report losing 10-45+ lbs over months.

product.title: The same 'seed' and cute design that annoy some are the very thing that keeps others coming back
product.plus: For a meaningful slice of users gamification is the draw, not a flaw: the cute seed pet, gems for streaks and a pleasant interface make routine logging fun and keep the habit alive.

product.title: Forced ads after an update killed long-timers' loyalty
product.minus: A recent update imposed unskippable ads that pop up seconds after opening and after every transaction or building upgrade. Users with 5-8 years of history are leaving en masse to find an alternative, even though ads used to be purely opt-in for a reward.

product.title: The paradox: an app about saving rewards you for spending
product.minus: The city only grows when you log expenses, so no-spend days bring no progress — the mechanic literally nudges you to spend in order to build. For a finance tracker, users feel this contradicts its whole purpose.

product.title: Gamification keeps logging fun for people who'd otherwise quit
product.plus: Building a cute city turns dull bookkeeping into a pleasure — users open the app daily and genuinely want to log expenses. Several specifically note it works for people with ADHD who struggle with normal budgeting apps.

product.title: Core tracking has been reliable for years
product.plus: Many users have tracked expenses here for 5-8 years, valuing the simplicity, the no-bank-connection self-tracking, and the clear visual breakdown of spending by category.

product.title: Basic budgeting and income tracking are locked behind a subscription
product.minus: Setting a budget, tracking income, and viewing trends sit behind a paywall, even though users consider those the whole point of a finance app. Many resent the logic of paying for an app meant to save money.

product.title: Login breaks and wipes out years of data
product.minus: After updates users get logged out, login hangs on a "credentials expired" error, and years of expense history vanish with no way to recover it. This is the most painful of the technical failures.

product.title: Crashes and incompatibility with OneUI 6 / Android 14
product.minus: After OS updates (especially Samsung OneUI 6 and Android 14) the app simply won't open, crashes at the logo, or sends the phone into a reboot loop. Users go weeks unable to track while waiting for a fix.

product.title: The growing city lags and won't zoom out
product.minus: The bigger the city, the worse the lag when merging and upgrading buildings — sometimes a 5-minute wait for a menu. On top of that there's no full zoom-out, so a large city can't be properly viewed or organized.

product.title: Ad-for-diamonds is broken: ads won't load, rewards aren't granted
product.minus: The key way to earn diamonds — watching an ad — has been broken for months: ads won't load, it says "no ads available," and the close button after the reward doesn't respond, so the developer gets ad revenue while the player gets no diamonds.

product.title: Steep subscription, and ads persist even after paying
product.minus: The yearly subscription runs as high as $77-200, which feels mocking for a finance app, and ads plus "watch a video" prompts remain even for paying subscribers. Many would rather pay once than subscribe.

product.title: No transfer between accounts — moving money inflates expenses
product.minus: You can't simply move money between accounts: you have to make two transactions (an expense + an income), so a transfer counts as spending and skews the stats. There's also no starting balance and no "transfer" option — a frequent ask that holds back the fifth star.

product.title: Rigid categories and currency that won't customize
product.minus: The default categories can't be edited or extended (education, etc.), which makes some users quit on day one. Currency handling is shaky too: entries still go in dollars and get converted, and amounts may not match the user's real currency.

product.title: Updates routinely break what used to work
product.minus: The defining pain: every update fixes one thing and breaks another — the app won't open and crashes, click-to-call from a note dies, freshly added features vanish. Rolling back to the old version is often the only fix.

product.title: The app icon is frozen on "31"
product.minus: A widespread irritation: the app icon shows a static "31" instead of today's date. Users want the number to rotate daily like other calendars and find the current behavior pointless and misleading.

product.title: The widget keeps going blank and breaking
product.minus: The calendar widget — vital for many — either shows a blank panel or disappears entirely after Android updates. Restarting and clearing cache only help temporarily, and people find the available widget sizes and formats too limited.

product.title: The monthly grid confuses with adjacent-month dates
product.minus: The new month view bleeds previous- and next-month dates into the empty cells, making it easy to lose track. People ask to show strictly the current month's 1–30/31, make its numbers stand out, and open on the week containing today.

product.title: Backlash over the new blue icon
product.minus: The icon redesign angered long-time users: the blue badge clashes with Google's rainbow set, looks "like a startup's," and people can't find the app among the rest. The ask is simple — bring the old one back.

product.title: Forced holidays you can't turn off
product.minus: The calendar auto-adds holidays with notifications — often from another country or religion, sometimes on the wrong date — with no in-app way to disable or delete them. Same goes for graphic banners injected on trigger words with no off switch.

product.title: Too many extra taps to create and edit an event
product.minus: Creating an entry means tapping a date, then a separate Event/Task/Birthday menu; editing means tapping the item, then a pencil. Needless confirmations like the "OK" button after the time wheel grate too.

product.title: Time handling: auto-shifts, DST and fraction parsing
product.minus: Time misbehaves: changing an event's start auto-moves its end, events aren't corrected for daylight savings, tapping a cell saves 15 minutes early, and typing a size like "3/4\"" in a note suddenly jumps you to March 4th 2027.

product.title: Sync stumbles with web and Exchange
product.minus: Sync isn't always smooth: events land on the wrong dates, deleted meetings keep popping up with notifications, web changes don't reach the app, and pairing with Microsoft Exchange forces keeping two calendars so nothing slips.

product.title: A reliable planning backbone that never loses data
product.plus: What users love: for years it loses neither events nor settings, keeps everything in sync across devices, and reliably reminds an hour, a day, a week ahead. For many it's the cornerstone of their organization they'd "be lost" without.

product.title: All-in-one: events, tasks and birthdays
product.plus: A strength: events, tasks and birthdays live in one app, with Google Tasks and Gemini integration — no separate apps needed. A clean interface and cross-platform reach make it handy for both personal and work planning.

product.title: Event colors are loved — but there aren't enough
product.plus: Color-coding events is loved and heavily used for categories — students color their subjects so they don't miss deadlines, and the newly added colors were a hit.

product.title: Demands a Google account and ignores other calendars
product.minus: The mandatory Google account grates: without one it won't work or pull in third-party app data. People also ask for alternative calendars — Islamic, Shamsi, Afghan, regional — while current support is either missing or shows the wrong dates.

product.title: Manual envelope method with no bank linking is the core reason people love it
product.plus: The devoted core stays for exactly this: you enter money yourself, no auto-sync to your account, and that gives a feeling of control and mindful spending. Many have budgeted here for 5-10 years and never left.

product.title: The free version caps you at 10 envelopes — and that's where many quit
product.minus: The most common newcomer complaint: 10 envelopes isn't enough for a real budget, so you either merge categories or pay. Many uninstall before even starting, calling the cap greedy.

product.title: Monthly and yearly cycles only — but people get paid and budget weekly or biweekly
product.minus: A huge source of churn: no weekly or biweekly cycle, yet that's exactly how many people are paid (Australia especially — fortnightly). The budget doesn't match the real account, so people leave for competitors or Excel.

product.title: Sync breaks and loses data — budgets built up over years get wiped
product.minus: The most painful bug: the app hangs on "trouble syncing", envelopes won't fill, and on a forced sync the phone's transactions get overwritten by the server's. Loyal multi-year users suddenly lose everything.

product.title: Half the functions live only on the web; the app just says "go to the website"
product.minus: Basic actions — adding income, paying a credit-card debt, importing CSV, fixing settings — get punted to the browser. People don't understand the point of the app and see it as an unfinished shadow of the website.

product.title: The Android version lags behind iOS and the web: no envelope groups, missing features
product.minus: Android users explicitly complain that features ship for iPhone while they only get bug fixes. The app ignores the envelope groups the website has, and lacks the biweekly cycle available on iOS.

product.title: The numbers just don't add up: envelopes go negative, income doubles, balances lie
product.minus: Fatal for a budgeting app: a $10 transaction posts but the envelope still shows the old amount; income clones and doubles; graphs and the unallocated total compute wrong. People stop trusting the numbers and leave.

product.title: Input gets wiped when you switch apps — the daily-grind annoyance
product.minus: A very specific, years-old bug: open a calculator or banking app to check a figure and all your unsaved input in Goodbudget is erased. Plus the list jumps back to the top after every refresh. It maddens even loyal fans.

product.title: A recurring subscription instead of a one-time purchase — a dealbreaker for many
product.minus: People are willing to pay, but once, not monthly for "digital envelopes". $50-70 a year feels steep for the modest feature set; many explicitly ask for a lifetime license or a one-time fee.

product.title: Dated interface: number entry via an on-screen calculator, text spilling off-screen
product.minus: The UI looks straight out of the 90s: an on-screen calculator instead of the normal keypad, no automatic decimal point, text overwriting elements and not scaling to the screen. For some newcomers it's off-puttingly confusing.

product.title: Stability and longevity: couples run a shared budget for years and save real money
product.plus: The loyal core's strongest plus: a shared two-person budget with synced edits, years without glitches, and concrete financial wins — a paid-off house, thousands saved. Many switched from pricey YNAB and are happy.

product.title: No instructions — the learning curve is steep, and "help" just nudges you to buy premium
product.minus: Newcomers can't figure out how to add an envelope, income, or split a spend; the help describes buttons that aren't in the app, and support replies "read the manual / watch YouTube". Some give up during setup.

product.title: Requests for percentage allocation, bank linking and photo attachments — the missing features
product.minus: Even happy users list gaps: no percentage-based income allocation (key for variable income), no auto bank sync, no attaching a receipt photo, weak credit-card debt handling.

product.title: Reminders silently fail — the app's one job goes undone
product.minus: The loudest, angriest complaint by far: notifications simply don't fire. People miss tasks and events, open the app manually to force a reminder out of it, and switch to other task apps — because firing a reminder on time is this app's entire job.

product.title: Seamless deep integration with Calendar and Gmail
product.plus: The fans' favourite trait: tasks auto-appear in Google Calendar, pull from Gmail, and show up on Google Home. You can drag tasks onto the calendar on desktop, set deadlines, and keep everything in one place — Google's real trump card.

product.title: No search — the app collapses once your list grows
product.minus: Dozens of users are stunned there's no search bar. Once you've piled up tasks, finding one is nearly impossible; people have begged for years for a basic feature that even the desktop version of Tasks already has.

product.title: Recurring tasks are buggy and hidden until they're due
product.minus: Recurring tasks only appear in the list on the day they're due, so you can't plan ahead. Completing one fails to create the next instance or jumps it to next year instead of next month, and rescheduling one instance breaks the whole chain.

product.title: A minimalism that genuinely helps you focus
product.plus: A huge camp loves the app precisely for its clean simplicity: add a task fast, check it off, no clutter and (on this account) no ads. Many — especially people with ADHD and students — call it indispensable for staying focused.

product.title: The new icon enraged users — it looks like the clock app
product.minus: The logo redesign triggered a wave of fury: the new round check-mark icon gets confused with the Clock app, Messenger and Bixby. People call it "ugly", "headache-inducing", and sarcastically "thank" Google for a pointless update instead of real features.

product.title: The widget got broken: won't refresh, no transparency, no colour control
product.minus: After an update the widget regressed: it won't refresh until you open the app, lost transparency and its custom black colour, stopped showing subtasks, and truncates the list behind a "show all" button. Former widget lovers now call it useless.

product.title: Too bare-bones: no priorities, colours, history or smart date input
product.minus: For many, the simplicity tips into feature poverty: no priorities, no colour categories, no completion history, no natural-language dates, no advanced sorting — all things Todoist and Microsoft To Do have had for years. Some call it "barely an app" stuck in maintenance mode.

product.title: No list sharing — useless for teams and families
product.minus: The lack of shared lists is a recurring pain: people want to split tasks with a partner, family, coworkers or assign them to their kids, and simply can't. For collaboration the app is a non-starter.

product.title: The Gemini pairing turns voice task-adding into a superpower
product.plus: A growing camp loves the Gemini pairing: you can dictate a task with a deadline by voice with one button press, and never open the app itself. For ADHD folks and busy people it's a "game changer" that keeps them organised.

product.title: Forced merger with Keep angered long-time users
product.minus: Google rerouted Keep reminders through Tasks and many are furious: picture reminders and location-based tasks vanished, the transfer is clunky, and Keep notifications now arrive late. People are begging to split the apps apart again.

product.title: Notifications are too easy to dismiss — no persistent alerts or alarm
product.minus: Even when a notification does arrive, it gets lost in the Android stream and is easily swiped away without staying pinned until the task is done. People want a loud alarm, full-screen alerts with snooze, and high-priority notifications like Samsung Reminder and Microsoft To Do offer.

product.title: «Server connection lost» makes the app outright unusable
product.minus: The single most common pain: with stable internet the app constantly drops the server connection, throws errors out of nowhere and won't even let you log in or check off a task — and for some it wiped all their progress.

product.title: The gamification genuinely motivates and makes dull chores fun
product.plus: The core of the value: turning tasks into an RPG with levels, XP and gold is, for many, the only thing that ever got them to stick with habits and beat procrastination.

product.title: No offline mode — you can't even tick off a completed task
product.minus: The app needs constant internet just to mark something done: on the road or without a signal the task tracker becomes useless, and entries made offline get lost.

product.title: No per-habit history or progress graphs
product.minus: As a habit tracker it lacks the one thing that matters: no calendar, heatmaps or per-habit stats to see where you're consistent and where you slip — and people leave for other apps just for that.

product.title: A lifeline for people with ADHD and a lack of motivation
product.plus: A distinct, vocal audience — people with ADHD: the visual rewards, dopamine from checkmarks and game framing help them start and keep habits better than any plain planner.

product.title: Drains your health and levels even when tasks are done
product.minus: The damage mechanic breaks: HP drains to zero, levels drop and coins vanish even when the user honestly completed everything — it's demoralizing and often coincides with bugs that block creating new tasks.

product.title: A confusing onboarding with no clear tutorial
product.minus: Newcomers drown: too many tabs and categories, no clear guide, the game side is opaque — people give up before they ever figure out how to use it.

product.title: Three sections — Habits, Dailies, To-Do — neatly separate your tasks
product.plus: The structure gets praise: splitting into Habits, Dailies and To-Do's helps prioritize and remember little things, and even people who skip the game pick up the task side easily.

product.title: Free, ad-free and open source
product.plus: A strong trust signal: everything essential is free, there are no ads, and purchases are cosmetic only — people specifically call out the honest monetization and offer to pay just to support the team.

product.title: The «Get Started» button doesn't work — you can't sign up
product.minus: A wall at the door: typing a username leaves the sign-up button dead, no account gets created via Google or email — people get stuck on the very first screen.

product.title: The game runs out of steam: too easy or just boring
product.minus: The game layer doesn't hold up: bosses deal no damage, you can max out in a week, fights amount to a «damage dealt» message — and after a couple of weeks you're left with a plain, lightly dressed-up to-do list.

product.title: Widgets don't roll over to a new day without opening the app
product.minus: The widgets work halfway: checkboxes don't respond and the list won't reset for the new day until you open the app — which defeats it for exactly the people who need the widget as their first reminder of the day.

product.title: Unfinished tasks vanish, and flexible scheduling is missing
product.minus: The scheduling logic falls short: unfinished tasks disappear as if done, there's no proper weekly task or multiple daily reminders, and the clock format and day-start ignore the user's timezone.

product.title: Life-changing over the long haul — for years, even a decade
product.plus: The most loyal cohort: people track habits here for 2, 3, 4 and even 10+ years, come back after breaks, and say the app genuinely rebuilt their discipline and their lives.

product.title: The free plan is capped at 3 habits — even basic check-ins hit a paywall
product.minus: The single biggest complaint: the free tier lets you create only 2-3 habits, and often the very act of marking something done demands premium. Users feel that checking off a daily habit is the bare minimum and shouldn't sit behind a paywall, so they leave en masse for free alternatives.

product.title: A wave of bugs turned a working app unusable: check-ins fail, fail/skip do nothing
product.minus: Long-time users repeat that the app "used to work great" but fell apart in the past month: you can't mark skipped or failed, check-ins don't save, undo doesn't undo. Many of them paid, which makes it sting more.

product.title: Off-by-one date bug: marking yesterday lands on today or tomorrow
product.minus: A distinct, persistent defect: dates slide. Mark something failed for yesterday and it logs today; mark today and it jumps to tomorrow. Successes silently turn into "skip" the next day. Reinstalling doesn't help.

product.title: Widgets are broken: empty container, forget habits, force you into the app
product.minus: Widgets are a sore spot. They show an empty frame with no icons, "forget" the habits you configured, refuse to log progress, and instead of a quick tap they open the app on a stats page. A bulky new 3×3 widget replaced the small 1×1 that many people cherished.

product.title: Marking a simple habit is oddly hard: extra steps, pop-ups, precise taps
product.minus: The most basic action — ticking a box — is turned into a quest. Editing a progress log takes convoluted steps; a habit with sub-tasks forces a precise tap on a tiny 0/3 line or you mark the whole thing; the new widget throws an "amount" pop-up even when a habit is checked off once.

product.title: Support goes silent or drags — especially painful for paid and Lifetime users
product.minus: People who bought a subscription or Lifetime write to support about bugs and hear nothing for weeks, or ever. The sense of having paid and been abandoned recurs across the angriest reviews.

product.title: Cancelling the subscription is made painfully hard — it alienates even loyal users
product.minus: A separate grievance is cancellation. Cancel and payment options are stripped from the app's menus, so you can only cancel with a receipt; the process is called "extremely convoluted" and something that "should not be allowed." It reads as a dark pattern.

product.title: Rigid scheduling: no flexible "N days a week", and streaks break on days off
product.minus: Flexible scheduling is missing: you can't set "3 times a week on floating days." Streaks only count for everyday habits, so if you rest on Sundays your max caps at 6 even with a perfect year. Rivals like Habitnow and Loop handle this.

product.title: Google Fit / Health Connect and Wear OS watch integrations work intermittently
product.minus: Health integration — a common reason people buy Lifetime — lets users down: steps and workouts stop syncing, data goes missing, manual entry isn't available. On Samsung/Wear OS watches notifications get skipped and the tile freezes.

product.title: A clean minimalist design and true cross-platform sync — what people actually love
product.plus: Habitify's core strength is a tidy, uncluttered interface and seamless sync across phone, web (Chrome/Edge) and desktop. For many it's the one tracker made equally well on iOS and Android, and that's exactly what makes them buy Lifetime.

product.title: "Don't break the chain", the tree reward and a Lifetime option genuinely keep people hooked
product.plus: For users where it works, the app genuinely changes routines: the "don't break the chain" method, the grid view, and the tree gamification give visual motivation to keep the streak. The one-time Lifetime purchase is seen as a fair, valued alternative to a subscription.

product.title: Premium is seen as overpriced: too steep for many regions, with no purchasing-power parity
product.minus: Even satisfied users call the price too high — $50-65 for what's essentially a simple tracker when iOS rivals cost $6. Complaints are loudest from weaker-currency countries, asking the devs to support purchasing-power parity.

product.title: Pushy notifications and share-progress nags annoy and can't be turned off
product.minus: The app buries users in reminders, fires them at night, and keeps begging to share progress. Some new notifications can't be silenced except by killing all of them in Android — which defeats the tracker's purpose. It also pushes premium fast.

product.title: The Android build lags behind iOS and keeps losing features it once had
product.minus: Paid users note Android is far behind iOS, with features arriving months late. Worse, the devs remove things that already worked — editing note dates, per-habit success rates, the small widget — which erodes trust in the product.

product.title: Only 4 habits free — and it undercuts the whole point
product.minus: The 4-habit free cap is repeatedly called a deal-breaker: a habit tracker that won't let you track your habits. People uninstall over this specifically, not over quality.

product.title: The design and heat-map grid feel almost physically satisfying
product.plus: The core draw is the visuals: a clean minimalist grid you want to fill in. The act of checking off a habit is its own reward, and progress is visible at a glance.

product.title: Widgets are paywalled — and often broken even after you pay
product.minus: The widget is the top reason people buy Pro, but it's a double hit: it's locked behind the paywall, and those who pay report it doesn't show up, breaks, demands a huge size, or looks out of place.

product.title: Lifetime one-time purchase — a relief amid endless subscriptions
product.plus: Many are won over by the lifetime one-time option instead of a subscription: the price is called fair, "the cost of lunch," and people buy to support the dev. For the 2026 market it's a rarity.

product.title: No cross-device sync — switching phones risks losing progress
product.minus: The most painful functional gap: no auto-sync, only manual export/import. The purchase is tied to one device, and on switching phones people face "pay again or start over."

product.title: Responsive solo dev — Sebastian replies personally and ships requests
product.plus: A real strength is direct contact with the creator: people message a question and get a fast reply from the dev himself, sometimes even a feature added. It turns the purchase into backing "their" indie.

product.title: Can't handle weekly/monthly habits — the grid demotivates
product.minus: For "3-4 times a week" habits the app falls short: on days you don't need the habit, the cells stay blank, so the board looks like a broken streak even when the goal is met.

product.title: No-ads, unobtrusive model — yet some see the freemium as a greedy cash-grab
product.minus: Opinions on monetization are split. Some praise the no-ads, calm paywall; others see overly pushy Pro prompts (up to 5 times in 3 minutes) and call it greed and "a glorified ad for a paid app."

product.title: No support for negative habits or fractional values
product.minus: A recurring request is a "negative habit" mode (quit smoking, cut down drinking) where a check means a relapse. Fractional values (7.4 hours of sleep, 6.7 miles) and time tracking are also missing.

product.title: Reminders fire intermittently — the one thing they must do
product.minus: Notifications are unreliable: here one day, gone the next, morning ones silent while evening ones fire. For a tracker you open "when you remember," that's critical — no reminder, habit slips.

product.title: No-bloat simplicity — a tracker you actually stick with
product.plus: People specifically value that it does one thing well: everything you need and nothing more, no fanfare and no guilt when you miss. The real habit-tracker problem — keeping the habit of opening it — is solved by simplicity.

product.title: Lag, old phones, and broken scaling on tablets/foldables
product.minus: Performance and adaptiveness wobble: it lags even on recent Pixels, an update can break launch, and the UI looks monstrously magnified on tablets and foldables — tiny text or bloated elements.

product.title: The free version hits a wall at ~7 habits
product.minus: Users quickly hit a ceiling of a handful of habits and feel pushed to buy premium, otherwise the app is just a bare minimum.

product.title: One-time payment instead of a subscription is the big draw
product.plus: A one-time lifetime purchase feels fair and cheap against a subscription-heavy market, and many pay willingly just to support the developer.

product.title: Reminders and background notifications silently fail
product.minus: Even with battery optimization off, notifications don't fire on time unless the app is open, so people miss things — nearly fatal for a habit tracker.

product.title: A simple, clean, uncluttered interface
product.plus: A tidy ad-free interface with no gimmicky AI features makes it feel like a tool, not a toy — people open it first thing every day for years.

product.title: The home-screen widget is loved, but out of sync with the app
product.minus: The widget is a top reason to choose the app, yet checking off a task in it doesn't turn off the alarm, and on one Android version it's completely broken.

product.title: No desktop app or cross-platform sync
product.minus: The lack of PC, Mac, Windows and watch versions plus weak cross-device connectivity drives people back to competitors despite loving the app.

product.title: Backups and data transfer are manual
product.minus: Without automatic sync, moving data to a new device is tiring, and switching phones sometimes wipes premium status and blocks cloud restore.

product.title: Deep customization of habits and schedules
product.plus: Per-habit flexibility — different reminders by day of week, colors, sub-tasks, quantity and time goals — gives people the sense they can do it their own way.

product.title: Stats and data visualization lag behind rivals
product.minus: The stats section feels underbaked: no quick glance at streaks and scores, no heatmap or overall daily progress, pushing some paid users toward Loop.

product.title: It genuinely helps build discipline and quit bad habits
product.plus: Long-term users say it changed their lives — helping them keep a routine, stay consistent, and quit smoking, vaping and sugar.

product.title: Notifications still fire even after a task is done
product.minus: Complete a habit or task early and the alarm and notifications still go off — a small but irritating logic flaw.

product.title: The timer and stopwatch don't run in the background
product.minus: The built-in timer stops as soon as the screen goes off or you switch apps, making the feature nearly useless for time-based tasks.

product.title: A generous, ad-free free tier is rare on this market
product.plus: Many note that even without paying the app gives almost everything they need and isn't clogged with ads, unlike rivals that hide everything behind a paywall.

product.title: Moving reminders to Calendar broke the core feature
product.minus: Reminders used to live inside Keep and just worked; after the update they were handed off to Google Calendar/Tasks — now you must install a separate app, edits in Keep don't sync back, and notifications frequently don't fire at all. For many users this killed the whole reason they used the app.

product.title: Account sync is the main reason to trust it
product.plus: Notes are tied to your Google account, not your phone, and sync across every device and back up to the cloud automatically. People have used it for years and decades without ever losing a file — for most this is the single biggest edge over the stock notepad.

product.title: Notes vanish after updates — trust is broken
product.minus: Despite the praised cloud backup, a slice of users report that an update wiped out years of notes, whole pages and shopping lists — and now note contents even change on their own. For an app whose whole pitch is reliability, this is the most damaging failure.

product.title: No search inside a note — you can't find a line
product.minus: There's no Ctrl+F equivalent inside a long note: you can't locate a specific word or line the way you can in a browser or Docs. The old yellow highlight of matches is gone too. With big lists and notes this makes finding anything painful — one of the most repeated requests.

product.title: Minimal and fast — you open it and just write
product.plus: A clean, fast, ad-free interface where you can jot a note or checklist instantly with no extra steps. For many it's exactly this simplicity, plus the checkboxes for shopping and to-do lists, that beats the bloated competitors.

product.title: Lag on big notes makes plain typing hard
product.minus: Once a note grows large (around 10k words and up) typing starts to stutter, with lag when entering text and fixing typos. The latest update made the interface slower to respond even on plain text — in an app where you're 'just writing letters'.

product.title: The new lightbulb icon instead of a notebook infuriates
product.minus: The redesigned lightbulb icon sparked its own wave of anger: a pencil or notebook would make sense for a notes app, and the bulb gets confused with other apps (like the Hue light controller). Some people even rolled back to an older version just to get the old icon.

product.title: Lists and checkboxes — the daily killer use case
product.plus: Shopping lists, to-dos and plans with tick-boxes are what people open the app for every single day. They keep recipes, year-long lists and study notes in it, and call the checklist feature the one they love most.

product.title: You still can't sort a list alphabetically — for years
product.minus: Basic alphabetical sorting of a shopping list still isn't there, even though people have asked since 2025. Add to that: you can't select and copy multiple list items at once to paste a list into a chat. The basic list handling feels unfinished.

product.title: The widget is great but renders notes badly
product.minus: The widget is called one of the best features, yet it's spoiled by details: single-line notes take two lines, the padding eats space, there's no indicator that notes didn't fit, and on some devices the widget shows no notes at all, forcing you into the app.

product.title: Forced AI and Gemini nobody asked for
product.minus: A chunk of users are irritated by the Gemini integration and 'AI slop' they never asked for: some left for FOSS alternatives precisely because of it, others suspect AI now maintains the app's code — which is why things keep breaking.

product.title: No app lock or private folder for notes
product.minus: There's no built-in protection: users ask for a password on a note, a lock on the app itself, or a private folder. On Samsung devices the app can't be physically locked, and this privacy request has been around a long time.

product.title: You can't place an image where you want in a note
product.minus: You can embed photos, video and audio, but an image always lands at the top of the document and can't be moved or placed between lines of text. For anyone mixing text and pictures, it breaks the whole layout.

product.title: Missing text formatting and headings
product.minus: Formatting is thin and in places stripped back: title styling was removed, you can't bold or underline, and formatting is lost on copy-paste. Users ask for bold, italic, headings and font size — without them the app only suits short notes.

product.title: People want more colors and backgrounds for notes
product.minus: The palette is stuck at 12 colors and a handful of background patterns, in 2026 no less. People want more shades, custom colors and the option to set their own gallery image as a note background — often the only gripe from otherwise happy five-star users.

product.title: "Free and ad-free" is the number-one reason for the love
product.plus: Parents repeatedly single out that the app is completely free, ad-free, and has no mandatory subscription — for a kids' learning app this is felt as a rarity and a reason to trust it.

product.title: Kids reach for it on their own — learning feels like play
product.plus: Many parents say the child is "hooked", wakes up wanting to open it, and doesn't notice they're learning — the lessons are disguised as play so well that it holds even toddlers' attention.

product.title: Crashes, freezes, and won't launch on a range of devices
product.minus: Stability complaints pile up: the app crashes on launch, freezes "on almost every other song", and lags or hangs even on brand-new flagships like the Pixel 10.

product.title: English-only — a barrier for non-English families
product.minus: The most common structural complaint: the language can't be changed, everything is English-only. Parents from India, Bangladesh, Arabic-speaking and other regions ask for localization and note that without it the app feels "for the rich" and their kids can't follow the content.

product.title: Content is too easy and stops at preschool age
product.minus: For first-graders and kids aged 6+, the material quickly turns dull: lessons are "too easy", there's no way to manually set the difficulty edge, and parents ask to raise the ceiling (around 2nd grade) up toward K-12.

product.title: Tablet incompatibility — and tablets are exactly what's needed
product.minus: A paradox: the best experience is on a tablet, yet it's tablets where the app often refuses to install or launch (Lenovo Tab M11, Galaxy Tab S11, etc.) — even when the parent bought the tablet specifically for it.

product.title: Especially valued by parents of neurodivergent kids
product.plus: A distinct strong note: parents of autistic, non-verbal and neurodivergent children report real progress — a child starting to learn opposites, to read, to speak — and thank the app for it.

product.title: An indispensable free homeschooling tool
product.plus: Homeschooling families use the app as a full supplement across subjects and stress that it covers reading, math, logic and writing — and many voluntarily donate to the developers.

product.title: Login loop: email/Google sign-in dead-ends
product.minus: Sign-in is its own pain zone: the app endlessly demands you re-check your email, falsely reports "no internet" over working Wi-Fi, or gets stuck forever on the loading animation after login.

product.title: Too-continuous flow with no clear activity boundaries
product.minus: The continuous format makes parental control hard: it's unclear where one activity ends and the next begins, you can't pick a single specific exercise for the child, and the only way "back" is to exit the app.

product.title: Managing child profiles is clumsy and inflexible
product.minus: Child profiles can't be deleted or corrected, you can't create a new one with the same names, and the level is locked to age — parents would rather have a placement test so the child lands at their real level.

product.title: The AI overhaul turned a beloved app into a mess
product.minus: The single loudest pain: people who loved the app for years woke up to a mandatory AI logger instead of the tracker they knew, and they're leaving in droves. The old ease, transparency and tidy layout they paid for are gone.

product.title: The AI invents calorie numbers you can't trust
product.minus: The AI calorie estimates wildly miss: 711 kcal for a cup of tea, 7000 kcal in a mug of coffee, 65,608 kcal for one serving of fish. It counts the same food differently every time, so the whole point of a food diary collapses.

product.title: The AI replaced search and made logging painfully slow
product.minus: Food used to take seconds to add via search; now you must dictate to an AI chat that types one letter at a time, picks the wrong item, and won't let you choose manually. What was instant is now a multi-step chore for every single meal.

product.title: "Sorry, something went wrong" — logging just breaks
product.minus: Paying subscribers hit "Sorry, something went wrong" for days on end and can't log food at all — not manually, not by camera. Restarting the phone doesn't help, and there's no button to report the issue.

product.title: Basic settings are locked behind the paywall
product.minus: Adjusting your own calories and macros for keto or diabetes is now premium-only, as is the AI scanner. Users are furious they must pay for what's free elsewhere and used to be free here too.

product.title: A "buy premium" takeover pops up mid-logging
product.minus: A full-screen subscription prompt appears every time you open the app and right in the middle of adding food — several times a day, for years. It's so aggravating it kills any desire to ever pay.

product.title: Beloved features quietly vanished: fasting, meal sharing, water
product.minus: The intermittent fasting timer, meal sharing with a partner, and the water tracker simply disappeared after updates — often the very features people paid for. No way to bring them back, no explanation.

product.title: Slow, laggy and crashing even for paid users
product.minus: Every action drags 10-30 seconds, sometimes times out, and lately the app crashes a couple seconds after launch. Even typing into the diary lags and drops characters.

product.title: Steps and workouts don't turn into burned calories
product.minus: Health Connect, Fitbit, Samsung — workout and step sync works poorly: 10,000 steps a day show 0 burned calories, or conversely walking and steps get double-counted. MyFitnessPal handles this better.

product.title: The free tier and clean interface still win newcomers over
product.plus: Despite the storm, many praise the generous free tier, the rich multilingual food database, and the clean, intuitive interface. For calorie-counting newcomers it's an easy, visual start with no intrusive ads.

product.title: Long-term results: real weight loss over the years
product.plus: For loyal users it genuinely works: people report losing 21, 30, even 150 pounds over years of consistent tracking. Keto mode with net-carb counting, recipes, and sustained results are why they pay and keep coming back.

product.title: Free, no ads, no subscriptions — the core reason people love it
product.plus: The overwhelming majority of rave reviews boil down to one thing: the app does its job completely free, with no ads, no account and no features locked behind a paywall.

product.title: Minimalism as the feature: nothing extra, focus on the goal, not the UI
product.plus: People value that the app is deliberately un-bloated: clean interface, zero frills, keeping attention on the habits themselves rather than on fiddling with the app.

product.title: No cross-device sync — you have to shuttle backups by hand
product.minus: The single most common request from fans: data lives only on one device, and moving it means manually exporting a full backup — there's no cloud and no account sign-in.

product.title: No categories/grouping — a long habit list turns into an endless scroll
product.minus: Power users with dozens of habits hit a flat list with no folders or collapsing: they scroll endlessly and hack grouping via color tags.

product.title: Widgets make ticking off fast, but the new combined widget disappointed
product.plus: The small tile widgets are praised for instantly marking completion right from the home screen. But a recent change cramming many habits into one widget broke people's setup, and they're asking to make it optional.

product.title: Measurable habits exist, but typing numbers by hand is painful
product.minus: The ability to track numeric habits is loved, but manual number entry frustrates: people want '+'/'-' buttons with a custom step right on the home screen and an increment widget.

product.title: Flexible habit frequency (X times in Y days) — what rivals lack
product.plus: A standout that long-term users single out: you can set 'X times in Y days' frequency, measurable goals and multiple tracking modes, and here it beats the others.

product.title: Reminders are unreliable — sometimes silent, sometimes ignore the schedule
product.minus: Some users complain notifications simply stop arriving (even with battery optimization off), and reminders also can't flexibly handle an 'every N days' interval.

product.title: People want the streak shown next to the habit, not buried in a card
product.minus: A recurring request: show the current streak right next to the habit on the home screen and widget — today you have to open the habit and scroll to see this key motivator.

product.title: Android-only, no iOS or web — feels dated and walled-off
product.minus: Being locked to Android alone puts people off: they want iOS, web and Google Drive sync, and without it the app feels dated.

product.title: The dev deliberately won't add features — the flip side of minimalism
product.minus: Long-time users are tired of waiting for long-requested basics (search, duplicate, skip-from-notification, categories) and drift to other apps: the developer is deliberately stingy with updates.

product.title: Charts and calendar don't always reflect the real data
product.minus: The analytics draw complaints: line graphs don't plot the actual entered values, days appear out of order, and 'unmarked' and 'not done' look identical.

product.title: Basic features that were free for years got moved behind a paywall
product.minus: The core grievance of loyal users: setting a daily calorie budget, viewing macros, the barcode scanner, manually entering calories — all of it used to be free, and now demands a subscription. People don't read this as «new features cost money», they read it as having something taken away that they already relied on.

product.title: An ad fires every single time you log a piece of food
product.minus: Ads aren't in the background, they're spliced into the core action: you have to watch a clip before you can log a food or scan a barcode. It kills the app's main advantage — speed of entry — and pushes longtime users with thousand-day streaks out the door.

product.title: An endless onboarding quiz before they ever show the price
product.minus: Before you can start, the app asks dozens of personal questions with no skip button, and only at the very end reveals it's paid. People came to log food, not to tell an AI their life story, and they uninstall en masse around question 18, 30, or 40.

product.title: Listed as «free» but paid after sign-up — the hidden price
product.minus: The app shows up under «free calorie counter», walks you through the whole onboarding and email capture, and only then mentions a 7-day trial and an $80/year subscription. You can't even see the premium price without making an account, and the website doesn't list it either. People call it false marketing and a dark pattern.

product.title: Forced account creation to harvest personal data
product.minus: Just to count calories, the app forces you to create an account and pulls a pile of personal data up front — even questions about your family. There's no guest mode to try it first, and users flat-out accuse the developer of collecting and selling data under the guise of «mysterious plans».

product.title: Billing surprises: charges without consent, cancellation that doesn't work
product.minus: A whole layer of money complaints: surprise charges of $42/$80/$87 to people who deleted the app long ago, double charges, and billing even after cancelling at the end of the trial. Finding how to unsubscribe is sometimes impossible. This isn't about «expensive» — it's about unpredictable billing behavior.

product.title: Fitbit/Google Health sync is broken: steps and burned calories don't pull through
product.minus: After Fitbit moved to Google Health Connect, sync fell apart: steps pull through intermittently and burned calories don't come at all — only the step count arrives. For people who paid for premium specifically to sync and compute their deficit, this makes the app useless and drives cancellations.

product.title: Food search dies with a «slow connection» error on a perfectly fine network
product.minus: After one of the updates, food-database search stopped working for many: an endless spinner or a «slow connection» message, even at 150 Mbps with a clean speedtest. The barcode scanner fails right after. Without search, a food-logging app loses its point.

product.title: UI updates break familiar flows: the «done logging» button got hidden
product.minus: The team keeps moving things and swapping colors: the «done logging» toggle got buried at the bottom of the log, the handy Quick Add was removed as «underused», and macros now require a toggle instead of a dropdown. Longtime users, including lifetime owners, just want the old version back.

product.title: The food database is huge but clogged with duplicates carrying wrong calories
product.minus: The crowdsourced database gives breadth, but searching one item returns a pile of variants with differing calories, and almost none are right — you end up creating your own. There's no thumbs-up/down to flag accurate entries, so the database fills up with useless duplicates.

product.title: Simple entry and a big database make logging fast — the thing people love most
product.plus: Over the years this became many people's most convenient tracker: a clean interface, a huge food selection (including Indian/Asian dishes), voice, photo, and scan entry. Logging is so simple it becomes a habit — it's exactly the speed and simplicity that keeps bringing people back.

product.title: It genuinely helps people lose weight — through the habit of honestly logging everything
product.plus: The headline outcome people praise: users drop tens of pounds and come back years later. It's not magic but the act of daily honest logging that raises food awareness — reviewers literally write «5 lbs in a week», «50+ lbs», «311 down to 154».

product.title: The barcode scanner and photo capture are the beloved feature — for speed, when they work
product.plus: Barcode scanning and snapping a photo of a meal are what users call the app's best part: it removes typing the product and brand, making tracking fast and nearly automatic. Many bought lifetime specifically for the scanner. The catch — after several updates the scanner started throwing errors for some.

product.title: You can't enter portions in grams — only weird «serving sizes»
product.minus: For people who weigh food on a kitchen scale this is critical: many items offer no grams option, only cups and spoons, which blocks an accurate count. Grams are more precise than measuring spoons, and without them the app becomes nearly unusable for some users.

product.title: Free, no ads, no subscription — the parents' headline reason
product.plus: The same point comes up again and again: the app is fully free, with no ads, no upsells and no paid subscription. For budget-conscious parents and volunteer teachers, that is precisely why they install it and trust it.

product.title: Kids genuinely start doing arithmetic — adding, subtracting, multiplying
product.plus: Parents describe concrete progress: a five-year-old learned to add and subtract within a couple of weeks, a child can now «add up to 20», a sibling learned to divide. These aren't vague compliments but an observed jump in skill.

product.title: Hints can't be turned off: a hand just points to the answer
product.minus: The core systemic bug: a parent unchecks «hints» in settings, yet after 5 seconds a hand appears anyway, pointing straight at the correct answer. The child never gets to think and just taps where it points — defeating the whole purpose of a learning app.

product.title: The Lucas character carries engagement — kids learn without noticing
product.plus: The bond with the character Lucas and friends turns the lesson into play: kids «don't even notice they're learning» and won't put the tablet down. Teachers and volunteers note it's the characters that hold a class's attention.

product.title: There's a mindless mini-game where the child hides from the math
product.minus: The app exposes a pointless point-and-click game, and the child slips into it without solving any problems at all. Parental controls don't block it — for a learning product that's a hole in the core mechanic.

product.title: A safe alternative to «violent» games — parents feel calmer
product.plus: Parents explicitly contrast the app with shooters and violent mobile games: the child is busy with age-appropriate educational content that builds thinking and focus. It's a strong emotional reason to stay.

product.title: It's hard to quit — even parents are baffled by the close button
product.minus: Quitting the game is hard even for an adult: a non-obvious close button turns «time to hand back the phone» into a fight, especially when the child won't let go of the tablet.

product.title: Crashes on the splash screen and freezes on the stickers — you just close it
product.minus: Some users can't get past the door: the app sticks on the title screen and never opens, or freezes at the stickers stage with closing it the only way out. There are also glitches that scare the child.

product.title: A lifesaver for homeschooling and the classroom when the parent is busy
product.plus: It fills a real need: it helps parents who don't have time to teach the child themselves, and first-time homeschooling teachers. Whole families use it (4 kids) and it's used in classrooms.

product.title: Safety alarm: the child reportedly reaches «adult» content
product.minus: Several parents are seriously alarmed: by their account, the child gets from the app to «adult» YouTube or an «adult only» tab via a basic number test. Even if it's an edge path, for an app «for the littlest ones» that perception is a reputational risk.

product.title: Too easy and «babyish» — older kids get bored
product.minus: The content is pitched at first-grade level, and for older kids (12+) the tasks feel primitive and dull: «a baby game because the maths is so easy». What's a plus for a preschooler is a reason for an older child to quit.

product.title: It used to work offline, but after an update it needs Wi-Fi
product.minus: Part of the app's value was working without a connection — key for kids on the go and families with poor internet. After an update users complain it now needs Wi-Fi, and ask whether it can be played offline at all.

product.title: The lifetime Pro people bought was voided, and now they're forced to re-pay via subscription
product.minus: People who bought lifetime access years ago find, after switching phone or account, that their purchase is no longer recognized, Pro is gone, and a subscription has taken its place. It reads as a betrayal of loyal paying customers.

product.title: Support goes silent for months, and emails bounce back
product.minus: Dozens of emails to support go unanswered, including paid issues like data loss, license transfer and refunds. Some users report emails bouncing outright, while the daily review-replies look like for-show theater.

product.title: The subscription is too pricey, and the one-time purchase is gone
product.minus: The move to subscriptions put many off: the price is called too high (e.g. ~7€/month or ₹2600/year), and losing the one-time option is the biggest grievance. Users flat-out ask for the single purchase back.

product.title: Data vanishes with no warning and no auto-backup
product.minus: One wrong tap or a phone change, and months of entries are gone for good — there's no automatic backup and no delete confirmation. For a finance tracker, this is the most painful failure of all.

product.title: Sync demands payment on every device — and still doesn't work
product.minus: To sync expenses across devices you must buy a subscription on EACH one, and even then the data often won't sync. Dropbox sync simply stopped working for many users.

product.title: Fast entry and the pie chart are the heart of the love
product.plus: Quick expense entry, a clear category pie chart, and a minimalist interface make daily tracking easy and even enjoyable. Many have used it for years as their main tool.

product.title: You can't edit categories, icons or sub-categories — even basics are locked in Pro
product.minus: Customizing categories, adding sub-categories, renaming and picking icons is either missing or paywalled. Many want a bigger icon set and the ability to upload their own.

product.title: Dark mode, currency switching and recurring entries sit behind the paywall
product.minus: Users are especially outraged that even dark mode is paid. Currency switching and a repeat-transactions mode are also locked in Pro, which many feel is greed over trivial things.

product.title: Freezes and crashes when typing notes and descriptions
product.minus: When typing a note, the app often hangs with a "close or wait" toast, and the recent version crashes right while entering an expense description. Heavy entry history brings performance issues too.

product.title: Budget mode and carrying balances over are poorly done
product.minus: You can't carry a surplus or deficit from month to month, and there's no balance forecast or cash-flow projection. Changing the budget figure rewrites it across all past months, making budget mode useless.

product.title: Side swipes accidentally flip months while scrolling
product.minus: Horizontal swipes switch months right as you scroll the expense list vertically, with no way to turn it off. Opening categories also sometimes refuses to register taps.

product.title: Missing receipt photos, category reports and auto-entry from SMS
product.minus: Users ask for attaching receipt photos, printing and exporting per-category monthly reports, and auto-entry of expenses from SMS notifications or voice, so they don't have to type every record by hand.

product.title: The free version is enough for daily tracking, with no ads
product.plus: For many, the free version is enough for everyday expense tracking, and it's especially praised for having no intrusive ads. That outweighs the gripes about paid features for a lot of users.

product.title: Past months' history suddenly locked behind a paywall
product.minus: Once-free, the app retroactively locked all past transactions: users are furious at being asked to pay just to view their own data stored right on their phone.

product.title: Lifetime premium vanishes after a phone change and won't restore
product.minus: People who bought a lifetime license years ago suddenly drop to free accounts after switching devices or reinstalling; the restore-purchase button finds no payment and support doesn't help.

product.title: Sync hangs on "syncing your data" and won't pull records on a new device
product.minus: After signing in on a new phone the app gets stuck on the syncing screen for weeks; premium users can't get their data, and some leave for competitors before it ever finishes.

product.title: Balances miscalculate: totals drift, go negative, double up
product.minus: The tracker's core job — accurate accounting — fails: totals don't match a manual count, and balances drift negative or double on their own without a single new transaction.

product.title: "Please check the update of Google service" blocks login and signup
product.minus: A cryptic "update Google service" error suddenly throws people out and blocks both login and signup — even though there's nothing on the phone to update.

product.title: Recent updates break what used to work: categories, design, navigation
product.minus: Long-time users complain updates strip familiar features and the comfortable old interface: global categories break nesting, detailed reports vanish, and the new design feels cluttered.

product.title: Nagging intrusive screens: surveys, rate prompts, motivational pushes
product.minus: Every launch greets users with pushy "share/take survey" screens and rate prompts that won't dismiss even after completion, plus new motivational notifications with no off switch.

product.title: Subscription creep and rising prices anger long-time users
product.minus: Those who once paid a single price resent the shift to a subscription model and price hikes, feeling the free version is deliberately crippled.

product.title: Freezes, lag, and duplicate transactions on save
product.minus: The once-smooth app now lags and hangs, especially with a lot of data; pressing Save sometimes fails, then spawns a pile of duplicate entries.

product.title: A years-loved tracker with a clear interface and multi-device sync
product.plus: Many have used it for years and call it the best: a clean, simple, intuitive interface with handy widgets and wallets makes daily expense tracking almost effortless.

product.title: One-time lifetime payment is the standout argument against subscription rivals
product.plus: For those whose lifetime works, the "pay once, use forever" model is a prized rarity and a strong reason to stay, unlike rivals' endless subscriptions.

product.title: Responsive support often rescues users from data trouble
product.plus: When things break — premium lost, transactions gone — the support team often responds and fixes it within a couple of days, which many cite as a real strength.

product.title: Web version in "read-only" mode kills the loved desktop-entry workflow
product.minus: The once-handy web sync for desktop entry now only allows viewing; people who bought premium for it lost editing and are asking for a proper desktop version.

product.title: No proper savings/goals and no bulk import of past transactions
product.minus: Users hit missing table-stakes features: no savings/goals tracker and no bulk import of old records, forcing a manual start from zero.

product.title: A simple, clean interface that keeps people for years
product.plus: The core reason people love it is the no-noise minimalism: the interface is clear, customizable, and fast for daily entries. Many say they've used it for 7–10 years and found nothing better.

product.title: Backup lives only in Google Drive — and people lose years of data
product.minus: There's no automatic cloud backup on the app's own servers: data sits in Google Drive, and if a user didn't set it up or switched phones, everything vanishes. Several people lost two years or more of transactions.

product.title: Paid premium doesn't kill the ads — they come back after updates
product.minus: People buy premium to remove ads, but after each update the ads reappear and they have to reinstall the app. Many ask for a login page so premium status doesn't reset.

product.title: Ads pop up right while you're adding money — breaking quick entry
product.minus: Even on the free plan, ads fire at the moment you add an entry, breaking the core use case of logging a spend quickly. Some tolerate it, knowing ads pay for the free tier, but ask to dial it down.

product.title: No automatic SMS reading — everything is entered by hand
product.minus: The most common request is automatic reading of bank SMS to log transactions. For some the feature simply doesn't work despite granting permission, and some leave for competitors specifically because it's missing.

product.title: Double-entry and subcategories give honest control over spending
product.plus: Power users value the real double-entry system, accounts, transfers between them, and subcategories — it gives transparent bookkeeping of daily spending. For those who know debit/credit, the app is near-perfect.

product.title: No cross-device sync — a couple can't share one budget
product.minus: One account doesn't work across devices: premium won't log in on PC, there's no phone-to-tablet sync, and spouses on iPhone and Android can't keep shared expenses in sync.

product.title: Years of reliability reshaped users' financial discipline
product.plus: People with 7–10 years of history say the app genuinely changed how they handle money: yearly trends are visible, they see where income goes, and they build financial literacy and a habit of control.

product.title: Free with no push to subscribe — a value in itself
product.plus: Many specifically note you can fully use the app for free, with no mandatory subscription to unlock features. Some buy premium out of gratitude rather than coercion.

product.title: Editing an amount wipes the whole number instead of one digit
product.minus: An everyday entry annoyance: you can't delete a single digit or edit part of an amount — the app erases the whole number and you retype it. There isn't even copy-paste.

product.title: Multi-currency management is a sore spot for movers
product.minus: Single-currency accounts work fine, but the moment you need multiple currencies or to change your main currency after moving countries, the exchange-rate recalculation breaks old transactions and balances go wrong.

product.title: Stats lack filtering and subcategory totals
product.minus: The charts get praise, but in stats you can't filter by specific categories, accounts, or period, and a subcategory's total isn't shown separately — only the parent category's sum. Analytics hits this ceiling.

product.title: The home-screen widget flickers and reloads endlessly
product.minus: The widget — the main reason people install the app — has been continuously flickering, stuck on "loading" or "all done," and ignoring taps for months for huge numbers of users. The only fix is deleting and re-adding the widget or restarting the phone, and even then only for a few hours. Reinstalling, clearing cache, switching launchers — nothing fixes it for long.

product.title: In long notes the keyboard covers the text and you can't scroll to it
product.minus: Once a task note grows past a certain length you can neither see nor edit the bottom: the on-screen keyboard covers the text and scrolling down stops working. Reviewers say the bug is literally years old (one counts from 2016), returned after an update, and turns note-editing into a guessing game.

product.title: Every launch it nags you to turn on notifications and won't take no for an answer
product.minus: Anyone who deliberately turned reminders off gets a "Reminder settings turned off" pop-up or an enable-notifications prompt on every single launch. There's no "never" option, so you dismiss the same dialog over and over — reviewers furiously write "No means No, Microsoft."

product.title: Simple, clean, ad-free — and that's exactly why people love it
product.plus: The core value is zero clutter and zero ads: nested lists, steps within tasks, "My Day," and sharing lists with family. People keep everything here for years — from grocery lists to career goals — and call it the best to-do app they've tried.

product.title: Free sync across phone, PC and Mac is the main hook
product.plus: Tasks appear instantly on every device, fit neatly into the Microsoft 365 and Windows ecosystem — and it's all free. For many that's the deciding factor: jot it on the laptop at work, see it on your phone.

product.title: Forces you to re-login every few days, even corporate users
product.minus: The app demands a login almost daily, while other Microsoft apps (Outlook) keep the session for 5 days under the same policy. For To Do this has gone unfixed for years, annoying people enough to leave for Google.

product.title: A painful Microsoft-account sign-in — too many hoops for a simple list
product.minus: Just to start a to-do list you're forced through multi-step verification — password, last digits of phone, a puzzle captcha, a code, a backup email, then verifying that. People give up at step 6 or 7. And tying it to a work/school account means losing your data when you leave the company.

product.title: The Wunderlist shadow: Microsoft is seen as having ruined what worked perfectly
product.minus: Long-time users remember Wunderlist and say in unison that after the Microsoft acquisition the app became less intuitive, buggier, and lost its charm. "If it ain't broke don't fix it" is a recurring refrain; for them it's a symbol of a good product being enshittified.

product.title: No way to bulk-delete completed tasks
product.minus: Completed tasks pile up forever and you have to clear them one by one — there's no "delete all completed" or "uncheck all." For recurring lists (groceries, packing, checklists) it's tedious; people openly envy Google Tasks' "Delete completed" button.

product.title: Recurring tasks and reminders get garbled — DST, time zones, snooze
product.minus: The reminder logic is unreliable: at DST changes the recurrence shifts by a day or hour, while travelling reminders stay in the old time zone, and dismissing one notification of a recurring task kills the next. Snooze glitches too. For an app whose whole point is reminders, that's critical.

product.title: Bottom-edge buttons land under the system nav and become useless
product.minus: The "More"/save/delete-list buttons sit right at the bottom edge and get covered by the gesture bar or the phone's Google button — you can't reach them. Worse, the delete-list button in the corner is easily brushed by your palm.

product.title: Won't merge tasks from multiple Microsoft accounts or show them in the calendar
product.minus: Anyone with work and personal life in separate MS accounts is forced to keep switching — the app won't show everything together. On top of that, tasks don't surface in the calendar and there's no Outlook integration on Android, pushing people toward the Google or Apple ecosystem.

product.title: Far too easy to accidentally complete a task — and it vanishes with no history
product.minus: A swipe or a stray tap on the widget instantly marks a task done and it disappears — you can't disable the swipe, there's no history and no trash for accidental deletions. It hits hardest for people whose hands shake or who tap with a thumb.

product.title: 2026 redesign: seeing your whole day now means tapping into each meal one by one
product.minus: The redesign's core wound: the single day-view is gone. The whole diary used to be visible at once; now breakfast, lunch and dinner are collapsed and you have to open each one. For people who logged daily for 10-15 years, it's extra taps at every meal.

product.title: Day-to-day swipe is gone — now you tap a date at the top and get stuck on it
product.minus: The left/right swipe between days was cut. To check yesterday you tap the date at the top, then must remember to return to today or you log food onto the wrong day. A small gesture people relied on for years.

product.title: Barcode scanner and basic features moved behind Premium after years of being free
product.minus: What stings isn't the price itself but the clawback: barcode scanning, adding your own foods, time-of-day logging — all free for years, now Premium-only at ~$20/month. Many read it as a betrayal and leave for competitors.

product.title: The huge food database is the one thing keeping many users from leaving
product.plus: Even the angriest reviews concede it: the food database is enormous, and it's what keeps people. Finding almost any food, saving your own recipes and meals — that's what they tolerate everything else for.

product.title: A genuine weight-loss tool: people credit it with dozens and hundreds of pounds lost
product.plus: Beneath the anger sits real gratitude: users drop 20, 30, 80, 150, even 160 pounds and name the app as the reason. The draw is the plain accountability mechanic — "the facts speak for themselves" — with no fad diet.

product.title: Post-update, Google sign-in mass-fails — people simply can't get back in
product.minus: A whole wave of it: after updating, the app logs people out and won't let them back in via Google — grey screen, endless spinner, "email incorrect". Some go weeks locked out and finally uninstall, losing years of history.

product.title: No way to delete a whole meal or multiple items — only one at a time
product.minus: You used to delete an entire meal or copy a whole day; now it's line by line. Meanwhile copying yesterday's food has become too easy, and if you slip you undo it one item at a time. A direct hit to the daily workflow.

product.title: Steps and workouts won't sync — or duplicate themselves five times over
product.minus: The Fitbit / Garmin / Samsung Watch / Health Connect link is a chronic sore: steps either don't pull through, arrive wildly off, or a workout duplicates 5 times and wrecks the calorie balance. And you can't enter steps manually.

product.title: Logging reminders are nagging and try-hard "cringe"
product.minus: The new reminder wording reads as manipulative and try-hard: "log your food it freaks us out", "the truest horror story — you not logging your meal". On top of that, streak notifications can't be disabled and fire at the wrong times.

product.title: It makes you configure everything, then springs a paywall and surprise charges
product.minus: The hated flow: spend 20 minutes configuring meal plans, then pay $99-180/year. Then come triple charges, deductions off a backup card, trials you can't cancel, and charges years after uninstalling. Many call it a scam.

product.title: Custom foods and goals need Premium — and even then they reset on you
product.minus: The database is user-built, yet adding your own food or nutrients is now Premium-only. And paying users can't set macro goals flexibly (only 5% steps), can't see protein and fiber at once, and watch their settings revert to defaults.

product.title: Boot loops, crashes and lost data after updates
product.minus: After updates the app often hangs in a loading loop ("Please wait...", the logo screen on repeat) or won't open at all. Worst of all is data loss: wiped workouts, vanished foods, months of history gone, calories duplicated into the past.
