product.plus: People use it for far more than groceries: recipes that push ingredients into the list, lists for camping, Christmas, trip packing, household chores. The flexibility and categories are especially valued by people with ADHD/autism.

product.title: One-time paid version and longevity — years without issues, many pay out of gratitude
product.plus: A one-time purchase (or lifetime) removes ads, and users pay even without needing premium — just to support a good product. Many have used it for 7, 10, 13, 15 years and won't switch even 'in the AI era'.

product.title: The free version is overloaded with ads and pop-ups on every action
product.minus: In the free version every added item triggers a pop-up about the paid version, ads have become intrusive, and some banners look outright obscene. Ad-preference settings are ignored and switch themselves back on.

product.title: No aisle/store tagging of items or moving between lists — a ceiling for serious shoppers
product.minus: Power users miss GroceryIQ-style features: assign an item to a specific aisle and sort the list by the store's aisle sequence, easily move an item to another list, or mark it 'not this time' without deleting it.

product.title: Lists randomly delete and reshuffle items
product.minus: After recent updates the shopping lists have a life of their own: items vanish, previously deleted ones come back, jump between categories and sink to the bottom. People spend time building a list only to have it erased the moment they finish.

product.title: Basic features moved behind the paywall
product.minus: It's marketed as a free calendar, yet anything past three days — let alone scheduling more than a month ahead — is locked behind the Gold subscription. Long-time users were suddenly cut off from past and future events, asked to pay just to see their own data.

product.title: Random logouts and unrecognized password
product.minus: The app randomly logs people out and then refuses their long-familiar password. Password resets often claim the email isn't registered at all — and people lose access to the organizer they set up for their whole family.

product.title: Sync between family members broke
product.minus: The core selling point — instant shared lists and calendar — stopped working: sometimes only one person can add things, sometimes one member's changes never reach the others. Mixed iPhone-and-Android households suffer the most.

product.title: Endless loading and lag after the update
product.minus: The calendar and lists take forever to open, a spinning "ring of death" hangs there, and every list entry lags 10–20 seconds. The widget goes blank. What used to be instant is now painfully slow.

product.title: Swipe-to-delete with no confirmation erases by accident
product.minus: List items get deleted from the lightest touch — with no confirmation and no Undo. In the middle of a store with a long list it becomes a disaster: brush the screen and you can't recall what was there.

product.title: Intrusive ads and pushy upsells
product.minus: Ads pop in on a delay exactly as you're typing an item — so you tap them by accident. On top of that, constant Gold/Max upgrade prompts that even paying subscribers can't dismiss.

product.title: No offline access to lists — fails right in the store
product.minus: Many supermarkets have no signal, and without a connection the app refuses to open the list or even tick an item off. Users say the developers deliberately removed offline use.

product.title: The Android build looks and works worse than on iPhone
product.minus: On Android the dates sit at the bottom of the calendar, the per-member color coding doesn't work, and the interface looks clunky. For mixed-OS families the Android app is at times simply unusable.

product.title: One shared grocery list for the whole family — what users love most
product.plus: Anyone can add an item from home and whoever's already at the store sees it instantly — no more texting around or photographing the fridge list. This is the very reason people keep Cozi for years.

product.title: A shared family calendar that keeps everyone in the loop
product.plus: Per-person color coding, events appearing for everyone instantly, and birthday reminders turn big-family chaos into a manageable schedule. For many it literally makes getting by with a single car possible.

product.title: Easy to learn and good for ADHD / less tech-savvy relatives
product.plus: The interface is clear enough that both non-techie relatives and teenagers manage it. Several users with ADHD note the to-do list and calendar help them hold complex tasks and contain the chaos.

product.title: Recipes, meal planning and birthdays as a welcome bonus
product.plus: Beyond lists and calendar, people value the built-in recipes that turn into a grocery list, weekly meal planning, and a perpetual birthday tracker with reminders. All in one place.

product.title: Every flyer in one place — the core value
product.plus: People keep the app for years for one reason: all the local sales and flyers gathered on one screen, with no need to drive store to store or dig through paper inserts.

product.title: Hangs on the loading screen and won't open
product.minus: For a chunk of users the app sits on the spinning Flipp logo for weeks and loads neither flyers nor list — reinstalling and clearing cache change nothing.

product.title: Search only shows what's in a flyer
product.minus: The core gripe with the very premise: search returns a price only if the item is in a weekly circular, so you can't compare regular (non-sale) prices or find what's genuinely cheapest.

product.title: Saves money and time on the shop
product.plus: Regulars say it genuinely saves hundreds of dollars a year: they track sales on staples and stock up, especially with prices so high.

product.title: Indispensable for price matching
product.plus: A standout beloved use is price matching: people show a flyer at checkout to get a competitor's price, and keep the app just for that.

product.title: Shopping list hides the last items under the bottom bar
product.minus: A recent widespread bug: the bottom menu bar covers the last list item and you can't scroll to it — for some the list stopped opening or accepting additions entirely.

product.title: Pick only your stores and the screen goes blank
product.minus: When a user marks favourite stores, the app keeps pushing others (often Walmart or stores across the country), and selecting only your own often leaves the screen blank.

product.title: Relentless review nagging and pushy pop-ups
product.minus: The "never miss a sale" pop-up and review prompts appear at every action — many drop a one-star purely on principle for the nagging.

product.title: One-tap add from a flyer to the list
product.plus: A beloved feature is tapping an item right in the flyer to drop it into the shopping list; it's what makes people rank the app above paper inserts.

product.title: Sort-by-price doesn't behave
product.minus: The app defaults to "best match" instead of cheapest-first, and sorting by price often makes the sale item drop out of results entirely.

product.title: Search clogged with junk and irrelevant hits
product.minus: Search either spits out twenty identical hits from one store or misses an item that's clearly in several flyers — and pads the top with sponsored "featured" flyers.

product.title: Alarm over tracking and data shared with stores
product.minus: Some users refuse to install over the amount of hidden tracking: browsing history and location go to stores, and you aren't allowed to decline location sharing.

product.title: No landscape mode — flyers too tiny to read
product.minus: After a recent update the app stopped rotating to landscape, and on smaller screens you have to keep pinch-zooming flyers just to make anything out.

product.title: Missing stores and shaky accuracy
product.minus: Users complain that needed chains (Wegmans, Harris Teeter, Canadian Tire) are absent, familiar stores suddenly vanish, and the data is sometimes just inaccurate or even made up.

product.title: Shared family list is the core reason people love it
product.plus: Spouses, kids, in-laws all add to one shared list and see changes in real time. It kills duplicate buys when shopping ("divide and conquer") and avoids return trips to the store.

product.title: Color categories map to the store layout
product.plus: Users color items by store zone (blue for frozen, green for produce) and walk the aisles in one pass without backtracking.

product.title: Simplicity left un-ruined by "improvements" — for years
product.plus: People keep it for 6–10 years precisely because it does one thing and doesn't bloat with needless features. It remembers past items and suggests them as you type.

product.title: Sync is either instant or takes "years"
product.minus: For half it's "synchronization is immediate and just works"; for the rest, updates don't reach family phones, local edits get discarded, and syncing takes "years".

product.title: Crashes and lost lists break the core trust
product.minus: An app trusted to hold the list suddenly crashes and loses EVERYTHING. For a tool whose whole job is to not lose the list, that's fatal.

product.title: Phantom items appear and vanish on their own
product.minus: Dozens of unwanted items get auto-added to a carefully curated list (even tampons for a guy), while needed ones vanish — so people get home without what they came for.

product.title: The home-screen widget is read-only
product.minus: The home-screen widget won't let you cross off items — you have to open the app, which defeats the point of the widget.

product.title: Browser access and cross-platform save you when you switch phones
product.plus: Cloud plus a web version let you sign in by code on a new phone and get the list exactly as it was — and iOS+Android couples share one list.

product.title: Aggressive Pro promos and rate-prompts boot you out
product.minus: Pro pop-ups and rate-prompts can't be dismissed, fire on open, and one literally kicked the user out to the rating page.

product.title: Pro purchase: won't activate, no refunds, silent support
product.minus: Paid-for Pro doesn't unlock, the subscription can't be canceled for months, refunds fail, and support either goes silent or loops you for info already provided.

product.title: Too easy to tick off an item by accident with a tap
product.minus: A short press marks an item bought — easy to trigger by mistake. Users want swipe instead of tap or a long-press, and for ticked items to stay in place.

product.title: Wishlist: alphabetical sort, manual order, price/budget
product.minus: Fans' most-repeated asks: alphabetical sorting, a way to set color order manually, a price column with totals for budgeting, and barcode scanning.

product.title: Shared family lists are the core of why people love it
product.plus: Most users keep it specifically for the shared list: one person adds at home, the other sees the update right in the store, and shopping stops getting duplicated.

product.title: Recipe import that feeds straight into the list
product.plus: Recipes import from almost any website into a standardized format, and ingredients drop into the grocery list with one tap — for many this turns it into a full meal-planning tool.

product.title: Auto-sorting by store aisle kills the backtracking
product.plus: The list auto-sorts items into categories/departments, and the order can be reshuffled to match your own store's layout, so people stop doubling back for forgotten items.

product.title: Simple enough that even elderly users get it
product.plus: The basics stay clear and fast: jot it down before you forget and ditch the paper scrap — many note it's easy even for older people to use.

product.title: Free tier is genuinely usable, and the paid tier is worth it
product.plus: Unlike the usual trial traps, the free version covers the basics, and people upgrade (folders, recipes, per-store sorting) voluntarily and don't regret it.

product.title: Voice input broke on the Google side
product.minus: Voice-adding used to work, but the Google Assistant integration was cut; Alexa still hangs on, while Android and new-phone owners lose a feature they loved.

product.title: Forced account sign-up scares people off at the door
product.minus: The app demands an account from the very first screen, no demo and no way to just try it — some users find it invasive and uninstall before they even start.

product.title: Paywalling basic functions feels petty
product.minus: Some users hit the subscription where they expected basics: no entering your own prices, no starter lists, no mass export — and it nudges them toward other apps.

product.title: Comes across as just another greedy subscription
product.minus: For the skeptics the price overrides everything: the app reads as expensive and subscription-pushy, with some saying they'd rather use pen and paper or a rival like ourgroceries.

product.title: Auto-categorization occasionally guesses wrong
product.minus: The handy auto-sort doesn't always pick the right category (grapes filed as a vegetable), so the list needs a sanity check — usually minor, but it irritates some.

product.title: Occasional sync hiccups and vanishing items
product.minus: Now and then the list won't sync with the second phone (usually after a system update), and items can disappear or get accidentally crossed off halfway through the store.

product.title: A list organizer families have loved for years
product.plus: A loyal core has stuck with it for 10+ years: it replaces paper lists, gets shared with a spouse, and has become a standard household tool people say they can't live without.

product.title: Ads are the dealbreaker — especially for people who paid for Pro
product.minus: Full-screen ads pop up mid-shopping and are hard to dismiss; worst of all for those who once bought Pro with an ad blocker — the ads came back and their purchase is no longer honored.

product.title: Constant crashes and a multi-second lag when ticking items off
product.minus: The app crashes and freezes for no reason, and checking off a bought item lags 4–5 seconds — people double-tap and the feature becomes useless.

product.title: Sync loses items, categories and entire lists
product.minus: Cross-device and shared-list sync is unreliable: it deletes categories, reverts to an old list version, never reaches the other person — and trust in the data breaks.

product.title: Categories and prices arranged to match the store layout
product.plus: The most-loved feature: lists sort into custom categories matching your route through the store, and saved prices show a running total before checkout — no surprises at the register.

product.title: A random update wipes all lists and categories
product.minus: "Automatic" updates suddenly delete all lists, categories and years of accumulated data — with no restore menu; exporting the data also fails because the app crashes.

product.title: Now demands an account and floods you with data-harvesting surveys
product.minus: You used to be able to log in or not — now a simple shopping list forces an account, asks you to fill out a survey on every launch, and pushes personal-data collection; users flat-out call it data harvesting, not a service.

product.title: Duplicate items and categories that breed and won't delete
product.minus: Auto-categorization randomly spawns a pile of categories you can't delete, and checked items duplicate instead of moving — users see "milk ten times" and waste time cleaning up by hand.

product.title: Shared lists and versatility beyond groceries
product.plus: A core strength is shared lists: the whole family adds what's needed and everyone checks off in-store; and people use it far beyond groceries — for to-dos, trips, gifts, passwords and TV shows.

product.title: A broken barcode scanner they've promised to fix for years
product.minus: Some users love the barcode scanner, but for many it simply doesn't work: scanned items don't move to the main screen, and the reported problem has gone unfixed for 3 years — even after they asked for suggestions.

product.title: Moving to a new phone doesn't work — re-enter everything
product.minus: Switching to a new phone doesn't carry data over: you rebuild categories from scratch and re-enter lists, and a purchased "lifetime" license becomes invalid — brutal for a simple shopping list.

product.title: Region lock cuts off longtime users outside the US and Canada
product.minus: The web version and app suddenly declare users "outside the service area" — even US residents get the error, and in Australia it simply stopped being supported, cutting off people who used it for years.

product.title: One stray tap deletes an item — with no confirmation
product.minus: Tapping an item instantly removes it, and the "delete everything" button sits right under your thumb — people wipe the whole list mid-shop by accident, with no confirmation before removal.

product.title: Simplicity and ease are the main reason people stay
product.plus: Despite everything, the core values its intuitiveness: "type a few letters and your favorite items pop up," custom categories and drag-and-drop make it easy even for non-techies, and it's exactly the "simple" thing people wanted.

product.title: Saves hours of note-taking on meetings and lectures
product.plus: The core reason people love it: they show up to a meeting or lecture, take no notes by hand, and walk away with a ready transcript, summary and action items. Students, people with hearing loss, ADHD and memory issues call it a lifesaver.

product.title: Hard paywall: the free tier is cut short and bites on the very first recording
product.minus: Free gives you only 30 minutes of transcription, and you find out mid-task: record an hour-long meeting and only 28-30 minutes get transcribed, the rest behind a paywall. Some are forced to buy after 24 notes, others get just 3 uploads once ever.

product.title: Demands access to your work email and calendar before you can even sign in
product.minus: The app won't open until you log in with Google, Microsoft or a work email — which means access to your whole company calendar and inbox. For people who just want to dictate a shopping list, it reads as forced surveillance, and they uninstall on the spot.

product.title: Joins your calls uninvited and spams everyone in your contacts
product.minus: The scariest complaint: Otter joins every calendar meeting as an assistant — even on leave and after access is revoked — and emails everyone you meet with an invite that looks like it came from you. The same person gets spammed after every single call.

product.title: Confuses speakers and chops sentences mid-thought
product.minus: In in-person meetings it often can't tell speakers apart: it merges two people into one or labels a single voice as five. It also breaks sentences where it shouldn't, forcing you to manually untangle who said what — which defeats the time-saving point.

product.title: Transcription stumbles on accents and fast speech
product.minus: Accuracy is a weak spot even on paid plans: it catches every third word, trips on accents (UK, Southern drawl) and fast slurred speech, so transcripts need manual proofreading. Some users flatly say Fireflies, Fathom and Read.ai do a better job.

product.title: Few supported languages — barely usable outside English
product.minus: Russian, German, Arabic, Bengali are unsupported or return nothing. For non-English users this makes the app useless, and they leave for Gemini or open models that handle their language.

product.title: Updates removed key features: copy-summary and the recording widget
product.minus: Paying users are furious that in early 2026 the ability to copy a meeting summary was removed (now you can only export the whole transcript), and the Android quick-record widget vanished for months with no ETA — the very feature many subscribed for.

product.title: After updates it loses recordings and just stops working
product.minus: Reliability slipped: recordings vanish without a trace, after the latest update tabs and buttons freeze and audio won't play. Several compare it to Google Recorder, which never failed over hundreds of hours, and switch to it.

product.title: Billing bites: charges after cancellation, slashed minutes, business plan unavailable
product.minus: People get charged after cancelling via Google Play, the subscription doesn't show under managed subs, and recording minutes get cut 75% with no price change. Upgrading to Pro/Business inside the Android app often fails: it demands admin approval even when you are the admin.

product.title: Summaries and action items are what people come back for
product.plus: Beyond the raw transcript, what hooks people is the meaningful digest: a clean meeting summary, extracted action items, and AI search across all your transcripts at once. For meetings full of acronyms and crosstalk, it pulls out what actually mattered.

product.title: Low-friction capture: open, talk, and it just works
product.plus: When you're not hitting the paywall or a language gap, the app is praised for being effortless: quick audio upload from your phone, dictation on the move, capturing both in-person and online meetings. Accurate even in a moving car, easy to drop the text into Word or email.

product.title: Free plan shows only the first 3 minutes of a transcript — you can't actually evaluate it
product.minus: People record an hour-long lecture or meeting and only get to see the first 2-3 minutes of text before hitting a paywall. That's far too little to judge whether the app fits their workflow, so many uninstall on the spot and call the limit misleading.

product.title: Charges hit after cancellation and during the 'free' trial — no warning, no refund
product.minus: Users cancel right after a short test or trust a free-trial promise, yet the annual fee is still pulled from their card. Support replies slowly or refuses refunds, so people describe a predatory subscription model and threaten to dispute the charge with their bank.

product.title: Transcription cuts off after a couple of minutes — an hour of meeting becomes three minutes of text
product.minus: People report the app captured a whole meeting or interview but only transcribed a tiny piece — two sentences, 2:45 of thirty minutes, three minutes of an hour — then froze in processing mode. The recording is effectively lost and the time wasted, even on a paid plan.

product.title: Accuracy collapses on non-English languages and multiple speakers — speech gets mangled or mistranslated
product.minus: In Farsi, Afrikaans, Tagalog, Malay, Indonesian, Hindi and Arabic the transcription and translation come out riddled with errors: the text turns to gibberish, the language gets swapped (Afrikaans recognized as German), and the app can't tell two speakers apart. Many say it only works properly for Japanese and English.

product.title: Transcript quality is shaky even on paid plans — errors, broken punctuation, repeated words
product.minus: Premium subscribers complain the text comes with no commas or full stops, three mistakes per sentence, and the same words repeated in the final output when it stalls. A pin mic adds random question marks, and the transcript still needs heavy editing.

product.title: Meeting recording stops when you switch apps or turn off the screen — the data vanishes
product.minus: The app randomly stops recording in-person meetings without notice, halts when you switch to another app, and won't record with the screen off the way rivals do. People hit stop and the notes simply aren't there — the meeting and the quota are gone.

product.title: Slow uploads and processing, freezes, and lost recordings on Android
product.minus: Uploading a single file drags on for half an hour and often fails, transcription crawls, and the app freezes mid-process and stops responding. On Android, recorded audio gets lost and never produces a transcript, while the share button and speech upload simply don't react.

product.title: Pricing stings: annual-only with no monthly option, plus paid add-ons on top of the sub
product.minus: Students and occasional users are offered only a pricey annual plan — no monthly option — with paid add-ons stacked on top that double the cost. Many feel there are too many limits for that money and leave for cheaper rivals.

product.title: The paid product holds transcripts hostage: download once, but lose access if you stop paying
product.minus: Even after paying and downloading a transcript, users can't reopen or re-download it without renewing the subscription. Share links lead to a 'file can't be accessed' screen, so the notes are effectively locked away until the next payment.

product.title: When it works it's a lifesaver for meetings, lectures and voice notes: fast, accurate, with AI summaries
product.plus: Happy users cite over 90% accuracy, praise the clean dashboard, situation templates and AI summaries. For meetings, lectures and voice notes it saves huge amounts of time — upload a recording and get clean text in seconds.

product.title: Strong on multilingual and bilingual conversations — a rare niche where Notta beats rivals
product.plus: Some users pick Notta specifically for the number of supported languages and its ability to transcribe bilingual lessons and conversations, which they couldn't find in other AI note-takers at the same price. It works notably well for Hebrew, Indonesian and language learning.

product.title: Surprisingly pulls text out of videos and even song lyrics — where others give up
product.plus: A few users highlight unusual use cases: the app pulled song lyrics that aren't even on Google, and it transcribes audio from videos and web pages. For drafting estimates on the fly in the field and for lectures, they call it a game changer.

product.title: The mobile app is stripped down versus the web version: fewer features, no bulk file upload
product.minus: Users note the phone can't upload multiple files at once like the desktop can, can't upgrade to a business plan, and some web recordings don't even show up in the app. That makes the mobile version feel nearly pointless for serious work.

product.title: Frees you from manual note-taking so you can actually be present
product.plus: The core reason people love it: you can listen and engage instead of frantically writing. Summaries and action items assemble themselves, and nothing important gets lost.

product.title: A paid subscription on top of pricey hardware is the number-one grievance
product.minus: People already bought the expensive hardware and don't get why the software costs extra on top. Many point out the same AI is built into plenty of apps for free.

product.title: Without a subscription the device is nearly useless — a hard minutes cap
product.minus: Without premium you get only ~300 minutes a month on the device you paid for, and the AI features simply don't function. People feel they bought a fancy paperweight.

product.title: Transcripts and summaries stay accurate even in noise and crosstalk
product.plus: The strongest technical side: clean transcription, speaker recognition, auto-extracted action items and mind maps. It holds up even when coworkers talk over each other.

product.title: The app crashes on launch — especially on Android, bricking the hardware
product.minus: Recurring complaints that after an update the app force-closes at launch or freezes on every action. Without the app the device is dead, and people head for refunds.

product.title: The recent redesign broke basic functionality — a mass regression
product.minus: The new app version removed or broke the basics: file import, renaming, multi-select, transcript visibility. A pretty rebrand at the cost of working features.

product.title: The AI marketing overpromises — cross-file search doesn't work as advertised
product.minus: The advertised "ask across all files" / Ask AI only keyword-matches rather than answering questions across your archive. Paying subscribers feel misled.

product.title: Support replies with bots and abandons you after the sale
product.minus: Support answers with canned AI emails or goes silent for days. One user got a refund and account deletion instead of help. Once they have your money, you're on your own.

product.title: File transfer is slow and fragile — export only one at a time
product.minus: Wireless transfer is slower than realtime, error-prone, and blocks app use while it runs. There's no bulk export — users feel locked into their software.

product.title: Language detection goes haywire — transcribes English as Welsh or Malay
product.minus: Auto-generation guesses the wrong language and outputs Thai, Welsh or Malay for English speech — and re-transcribing eats your paid minutes.

product.title: Small, discreet and genuinely life-helping — medical, legal, study use
product.plus: An emotional bond: it helps with illness and memory, at doctor and lawyer appointments, in lectures in another language. And it doesn't drain your phone battery.

product.title: It's hidden pre-purchase that the app requires buying a separate device
product.minus: People install the app expecting a trial and hit a "connect device" wall. You can't even feel the interface or upload your own audio without buying the hardware first.

product.title: No dark mode — the glaring white background hurts the eyes
product.minus: A long-unanswered request: a blinding white UI. Many say they'd bump to five stars the moment dark mode lands — and it still isn't here, despite the feedback.

product.title: The hardware is unreliable — won't charge, won't reset, dies in a weekend
product.minus: Some units simply won't come to life: red light instead of white, no factory reset while charging, dead after a single weekend of notes. With no working device, nothing matters.

product.title: Sketchy billing — charges early and no cancel reminder before the trial ends
product.minus: The subscription bills days before the trial ends, there's no cancellation reminder, and purchased minutes don't credit. Users talk chargebacks and a "low level scam."

product.title: "Free" is just a label — your card is required before the first call
product.minus: Users are furious that the store lists the app as free, yet nothing runs without a subscription: you're walked through setup, your number is extracted, then you hit a paywall. Many call it outright false advertising.

product.title: The trial demands a card, then charges you on the sly
product.minus: To try it "free" you must enter card details, and users report being charged despite cancelling during the trial. Amounts run into tens of dollars, and many feel trapped.

product.title: Even after paying, the call just says "check your subscription"
product.minus: The most painful complaint: people subscribed, granted every permission, yet when they try to record, the app throws "check subscription" and records nothing. This isn't a one-off glitch but a recurring pattern.

product.title: Recording only works by merging in a call to a random access number
product.minus: The recording mechanic annoys almost everyone: you put the caller on hold, dial an "access line", and merge the calls into a conference. It's extra steps, interrupts the conversation, and is rarely quick to pull off.

product.title: The other party sees "conference call" — zero discretion
product.minus: For anyone needing a quiet recording this is a dealbreaker: the other person's phone flags a conference call, and the app essentially snitches on you. Several users say this defeats the entire purpose.

product.title: Records only your voice, not the other side
product.minus: A frequent functional failure: the recording captures only the user, while the other party's voice is missing or unintelligible. For a call recorder that's a total breakdown.

product.title: Support goes silent and refunds never arrive
product.minus: When something breaks or a refund is needed, users email for weeks and get either silence or a canned reply. Many complain the promised refunds never came.

product.title: The subscription can't be cancelled — it's not in Play
product.minus: Charges keep coming but cancelling is impossible: the subscription doesn't appear in Google Play, the FAQ steps are iPhone-only, and website attempts fail. People feel locked into the payment.

product.title: Prices jumped sharply, with no mercy for loyal users
product.minus: Long-time users are stunned by the price hikes: $3.99 a month became the same per week, and the yearly plan rose from $39 to $89. People who paid for years leave to find alternatives, feeling betrayed.

product.title: Recordings vanish after a reinstall or phone change
product.minus: Several users lost important recordings — after a reinstall, a new phone, or a lapsed subscription, old files vanished from the server, even after paying again for storage. For those keeping evidence, it's a disaster.

product.title: When it works, it's the only one that truly records both sides
product.plus: Those for whom it works praise it as a rare tool that genuinely records both parties clearly and loudly — where free alternatives (Cube ACR and others) failed. For many it saved important conversations.

product.title: Keeps recordings for years and adds transcription and sharing
product.plus: Happy users value that recordings persist for years (even across phone changes), with text transcription and easy sharing via link or email. For interviews, client notes and legal use this makes the app genuinely useful.

product.title: Phone number and broad permissions feel like surveillance
product.minus: Users are alarmed that just to record a call the app demands a phone number and access to nearly everything on the device. Many suspect spam, spyware or data-selling and refuse to install.

product.title: It records, but the file plays back silent
product.minus: The most frequent and most painful complaint: the app shows it's recording (duration, meeting minutes), but on playback there's total silence or only the first few seconds of audio. Users only discover it after the interview or important call, when nothing can be recovered.

product.title: Files are trapped inside the app — no way to export
product.minus: Sharing, export and backup are broken: email and Dropbox buttons throw errors, leaving only Bluetooth that also fails. Recordings are literally stuck in the app, and hours of work can't be moved to a computer.

product.title: Advertises call recording that Android doesn't actually do
product.minus: The website and store listing promise phone-call recording, but on Android the app only captures the mic. Calls come out silent or last a few seconds, and the Android build is fundamentally different from iOS, which does record calls.

product.title: The $10 promo vanishes and the card gets charged anyway
product.minus: The same script hits dozens of users: a $10 promo on first launch, then after entering a card it says "you've already used this promo" though no transcription happened yet. Money is charged immediately with nothing delivered, and many call it an outright scam.

product.title: Best-in-class speech recognition
product.plus: Users who get to the transcription praise it as the most accurate on the market — better than built-in iOS/Android, handles long recordings better than ChatGPT, and copes even with poor diction. For many it's the one reason they tolerate everything else.

product.title: A hidden subscription you can't cancel
product.minus: The subscription is billed outside Google Play, so it can't be cancelled there, and the app itself has no account management. Meanwhile the website shows a "Free" plan — nothing to cancel, yet money keeps leaving. Deleting the account is blocked too.

product.title: Forced account just to record
product.minus: To simply use the recorder, the app demands you create an account and hand over personal data. This scares people off at the very first screen — especially the question of why a recorder needs their recordings and banking details — and they uninstall before ever using it.

product.title: Crashes and updates that wipe your recordings
product.minus: The app crashes when the screen locks or on launch and stops working after updates, taking already-made recordings down with it. "Error saving recording" and files gone after an update are a recurring theme among formerly happy users.

product.title: You pay for transcription blind — no preview
product.minus: Pricing stings ($1.25–1.5 per minute) and you can't check quality before paying. Many find it absurd next to Google Live Transcribe doing similar for free; the recording stays "locked" until you pay, even when no transcription is needed at all.

product.title: Saves time on meetings, interviews and notes
product.plus: When it works, it's a beloved daily tool: journalists, researchers, students and doctors dictate thoughts on the go and get clean text back. A simple interface, instant start and good recording quality make it indispensable in everyday work.

product.title: Clean mic capture — even for music
product.plus: As a pure recorder the app earns separate praise: crisp sound with no app noise, no ads and no time limit. Musicians capture guitar and vocals, some use it as a journal — for basic recording it's among the best options around.

product.title: No navigation in a recording, no copy of the text
product.minus: In a finished transcript you can't select and copy the text — only share a link, which infuriates journalists and anyone wanting to paste it into ChatGPT. You also can't jump to a point in a recording: you have to listen from start to finish.

product.title: The paywall hits exactly when the transcript is already done
product.minus: People dictate or upload a long recording, see a chunk of the result on screen, then run into a payment request right before they can download or copy their own text. The transcript exists, but it's held hostage.

product.title: The "free" version turns out to be a clipped first line
product.minus: What's billed as a free try is really a couple of words or half a sentence: one word for a minute of audio, the first two words of a video, and the rest behind the wall. You can't actually evaluate it, so it feels like bait.

product.title: The 5-minute trial only reveals itself after you've recorded for ages
product.minus: The ad promises 90 minutes, but the trial actually caps at 5, and you find out only after you've already recorded a whole meeting. Then you have to redo everything in another app.

product.title: Cancellation is broken while the charges keep coming
product.minus: Users report cancellation simply doesn't work: an error on attempt, the account still shows "trial," yet money is debited annually — sometimes years after last use. The account can't be deleted either.

product.title: You paid, and the app still treats you as "trial"
product.minus: A separate pain for paying users: the premium money is gone but the status stays trial, the transcript caps don't lift, and the product "gives nothing." Support tickets go unanswered.

product.title: The price reads as out of proportion — especially to students
product.minus: A tag of $30/mo or $120/yr feels inflated to many for something "you can get on Google for free." Students openly beg for an affordable tier or a token model instead of a fixed monthly fee.

product.title: Given a real run, the recognition core is genuinely strong
product.plus: Those who get past payment praise accuracy even on noisy audio and long files: a 40-minute call becomes a full transcript plus summary in a couple of minutes, with format choices. For journalists, producers and researchers it's part of the daily workflow.

product.title: Auto-summaries and speaker labels save hours of note-taking
product.plus: A strength called out on its own: the app doesn't just transcribe — it produces summaries and key points, labels different speakers, and lets you edit. For meeting minutes, lectures and thesis work it saves dozens of hours.

product.title: One language per file — bilingual meetings collapse into errors
product.minus: A structural limit: only one language or accent per file. In meetings that mix two languages, the chosen one works while everything in the other turns to garbage. Many specifically need bilingual lecture transcription.

product.title: Weaker languages and accents come out as gibberish
product.minus: For non-English languages quality drops sharply: Amharic, Marathi, Arabic, Afrikaans come out as unreadable nonsense or get swapped (a Sinhala video transcribed into "some Indian language"). The summary is sometimes perfect anyway — which only makes it weirder.

product.title: Uploads and processing silently fail with no explanation
product.minus: The basic flow breaks for no reason: uploading a file and "nothing happened," a recorded meeting with no transcript, YouTube links rejected as invalid URL or failing at the last step. Not even an error explanation is offered.

product.title: Excess permissions and post-install spam raise alarm
product.minus: The app demands permissions beyond what its basic functions need (including an overlay that's awkward for security), then floods your inbox with mail and push right after install. Trust erodes before the first transcript.

product.title: Recognition drops chunks of speech — half the words vanish
product.minus: The most frequent complaint: during longer dictation the app swallows whole phrases and chunks of sentences, especially in lectures and with accents. People speak slowly and clearly yet get fragments back and have to constantly correct the text.

product.title: Uninterrupted stream-of-thought into text — the core thing users love
product.plus: Fans love being able to speak as long as they want without losing the thread: the app buffers speech and waits for you to finish. For writers, notes on the go, and quickly capturing ideas they call it a game changer and a godsend.

product.title: No auto-punctuation — periods and commas must be dictated or added by hand
product.minus: Unlike GPT-based engines the app won't punctuate on its own: you get one long stream with no periods or commas, and capitalization has to be fixed by hand. Commands like "period" and "new line" also sometimes get typed as text instead of acting.

product.title: Offline mode is advertised but broken — no internet, no transcription
product.minus: Many came specifically for offline, and offline is exactly what fails: with no network the app won't transcribe at all, and after updates or moving to a new device the offline languages vanish — even for paid users. People call it false advertising.

product.title: Accessibility for the deaf and hard-of-hearing — the app rescues communication
product.plus: A distinct, deeply emotional cluster of reviews: people who've gone deaf and their families use the app to understand a doctor, a conversation partner, loved ones. For them it isn't a utility but a way to communicate again.

product.title: Recording cuts off after a few seconds and won't hold in the background
product.minus: Even with "listen in the background" toggled on, the app stops recording after 5-6 seconds or a few words, breaking the flow. Long lectures and conversations can't be captured — you never know if the recording will make it to the end.

product.title: Free, no subscription, no forced AI — that's why people choose it
product.plus: For a chunk of users the deciding factor is that it's free, privacy-respecting, and doesn't shove AI in your face. A one-time ~$30 license and a solid privacy policy outweigh the imperfect accuracy.

product.title: Censorship of swear words — can't be turned off, ruins private notes
product.minus: The app bleeps out "bad" words or simply won't transcribe them — even in private notes, with no way to disable it. For authors and anyone who needs fidelity this is critical: along with profanity, important words can be dropped too.

product.title: Multilingual support and switching languages on the fly — a real strength
product.plus: Bilingual users are thrilled: you can dictate in Hindi, Hebrew, Persian, Kannada, and switch English and German mid-note. Many note it beats Google at telling languages apart.

product.title: Porn-style ads at the bottom of the screen — scare users off before first use
product.minus: Several people deleted the app without even trying it because of ads designed to look like pornography. Parents warn each other it's a danger around kids.

product.title: Hidden subscription instead of a one-time buy — charged for months
product.minus: Users thought they paid once, then discovered monthly charges. Plus a pushy paywall: on the free version the payment prompt pops up several times and key functions are locked behind it.

product.title: Bluetooth microphone unsupported — despite being promised otherwise
product.minus: Those who bought Pro specifically to use a Bluetooth mic on Android feel misled: it doesn't work and support is unresponsive. For others, BT mic support was dropped after an update.

product.title: Just stops working — works once, then nothing but "error"
product.minus: A recurring pattern: the app works for five minutes or once, then dies completely and a restart doesn't help. For some it shows nothing after they speak, and in one case it allegedly froze the whole phone.

product.title: High accuracy for those it clicks with — better than Google and Dragon
product.plus: Happy users cite 85-99% accuracy and rank it above Google Voice-to-Text and even Dragon — especially for voice punctuation and understanding Indian and Thai accents. For writers and professionals it's a working tool for years.

product.title: Cluttered interface and unclear instructions — hard to figure out
product.minus: Some users get lost in a pile of buttons and options with no clear help: it's unclear where notes are stored, how editing commands work, or where to log into a purchased account. The tiny punctuation keyboard also annoys.

product.title: A lifeline for people who can't write fast or hold focus
product.plus: Users with hearing loss, memory issues, ADHD, or hand disabilities say the app literally solves their problem: they can go back to the recording, search the conversation, and stop losing details.

product.title: Meeting summaries and action-item lists are the killer feature
product.plus: Users value not so much the raw transcript as the ready-made meeting summary and auto-extracted action items — it saves hours and lets them engage in the conversation instead of scribbling notes.

product.title: Forced sign-in via work email blocks people at the door
product.minus: The app won't even open until you sign in with Google, Microsoft, or a work email — and that login often fails with an error. Many uninstall before reaching a single feature, seeing it as a grab for corporate data.

product.title: It crashes your meetings and spams your contacts
product.minus: The bot auto-joins any meeting with a Zoom link even after the calendar is disconnected, and it emails everyone you've met with invites sent in your name. People say they can't stop it and that it publicly embarrassed them on work calls.

product.title: The free tier was cut to 30 minutes and stops mid-recording
product.minus: Free users get only 30 minutes of transcription, and you find out when a lecture or meeting cuts off halfway. Often you can't upgrade or top up from the app itself — the upgrade offer appears, but there's no way to actually pay.

product.title: Confuses voices and struggles with accents
product.minus: In in-person meetings the app often fails to tell speakers apart, runs the end of one person's line into the next, or labels multiple speakers when there's only one. Accuracy drops with accents and fast speech, forcing manual proofreading.

product.title: Plans get reshuffled: fewer minutes, same price
product.minus: Long-time paid subscribers complain their recording minutes and exports get slashed with no price drop, while their archive is held hostage. Loyalty counts for nothing: minutes can fall 75% in a month, and people leave for rivals.

product.title: Updates break the app and remove working features
product.minus: After updates, tabs stop switching, playback dies, settings won't open. They also stripped out familiar things: copying summary text, meeting start times inside the app, in-meeting search — and users go hunting for another note-taker.

product.title: The recording widget vanished and won't come back for months
product.minus: The Android widget with a quick-record button disappeared after a "bug fix", and support has no idea when it'll return. For many it was the key reason they subscribed — without it, starting a recording is clumsy.

product.title: Google Play billing glitches and unwanted charges
product.minus: Google Play payments turn into charges for a subscription that isn't even listed as managed, continued billing after cancellation, and downgrades to free despite a paid renewal. Support admits a "known issue" but only offers a refund and re-signup.

product.title: Accurate for clean English, useless for other languages
product.minus: On clear English the transcription is rightly praised as accurate, but Russian returns nothing, German is called "complete junk", and Arabic, Bengali and many others simply aren't on the menu. For non-English content the app is a dead end.

product.title: On clean speech the transcription really is best-in-class
product.plus: When the language is English and speech is clear, users call Otter the most accurate transcriber they've tried: it catches words even in a moving car, tidies up rushed dictation, and works for both Zoom and in-person meetings.

product.title: The paywall stays hidden until the recording is done
product.minus: People record a whole meeting and only learn the full transcript is paid afterward, when there's no way back.

product.title: Five stars are demanded before the first use
product.minus: Access to the "free" plan is traded for a rating, so the store is full of reviews from people who never opened the app.

product.title: The free tier only returns a fragment of the recording
product.minus: A roughly five-minute cap (sometimes less) cuts the text off halfway, so you can't even test quality on your own recording.

product.title: Onboarding is a wall of promo screens instead of an app
product.minus: Before getting to work you have to fight through endless pricing and ad screens — dodging them takes longer than the transcription itself.

product.title: The app freezes on the very first "Continue"
product.minus: Some users never get past the start screen at all: the button taps, then there's a blank page or a crash.

product.title: The payment goes through — the access doesn't
product.minus: Money is taken (sometimes twice), yet premium never activates; there's nowhere to log in or check the subscription status.

product.title: Accuracy wobbles, especially outside English
product.minus: On songs, multiple speakers and non-English languages the text comes out incomplete and wrong, and some languages aren't supported at all.

product.title: Suspicions of fake AI and watermarks inside the text
product.minus: Users notice missing key passages, made-up summaries and watermark phrases pasted into the transcript — and call it a scam.

product.title: Those who break through praise the speed and simplicity
product.plus: Once they reach the work, users get fast, accurate text in seconds, export to PDF/Word, and genuine time savings on busy days.

product.title: On clean speech it transcribes almost word for word
product.plus: When the recording is good, the text comes out spot-on — a couple of slips in the first sentence, then dead accurate, even across a language switch.

product.title: The icon doesn't install and the transcript can't be edited
product.minus: Even happy users hit splinters: the app doesn't create an icon so you open it via Google Play, and you can't name speakers or fix mistakes in the text.

product.title: You can't evaluate it without paying
product.minus: Users' core ask is a 1-3 day trial or at least a couple of attempts; without a real test nobody will hand over $60 a year blind.

product.title: Lives up to its name: one tap and you're recording
product.plus: Over and over, people praise it for doing exactly what it promises — no extra steps, no clutter. One button to record, one to listen, and it's clear even to the least tech-savvy users.

product.title: Recordings vanish overnight — sometimes years of work in a single day
product.plus: The scariest complaint: people open the app to record something new and find that everything they'd saved over years is simply gone, even though they deleted nothing. Songs, musical ideas, precious memories — with no way to recover them. After that, trust in the recorder is broken for good.

product.title: Clean capture: voice and sound come out crisp, with no hiss
product.plus: Sound quality gets steady praise — recordings come out clear, free of static, often better than the phone's built-in mic. Good enough for singing, for a church choir, and for important meetings.

product.title: Records with the screen off and in the background
product.plus: Many value that recording keeps going with the screen off or while other apps like Zoom, YouTube or iHeart run on top. For people capturing lectures, meetings or long sessions, that's the deciding feature.

product.title: Wear OS watch sync barely works
product.plus: Galaxy Watch owners get stuck: recordings are marked synced but never appear on the phone, and long files stay "locked" on the watch because Bluetooth transfer keeps timing out. Even Pro users can't retrieve their files, and the recording date gets overwritten with the sync date.

product.title: A pocket scratchpad for musicians: catches riffs and songs on the fly
product.plus: A big slice of fans are musicians, singers and songwriters who capture melodies and ideas the moment inspiration hits, then loop them back to learn. Double-tracking, harmonies and a loop for memorizing cover their rough music work.

product.title: No transcription — a letdown in the AI era
product.plus: Several people say it outright: in the AI era, the lack of speech-to-text transcription is reason enough to uninstall. Even those who love the cloud sync see it as a painful gap.

product.title: Unobtrusive ads — but sometimes deceptive and alarming
product.plus: Most praise the ads for being quiet and tucked into a small top banner. But spammy, deceptive ones surface too — like "We are about to disable your account, ACT NOW!" — and some complain ads remain even after paying.

product.title: Flexible storage: record straight to the SD card, no phone clutter
product.plus: People value choosing a storage folder at install and writing to the SD card so phone memory stays free. Quality settings and WAV support add flexibility that built-in recorders lack.

product.title: Long recordings cut themselves off before you stop them
product.plus: People recording for hours hit a nasty surprise: the app used to run until you manually stopped it, but now it cuts off after an hour. You think you've captured 4–8 hours, then on playback find only a fragment.

product.title: A sensitive mic catches even distant and ambient sounds
product.plus: A special kind of love is for the mic's sensitivity: tune it up and you hear trains, birds, insects, a neighbor's barking dog. A distant animal plays back louder and clearer than the original — perfect for capturing ambient sound.

product.title: Files get lost and stop being readable after updates
product.plus: Beyond vanishing recordings, another pain surfaces: after an update files stop being recognized — by this app or any other. And some simply can't find where recordings are even saved, and lose them for good.

product.title: Won't work without unrestricted microphone access
product.plus: Some users hit a permissions wall: the app seems to demand unlimited microphone access, and the "ask every time" mode just won't function. For the privacy-conscious that's a blocker — ironically, others praise it precisely for being clean about permissions.

product.title: The diary eats entries: whole writing sessions vanish without saving
product.minus: People repeatedly lose paragraphs or entire sessions: an entry won't save, disappears after adding a photo, or is gone after a phone reset. For a memory-keeping diary this is the most painful failure — and it drives users away.

product.title: Forced AI with no off switch — users read it as a privacy threat
product.minus: An update added AI features that stay visible even when supposedly off and can't be removed. For a journal that's taboo: people fear their private entries become training data, and many say outright they're leaving for a competitor.

product.title: A free app holds you hostage: after a subscription change, entries get locked behind a paywall
product.minus: People who joined a "free" app suddenly hit a login-to-payment loop and can't reach years of past entries. It reads as blackmail and provokes genuine fury.

product.title: Autocorrect bug: fixing a typo duplicates the whole word
product.minus: Delete a couple of letters to fix a typo and the app brings back the whole word: "examp" becomes "exampexample", "60kg" becomes "6060kg". The bug has lived for years and breaks the one core function — writing.

product.title: Endless syncing blocks input — even with sync off or no account
product.minus: The app freezes on "Synchronization" every time you switch apps, drains battery and blocks writing. What stings is that it happens with sync disabled and even without an account.

product.title: A simple, clean, uncluttered interface that's pleasant to write in daily
product.plus: The top praise: the interface is simple, clean, ad-free and not overwhelming like Notion or Obsidian. It's comfortable from day one, and many write in it daily for years.

product.title: Multiple separate journals in one app — a beloved way to organize thoughts
product.plus: Having many separate journals in one app is a standout favourite: from work to existential ones, people sort their thoughts and keep up to 20 journals.

product.title: Streaks, prompts and the "On This Day" memories genuinely pull people back to daily writing
product.plus: Streaks, daily prompts and the "On This Day" memories act as a motivator: people keep 1000+ day streaks, reread past years, and credit these features with getting them back into the writing habit.

product.title: The ~$50/year subscription with no lifetime option grates — especially with free Apple/Google Journal around
product.minus: A ~$50/year subscription feels "bonkers" for a diary, especially with no one-time lifetime option. People point to free Apple and Google journaling apps and question what they're paying for.

product.title: Heavy login and encryption demands: easy to be locked out forever over an "encryption key"
product.minus: Mandatory sign-up with a complex password and end-to-end encryption feel like overkill for a diary — and worse, losing the "encryption key" can lock you out of all past entries forever. Plus nagging encryption pop-ups on every launch.

product.title: The free tier chokes attachments: one photo per entry, video and audio paywalled
product.minus: The most common free-tier frustration is the one-photo-per-entry limit, with video and audio locked behind premium. For people who journal around photo memories, this breaks the main use case.

product.title: Google login and second-device sign-in often fail — some never get to use the app at all
product.minus: Google login fails with errors on phone and desktop, the sign-up link never arrives by email, and entries don't sync on a new device. Some people never managed to log in at all and rated one star without ever seeing the app.

product.title: The «lifetime» license got re-played as a subscription — what users paid for once is asked for again
product.minus: People who bought premium or lifetime years ago find, after an update, that their features (web access, email-to-entry, export) were moved behind a new membership subscription. They are asked for a nine-year-old receipt or told to pay again — for what they already paid for forever.

product.title: Entries vanish: years of journaling disappear after a phone swap or a sync glitch
product.minus: The most painful pattern is lost entries. After a new phone, an update or a cloud glitch, users lose years of journaling, photos of deceased loved ones, baby journals. Sometimes an entry is wiped in the moment: wrote for an hour, added a photo — all gone.

product.title: No support: just an AI bot and a queue where replies take days or weeks
product.minus: When something breaks, there is no human to reach. The chat is an AI bot in a loop, the auto-reply promises 24 hours, but in reality there is silence for 4-5 days, a week, months. Email and forums go unanswered too. It hits paying members hardest.

product.title: Basic formatting costs money: bold, italics and underline got locked behind subscription
product.minus: What stings isn't the price itself but WHAT got locked: bold, italics, underline — the things free Notes gives out of the box. Users who once had this suddenly lose access to the basics after an update.

product.title: Billing trap: silent auto-renewal, a price jump, and no way to cancel or refund
product.minus: Subscriptions renew without warning, the price doubles ($39 to $75, $50 to £70), and cancelling or refunding is nearly impossible. Cancellation was deliberately moved out of the app to the website so users give up. Refund requests are ignored.

product.title: Relentless upsell: buy-premium popups on every open — even for those who already paid
product.minus: Every launch throws a «buy membership» screen, sometimes before you even get to try it. Worst of all, the popups continue for those who already bought premium or lifetime: the ad comes back even after you tap «cancel».

product.title: «Free» on the listing, paid in reality: a 3-day trial that sometimes charges instantly
product.minus: The app is listed as free but opens straight into a subscription: a measly 3-day trial, then $50-75 a year. Worse — for some the «3-day trial» button charges money instantly, with no trial, which reads as a bug or a scam.

product.title: Sync and backup let you down: Google Drive failures, a 275-entries-at-a-time cap
product.minus: Cloud sync — the headline feature — breaks regularly: Google Drive stops working, entries won't pull onto a new device. And restoring is agony: the download runs ~275 entries at a time, so with thousands of entries you restart it by hand for hours.

product.title: A decade of loyalty: people journal here daily for 8-10 years
product.plus: A huge share of 5★ are multi-year users: 6, 8, 10 years of daily entries. For them it's not just an app but an «external brain and heart», a companion through hard times, a habit they don't want to drop. Retention this deep is rare.

product.title: Simple, clean and fast: free-form writing without forced templates
product.plus: What users love most is the simplicity: a clean tidy interface, no clutter, you can write freely like in a paper diary, with templates optional rather than forced. Calendar, photos, tags, PIN — all at hand and out of the way.

product.title: «Throwbacks», photos and media turn entries into a living memory archive
product.plus: The throwback feature plus attaching photos, video, geotags and tags make the diary not text but a memory archive. People keep «how I look» and «weather» journals for years, print entries as a book for their kids — the app brings back forgotten moments.

product.title: Endless rate-us prompts and nag popups annoy even happy paying users
product.minus: The app constantly begs for a rating — after every entry, almost daily. It annoys even premium buyers: «organizations are not owed reviews». Some people deliberately lower their stars precisely because of the nagging.

product.title: Privacy gaps: entry snippets show in recent-apps and in flashbacks despite the lock
product.minus: Although the PIN and lock are praised, there are leaks: the recent-apps screen shows snippets past the lock, and flashbacks pop up without authorization even with fingerprint enabled. For a diary where privacy is the point, that's a serious flaw.

product.title: Paid for premium — access never unlocked
product.minus: The single most common complaint: people pay (especially for the «lifetime» plan), the money is taken, but the account stays Basic and the «restore purchase» button does nothing.

product.title: Support is dead, emails bounce back
product.minus: The contact email and the «contact support» button either go unanswered for weeks and months, or the message bounces as undeliverable — people have literally nowhere to turn.

product.title: Logged out once and can't get back in
product.minus: One accidental logout and the user is stuck on a login error: resetting the password doesn't help, and they're forced to make a new account and lose their history.

product.title: Can't add photos: storage permission is missing
product.minus: The app tells you to enable storage access to attach a photo to a challenge, but the option simply isn't in the permission settings — so the challenges can't be completed.

product.title: Stats are dangled for N days — then locked behind premium
product.minus: Users are told to journal for 4-5 days to unlock stats, only to find at the end that they still have to buy them — which feels like a bait-and-switch and wasted time.

product.title: Premium pop-up on every single launch
product.minus: Every launch is met with a nagging prompt to buy premium — for an app meant to calm you down, it's grating and often the reason people uninstall.

product.title: The home screen suddenly goes blank
product.minus: After an update some users lose the whole home screen with check-in, quote and challenges — it just goes blank, and it's unclear whether it's a bug or a premium restriction.

product.title: Too expensive for too little
product.minus: A price tag of tens or hundreds of dollars feels disproportionate: premium, users say, mostly adds extra quotes and doesn't even remove ads.

product.title: No back-dating and no autosave loses your text
product.minus: You can only write an entry for today, and a long entry vanishes if you step away and come back later — the lack of autosave wipes out an hour of work.

product.title: Cozy, simple and beautiful — what people love
product.plus: When it works, people are won over by the soft aesthetics, smooth animations and pressure-free simplicity: it's easy to write without being forced to churn out paragraphs.

product.title: Genuinely helps with mood and anxiety
product.plus: Many say the daily check-ins, quotes and the chance to vent visibly lift their mood and help with anxiety — almost like having a therapist's support.

product.title: Challenges and quotes keep the habit alive
product.plus: Daily challenges, motivational quotes and playful prompts turn journaling into a pleasant ritual people come back to for years.

product.title: A private place to vent that syncs to the cloud
product.plus: Users value it as a safe private corner to dump any thoughts, with entries auto-synced to the cloud so they're not lost when switching phones.

product.title: One-time purchase, not a subscription — the main reason people love it
product.plus: People are sick of subscription traps and come here precisely for the one-time, lifetime payment. It is repeatedly named as the key reason to choose Diarium and recommend it to others.

product.title: You buy the app, then pay all over again for each platform
product.minus: The license is tied to a single ecosystem, so Windows, Mac, or iPad each cost extra. With several devices this becomes paying twice, three, or four times for the same diary — and many call it ridiculous.

product.title: Cloud backup suddenly moved behind a paywall
product.minus: Some users saw free cloud sync as the app's core feature, only to be asked to pay just to keep their diary in sync. For a few, that was reason enough to uninstall.

product.title: Attaching photos to entries — the thing that keeps people coming back
product.plus: Easily adding photos, videos, and audio makes entries richer, and auto-collecting the day's pictures becomes a daily ritual. For many it has turned into their favorite part of journaling.

product.title: The "on this day last year" reminders spark reflection
product.plus: Daily pop-ups with entries from previous years give a reason to look back and notice what has changed and what has stayed the same. This feature is named as one of the warmest and most valued.

product.title: Tags and trackers turn the diary into a searchable tool
product.plus: Hashtags, tags, and trackers let users sort entries by topic and find anything instantly — from recipes to answered prayers. The lightning-fast search across all entries is called especially powerful.

product.title: Strava, maps, and weather integrations auto-fill the day
product.plus: Linking to Strava, Maps, Weather, and even GitHub automatically pulls in everything the user did that day. For power users this turns the diary into a rich chronicle with no manual entry.

product.title: Easy import from other diaries removes migration fear
product.plus: People move here painlessly from Day One, Diaro, and others, carrying over entries, photos, and tags intact. Being able to escape another app's lock-in is named as a reason for gratitude.

product.title: Entries vanish: lost diaries break trust
product.minus: Despite cloud backup, some users lost their diary when switching phones, after a crash, or through sync failures — sometimes multiple times. For an app holding years of personal entries, such losses feel catastrophic.

product.title: Unobtrusive reminders help keep the habit
product.plus: Gentle end-of-day reminders and prompt suggestions help people write consistently without pressure. Users note the app genuinely got them journaling more often than a paper or Google-doc journal.

product.title: No ads, no tracking — privacy by default
product.plus: No ads, end-to-end encryption, and storing data in the user's own cloud give a sense of control over personal entries. For a diary holding intimate content, users call this crucial.

product.title: SQLite backup feels like a "proprietary lock-in"
product.minus: The SQLite-database backup format, rather than a plain txt or JSON, alarms some users who fear losing access to years of entries if the app ever disappears. Not being able to export their data for free deepens that worry.

product.title: A simple, clear interface lowers the barrier to writing daily
product.plus: A clean, lightweight, flexible interface makes the app easier than picking up pen and paper, which matters most on hard days. Users call it a tool for mental health and daily writing.

product.title: Basic writing features are locked behind the paywall
product.minus: Bold, italics, headings, bullet points, tags and even font size require premium — users are asked to pay for what any diary treats as a given.

product.title: Simple, ad-free, does exactly what it promises
product.plus: The core love for the app is its minimalism: jot a thought with date and time in two or three taps, no ads, no clickbait, nothing extra.

product.title: Entries just vanish or roll back
product.minus: People lose what they wrote: the app erases parts of text, reverts to an older version after they hit save, and an accidentally deleted entry can't be recovered — fatal for a diary.

product.title: Gmail-linked = entries survive for years
product.plus: The loyal users' strongest argument: everything is stored in your Google account, so switching phones or reinstalling doesn't wipe the diary — many still have entries from 2018-2021.

product.title: The subscription price feels absurd
product.minus: For a notepad with a calendar the app asks sums users call insane (2500 CZK, 4550 PHP) and compare the model to Adobe — for a diary the price tag feels like a joke.

product.title: Support simply goes silent
product.minus: Emails and Facebook messages go unanswered for months, the chatbot throws "Authentification failure", and help seems reserved for those who already paid — which stings most after buying premium.

product.title: A private vault for your thoughts
product.plus: Users value being able to pour out anger, fear or complaints about loved ones with no one seeing — privacy and the lack of data collection make the app a therapeutic outlet.

product.title: The premium prompt hits you at every launch
product.minus: The upgrade screen pops up before you can even do anything and recurs at every opportunity — the pushiness of the upsell repels even people who liked the app.

product.title: The privacy lock doesn't always work
product.minus: The advertised PIN protection is unreliable: sometimes it doesn't lock at all, sometimes it leaves the last screen open — leaving private thoughts exposed to anyone who picks up the phone.

product.title: Doesn't work without internet
product.minus: Some users find it absurd that a diary requires a connection and forced email login, while others praise it working offline — the behavior clearly varies by case and confuses people.

product.title: Users ask for a widget, reminders and a character counter
product.minus: Recurring requests from loyal users: a home-screen quick-entry widget, pop-up reminders for future plans, and a character counter — especially because of the 6,000-8,000 character per-entry limit.

product.title: Cross-device sync breaks down
product.minus: Cross-platform sync is both the headline draw and the pain: bullet points don't carry between phone, tablet and PC, tags fail to sync from iPad, and on a new phone entries sometimes disappear.

product.title: The grid of customizable prompts removes the blank-page fear
product.plus: The app's core win is the grid where each cell becomes your own prompt-question. People who could never keep a diary finally write daily, because the guiding questions break through the blank page and help them sort their thoughts.

product.title: Sync and backup are gated behind the subscription
product.minus: To sync between devices or have a cloud backup you must pay. Users don't understand why they can't just link a normal Google Drive or OneDrive, and when they switch phones they risk losing everything.

product.title: Entries silently vanish after an update or after saving
product.minus: The most painful failure: people write an entry, hit save, and it disappears. Many lost year-old entries and entire journals after an update. It destroys trust in an app whose one job is to keep your writing.

product.title: Deep customization bends to anything — from a bullet journal to a dog-health tracker
product.plus: The grid reshapes to any use: gratitude diary, planner, bullet journal, workout tracking, even pet-health logs. Day/week/month/year templates give a rare mix of freedom and structure.

product.title: No web or Windows app leaves desktop users stranded
product.minus: The app lives only on phone and tablet, with no PC sync (and in one case it syncs only to Macs). People want to write longer reflections on a real keyboard at home and keep begging for a web client or Windows app.

product.title: The free tier allows only one journal
product.minus: The free version allows just one journal; a second one (say, a separate gratitude log or one shared with a partner) requires a subscription. Many accept the single journal but ask for at least two or three for free.

product.title: A clean, ad-free interface that never nags
product.plus: A minimalist, tidy design with daily quotes, no ads and no push notifications wins over people tired of nagging apps. Many praise the lack of pressure and the calm feel.

product.title: Some find the interface cluttered and confusing
product.minus: The same richness that delights some scares others: reaching an entry takes several taps and picking a question. Some want a plain free-writing mode without a mandatory prompt.

product.title: Subscription-only with no one-time buy, and the price stings
product.minus: People object on principle to paying for a diary "for the rest of your life" and want a one-time purchase. The roughly $100/year price feels steep for a simple journal, especially when basics like changing the colour scheme are paywalled too.

product.title: Responsive support that fixes bugs and wins users back
product.plus: When the team does respond, it acts fast: fixes crashes, communicates progress clearly, updates default settings, and turns three-star reviews into five. This sharply contrasts with the users who were ignored.

product.title: Login, verification and startup crashes lock out new users
product.minus: Many never reach their first entry: Google login fails with http 422, email verification doesn't work, and guest mode or the Terms/Privacy buttons crash the app or show a blank page.

product.title: Requests for handwriting, stats and media show real feature gaps
product.minus: Loyal users want the app to grow with them and ask for specifics: stylus handwriting, stats on moods and tags, audio/video in entries, reminders, and the ability to reorder grid cells.

product.title: Autosave silently eats text while you're still writing
product.minus: The single most common and painful complaint: users write a long entry, exit or just switch tabs, and everything but the first line vanishes. A manual save button was added, but even that doesn't help.

product.title: The cursor jumps to the top and deletes a paragraph mid-typing
product.minus: A distinct Android input bug: while typing, the text gets flung to the top, the last paragraph is deleted, and people end up retyping the same thing several times within minutes.

product.title: Broken sync: versions diverge and overwrite what you wrote
product.minus: Sync between phone, PC and web has gone unfixed for years: refreshing the browser loses progress, desktop changes never reach the phone, and the app itself hangs on "syncing" and locks you out of writing.

product.title: Forget the journal password and your entries are gone forever
product.minus: The encrypted journal has no password reset: people who kept entries for years forget a pin or password and are permanently locked out, with no email-based recovery.

product.title: Account login and password reset are broken too
product.minus: Beyond the journal, account login itself breaks: reset emails never arrive, a correct email is rejected as "not valid," and after three reset attempts people get locked out entirely.

product.title: The app crashes on open after an update
product.minus: Successive updates render the app unusable: it crashes on launch, at the unlock screen, or when opening an entry, leaving people with no access to their own journals.

product.title: You pay for Pro, don't get Pro, and can't get unsubscribed
product.minus: Billing genuinely fails: Pro features don't unlock after payment, subscriptions cancelled years ago keep getting charged, and even the bank can't stop the payments.

product.title: Support is locked behind a subscription, and there are no replies
product.minus: When something breaks, there's no help: you can only reach support from a paid account, and emails get only irrelevant automated replies, leaving people feeling abandoned.

product.title: The journal emails your entries back to you — a creepy privacy flaw
