product.title: Custom drinks got cut and broken
product.minus: The make/edit-your-own-drinks feature people stayed for is gone or corrupts past entries; there's no white color, and you can't reorder or delete the preset drinks.

product.title: Onboarding survey-before-use grates
product.minus: The app asks for an opinion and pushes a questionnaire before you've even tried it, and a nagging "Yay, you" pops up after your first sip that you have to dismiss.

product.title: Users want graphs, stats and data export
product.minus: History is a narrow list of numbers with no weekly/monthly graphs and no CSV export — visual users miss a clear view of progress and a copy of their own data.

product.title: No dark mode even in the paid version
product.minus: The harsh all-white interface with no dark mode hurts the eyes and bothers light-sensitive users — and it's missing even after buying the full version.

product.title: Weak watch and Wear OS support
product.minus: On the Galaxy Watch 4 the app either refuses to run or won't let you pick a drink type and makes you guess the milliliters with no reference — breaking the use case for watch-first buyers.

product.title: Ads now block the act of logging water itself
product.minus: The top complaint from longtime users: after an update, full-screen or banner ads sit right between you and the «add water» button. Logging is a one-second action, and people refuse to watch videos or dodge banners for it, so they leave in droves.

product.title: The free widget suddenly went pro-only
product.minus: The handy widget is exactly what drew many in — and it's exactly what got moved behind the paywall retroactively. To users this feels like a bait-and-switch: what they'd used for years suddenly demanded an upgrade overnight, and without it the app loses any edge over a plain reminder.

product.title: A paywall pop-up on every launch infuriates
product.minus: Some opened the app expecting a free tracker and hit an aggressive subscription screen that's hard to dismiss. The feeling of being forced to pay, plus a hidden back button, reads as a scammy dark pattern.

product.title: Stats silently drops whole days and breaks streaks
product.minus: A serious trust-breaking bug: the entry shows in history but the day reads zero in statistics. This snaps streaks and withholds milestones — most galling for people who logged faithfully and even paid for premium.

product.title: The day hard-resets at midnight — a mess for night shifts
product.minus: Night-shift workers and late risers ask to set their own day start and end. Right now the counter resets exactly at midnight even if you set a late bedtime, so you physically can't hit your goal before it wipes.

product.title: Migrating to a new phone and restoring purchases breaks
product.minus: Backup and restore are a weak spot. People lose all their history when switching phones, the «restore purchase» button doesn't work, and emails to the developer go unanswered even though the app is paid.

product.title: Reminders fire unpredictably or go silent
product.minus: The core job — reminding — simply fails for some: the notification fires once and stops, the sound silently switches itself off, and one user's 2-hour interval suddenly became every 15 minutes. For a tracker, that's critical.

product.title: Tracking is imprecise: drinks count as 100% water, measures are limited
product.minus: Users who want accuracy hit crude assumptions: beer and coffee count as pure water, you can't enter a standard 16.9 oz bottle (the decimal button doesn't work), and the app blocks anything over 5L as «unhealthy».

product.title: Simplicity and minimalism are the top reason to love it
product.plus: The most frequent praise: «open, tap, done». No extra screens, no trying to be more than it is — the clean interface does exactly one job, and that's precisely why people pick it over fancier trackers.

product.title: It genuinely raises water intake and improves well-being
product.plus: For many, the app does its job: people drink far more than before, acne and migraines clear up, and chronic conditions or medication side effects become easier to manage. It's not cosmetic — it actually changes the habit.

product.title: Cute design and a pleasant water sound make the routine non-annoying
product.plus: The app's emotional hook is its cute «smiling water drop» character and a soft trickling sound instead of a harsh alarm. Reminders feel gentle, even fun, which sets it apart from «pushy» rivals.

product.title: A cheap one-time payment instead of a subscription — what people praise
product.plus: For happy users, a key strength is premium at a small one-time fee (about the price of a cup of tea) that removes ads and unlocks drink types. It reads as a fair deal and a reason to support the devs.

product.title: Customizable cup sizes and fast one-tap entry
product.plus: A practical favorite: cups and volumes are easy to customize, and picking a size is just an arrow tap with no extra menus. Logging is faster than rivals and you can backdate the time.

product.title: Fish-as-reward is the real motivation hook
product.plus: People drink on schedule not for health but to earn the next fish — the gamification works where dull trackers fail.

product.title: Subscription for a basic feature feels absurd
product.minus: A water-reminder by subscription is the biggest irritant: $2/mo or $18/yr for what competitors give free, and the aquarium — the only draw — is locked behind the paywall.

product.title: Reminders work, then go silent for days
product.minus: The app's whole job — to remind you to drink — fails at random: notifications work a couple of days, then vanish for weeks, and without them the app is useless.

product.title: Gentle, non-nagging reminders when they do fire
product.plus: For users whose reminders work, the gentleness wins them over: custom intervals, subtle alerts, and an app that never shames you for missing a goal.

product.title: Stripped-down simplicity others couldn't match
product.plus: After trying dozens of water trackers, people settle here precisely for the minimalism: no clutter, easy logging, it does exactly what's needed.

product.title: The home-screen widget just opens the app, doesn't log
product.minus: The widget promises quick logging from the home screen, but it merely opens the app and routinely freezes for hours — the one thing it's for doesn't work.

product.title: Flat fish-on-a-stick animation kills the upsell
product.minus: The fish animation looks like flat cardboard cut-outs on sticks over a painted backdrop — and it's that cheap visual that stops would-be payers from going Pro.

product.title: Drains battery, freezes, and crashes after OS updates
product.minus: A lovely idea undone by a heavy runtime: it drains the battery, freezes the phone, and crashes over conflicts with Pixel updates — enough to make people uninstall.

product.title: Switching phones wipes data and your purchase
product.minus: There's no proper sync: moving to a new phone loses progress, fish, and even a purchase you bought "forever" — you end up paying again.

product.title: Ads exist, but are so unobtrusive people praise them
product.plus: Unlike rivals with aggressive pop-ups, here it's just a quiet banner at the bottom — users specifically note the ads never interrupt or get in the way.

product.title: Flexible custom cup sizes and goals
product.plus: You can set your own cup sizes, edit the log by hand, and adjust the ounce goal rather than being locked to a weight-based number — a genuine pain solved.

product.title: Counts water only — no other-beverage tracking
product.minus: It can't account for the water content of tea, coffee and other drinks, forcing users to look it up and recalculate by hand every time.

product.title: Blocking senders and spam filters are locked behind the subscription
product.minus: A basic thing — blocking an annoying sender — is paid in Spark. Users are stunned they must pay for what Gmail and other clients do for free, and several leave specifically over this.

product.title: "Free" turns out to be a 7-day trial with a pricey subscription
product.minus: The app is presented as free, but the real price (tens of dollars/pounds a year) only surfaces after you've logged in and handed over your data. Many call it bait-and-switch and uninstall on the spot.

product.title: Forced AI with an un-hideable button floating over the inbox
product.minus: After the AI pivot, a star button sits next to compose everywhere and can't be removed — support tells users to "simply ignore it." Even with AI off the widget stays, and longtime fans see it as ruining a beloved app.

product.title: Emails take painfully long to open and often won't load at all
product.minus: Opening a single email can take 4–10 seconds, and sometimes it just spins forever and never loads. Next to Gmail it feels especially slow, and for business use it becomes nearly unusable.

product.title: Constantly logs you out and resets accounts and settings
product.minus: Especially after updates, the app signs you out and forces you to re-add every mailbox each morning and reconfigure everything from scratch. For people with five or six accounts it becomes the last straw.

product.title: Typing bug: letters double up and scramble
product.minus: While composing, the cursor jumps back, the first letter of each word doubles, and characters get scrambled — you end up typing almost blind. After updates this went from a quirk to a reason to uninstall.

product.title: Deleted and archived emails reappear in the inbox
product.minus: Swipe to archive or delete and the email pops back into the inbox on the next open. Read-state sync is broken too: the phone shows as unread what was opened on Mac or desktop hours ago.

product.title: You can't turn off conversation threading
product.minus: Emails are force-grouped into subject threads with no way to disable it — even on premium. An older email that later got a reply hides inside the chain and can't be found by date; for many it's a clean reason to leave.

product.title: On Android tablets and foldables it's just a stretched-out phone
product.minus: Unlike the iPad version, tablets and foldables get no two-pane view, no landscape, and no proper scaling — the UI is just stretched and looks shabby. Some users switch from iPad to Android and are let down specifically by Spark.

product.title: The unified inbox across all mailboxes is what keeps people for years
product.plus: The thing users love most is pulling Gmail, Outlook, Yahoo, and IMAP into one smart inbox with cross-device account and settings sync. Many try competitors and come back within weeks precisely for this.

product.title: Support replies fast and actually solves problems
product.plus: Despite some complaints, many praise support: fast, friendly replies, real fixes (often a VPN or antivirus setting), and attention to feature requests. For loyal users it's a meaningful plus.

product.title: Clean design and thoughtful swipes make triaging mail a pleasure
product.plus: A tidy modern UI, action buttons at the bottom under your thumb, customizable swipes, and smart categorization — this is why people call Spark the best email client and say it genuinely cuts "email overwhelm."

product.title: Every update breaks something: crashes and regressions
product.minus: The recurring theme: "it was great until the update." The app crashes on launch or while clearing spam, force-closes seven times in a row, removes favourite widgets, and lags even on flagships like the S25.

product.title: The bottom of emails gets clipped by whitespace, hiding the unsubscribe link
product.minus: On HTML emails the bottom is replaced by a blank white block that crops the content — right where the unsubscribe link sits. Some users even suspect it's deliberate so you can't unsubscribe from spam.

product.title: A long onboarding questionnaire grates right at the entrance
product.minus: Before you reach the inbox, Spark drags you through a survey and tutorials with no skip option. People don't get why an email client needs to know how they'll use it — and some uninstall right at this step.

product.title: One unified inbox for every account is the main reason people stay
product.plus: People keep 4-8 accounts from different providers here and see all mail in a single list without switching apps. This is the single most-praised thing.

product.title: Moved emails snap back to the inbox after a sync
product.minus: The most painful breakage: you file or delete messages, reopen the app, and they're all back in the inbox. People re-file the same mail several times a day.

product.title: Mail says "sent" but never actually goes out
product.minus: Sending is a weak spot: mail hangs, won't go unless the app stays open on screen, or shows as sent but arrives days later. Attachments make it worse.

product.title: Updates turn a working app into a glitchy one
product.minus: A recurring arc: worked fine for years, then an update lands and emails flicker, overlap, the screen skips. Many beg for the old version back.

product.title: Mail simply doesn't arrive or won't display
product.minus: The basic job of email sometimes fails: the inbox won't refresh, mail doesn't come through though it's there in the web mailbox, or shows up blank.

product.title: Better than Outlook is a common switching argument
product.plus: Lots of people came straight from Outlook and Gmail: unified inbox, no crashing, lighter and faster. It's an explicitly named reason to install.

product.title: When stable, instant notifications at tiny battery cost
product.plus: For those it works for, mail and pushes land near-instantly — where Gmail and Yahoo lagged by an hour — with barely any battery drain.

product.title: The paid tier feels expensive and is pushed via pop-ups
product.minus: Basic rules and filters sit behind a subscription people call overpriced; pop-ups nag to buy, and the buy button is placed so people subscribe by accident.

product.title: Sudden sign-outs and lost access after an update
product.minus: The app randomly signs people out with no warning, and sometimes an update locks them out of every account — users fear losing decades of accumulated mail.

product.title: Responsive support rescues the rating
product.plus: When the team responds, people praise it: they dig into the problem, reply fast and thoroughly, even for the free tier — and it often keeps the user on board.

product.title: The spam filter works for some and fails others
product.minus: The advertised spam protection is inconsistent: some praise the blocking, others drown in porn spam and watch blocked addresses come right back.

product.title: Accounts won't connect: Office 365, IMAP/Gmail, Comcast
product.minus: Connecting specific providers is a frequent wall: Office 365 demands admin approval, out-of-the-box Gmail IMAP won't sync, and Comcast accounts drop daily.

product.title: The app locks you out in an endless login → captcha → logout loop
product.minus: People simply can't get into their own mail: the app logs them out after updates, rejects a password that is definitely correct, or traps them in an endless cycle of captchas and codes. Meanwhile the web version works fine.

product.title: You can't even create an account: "Something went wrong" at the captcha
product.minus: Sign-up breaks before the first email even arrives: the puzzle captcha and code verification repeatedly throw "something went wrong" or "connectivity issue." Some have to fall back to a computer, others just leave.

product.title: Privacy and peace of mind are the main reason people stay
product.plus: Exactly what people come for: the feeling that only you read your mail, with no tracking or data selling. For many it's a straight replacement for Gmail/Outlook and a reason to migrate everything to Proton.

product.title: A clean, uncluttered interface with no ads or junk
product.plus: The happy users single out the simple, tidy look: nothing extra, dark theme, no ad banners — after bloated Gmail and Outlook it feels like a breath of fresh air.

product.title: Slow and frozen: it only loads through a VPN
product.minus: Basic mail handling drags: the app takes minutes to fetch messages, freezes, won't refresh, and a message only sends after several tries. Many admit it only behaves with a VPN turned on.

product.title: Email notifications only arrive in a batch after you open the app manually
product.minus: The most common gripe even among satisfied users: push alerts for new mail don't arrive until you open the app yourself — then they all dump at once. Settings have been double-checked; other apps notify fine.

product.title: Google dependency: to leave Gmail, you need Gmail
product.minus: The product's core contradiction: people come to de-Google themselves, only to find sign-up needs a Google account, payment goes through Google Play, and notifications depend on Google Play Services. It feels like a betrayal of the whole premise.

product.title: Basic email features are locked behind the paywall
product.minus: What grates is that the paywall hides not advanced tech but the basics: folders, labels, multiple addresses, auto-emptying trash, even the desktop app. To many it reads as "everything costs money," and they leave for more generous free rivals.

product.title: 1 GB free is too little next to Gmail's 15 GB
product.minus: Even loyal users uniformly ask for more space: 1 GB fills up instantly, old mail has to be deleted one by one, while Zoho gives 5 GB free and Gmail 15 GB.

product.title: Spam gets through while unsubscribe and block don't work
product.minus: Painful for a service that sells protection: people keep getting newsletters from senders they unsubscribed from, can't block addresses inside the app, and some get buried in scam mail.

product.title: A password reset = losing access to all your old mail
product.minus: The flip side of encryption: after a password reset old mail stays encrypted, and the recovery options (a prior device / a recovery file / a second password) are unworkable for a normal person. People lose access to mail full of clients and important data.

product.title: Pushy "Upgrade" prompts and in-app spam, even for paying users
product.minus: The company that promises no ads buries the interface in "Upgrade" buttons, a fake notification dot on the icon, and VPN pitches — even to paying subscribers. That dents trust harder than any bug.

product.title: After updates the app crashes on launch and won't open
product.minus: A whole wave of reviews about updates that break things: the app closes a couple of seconds after launch, hangs on the splash screen, won't open across different devices — and reinstalling or clearing the cache doesn't help.

product.title: No search across your mail — even after years
product.minus: A stunning gap for a mail app: you still can't properly search your mail by content, only manually scroll through thousands of messages. Add to that no editing of filters or contacts on the phone.

product.title: Text and attachments break: mangled formatting, tiny file limits
product.minus: A real problem for work mail: text formatting falls apart on paste, there's no font or size choice, images in emails don't load, and attachments over 4-5 MB simply won't send.

product.title: An all-in-one ecosystem: mail, VPN, calendar, passwords together
product.plus: A strength for loyal users: one paid bundle covers mail, VPN, calendar, storage and a password manager. People value being able to remove Google almost entirely and keep everything in one ecosystem.

product.title: Support goes silent for weeks; cancelling a subscription is near-impossible
product.minus: When something breaks, help doesn't come: people sit locked out of paid accounts for 3-4 days with no reply, and you can't cancel a subscription or delete an account from the app — you hunt for settings like a game of Where's Waldo.

product.title: Deleted emails keep coming back to the inbox
product.minus: The single most common complaint: you delete a message, reopen the app later, and it's back in the inbox. Same with archive and spam. The app blames a 'poor connection' even on full 5G or home Wi-Fi.

product.title: The notification arrives, but the email isn't in the app
product.minus: A push for a new email lands, but the inbox doesn't show it — sometimes it surfaces 20–45 minutes later, sometimes never. Tapping the notification often opens a blank page, forcing you to hunt for the mail manually.

product.title: Painfully slow at loading emails
product.minus: The mailbox never refreshes in the background: you open the app and wait while it starts fetching. Opening a mail from a notification takes 10–45 seconds, threads spin forever. Flagship owners complain too — it isn't the hardware.

product.title: Pay separately for every platform
product.minus: Buy Pro or even a lifetime license on one device and you have to buy it again on Android/Windows/Mac — subscriptions don't carry across platforms. People discover this only after paying, and refunds are often refused.

product.title: Accounts keep disconnecting and demanding re-login
product.minus: The app constantly shows 'offline' or hangs on 'authenticating', and on nearly every launch makes you reconnect accounts and re-enter the password. Support's advice to 'sign out of all your devices' just infuriates people.

product.title: The AI assistant butts in where it wasn't invited
product.minus: The AI pops up intrusively when you reply, Copilot buttons are everywhere and can't be hidden, and people want to answer in their own words. In one case the app sent an email with a Canary signature on its own, without permission.

product.title: Swipes and stars only work on the third try
product.minus: Gesture handling is over-sensitive: trying to swipe a message selects it instead, and starring or marking as read often takes two or three return trips to the same email. For anyone who triages mail this way it's a time sink.

product.title: Attachments won't download or open
product.minus: Tapping an attachment often does nothing, PDFs won't load, and downloaded files save in an unreadable format. Forwarding can drop attachments entirely — a dealbreaker for work mail.

product.title: Crashes when you tap a notification
product.minus: For some users the app crashes when opening a mail from a notification or right at launch, often after an update. Sometimes it crashes when attaching a file — and reinstalling doesn't always fix it.

product.title: Emails arrive as an unreadable wall of text
product.minus: The client drops line breaks, turning emails into one long line of micro-characters. With dark theme the recipient gets white-on-white unreadable text. It's a long-standing complaint that feels ignored.

product.title: No calendar — can't replace Outlook/Gmail
product.minus: Android has no calendar and no task or contact sync, while iOS does — and users know it and want parity. Without it the app can't cover work scenarios and stays a personal-mail-only tool.

product.title: A beautiful unified inbox is the main reason to stay
product.plus: When it works, it's a favorite: a clean native UI, a tidy unified inbox across many accounts, sender icons, no ads. Many find it visually nicer than BlueMail, Thunderbird and FairEmail.

product.title: Real human support that actually fixes things
product.plus: A share of users praise fast support: they refund wrong charges, fix bugs within a couple of weeks and follow up, and one user got a higher plan as compensation for a lost lifetime license. It keeps people even after stumbles.

product.title: When the AI nails a draft, it's a wow
product.plus: For some users the AI is the reason to stay: it writes a short email that captures their thoughts instead of bloating it like ChatGPT, and the AI briefings and summaries save time — even if not everyone wants them.

product.title: Basic features locked behind paid Pro
product.minus: Snooze, dark compose, pinned mail, fetch frequency, send-later — all gated behind Pro, which feels like a bait-and-switch. The price is called high and the billing opaque: you learn you must pay only after installing.

product.title: The 2026 redesign turned veteran loyalty into rage
product.minus: The backbone of the reviews is people who used the app for 5-10 years at 5 stars, then dropped their rating after the May-June update and are leaving. They all describe the same arc: "used to be great, now it's trash." These aren't newcomers — they're the most loyal users, driven out by the update.

product.title: Forced "GemAI" reads as a betrayal, not a feature
product.minus: Users say it flat out: they don't want AI, the GemAI button can't be removed, it crowded out functions they actually used, and worst of all it opts them in by default to sending emails to an outside AI — read as a privacy breach. On top of that, even support now replies with AI canned responses, which finishes off any trust.

product.title: After the update, mail stops syncing
product.minus: The most common functional failure: an endlessly spinning loading wheel, new mail never arriving, read/deleted server-side messages not reflecting, and phone-vs-PC going out of step. For some, sync dies weekly and the only fix is a full reinstall.

product.title: Open one email, it shows you a different one
product.minus: A nasty bug for an email client: tapping a message opens a completely different one, with one email's body stuck under another's header. For business correspondence this is critical — users can no longer trust they're even reading the message they tapped.

product.title: Constant re-authentication that dead-ends in "not found"
product.minus: The app keeps logging accounts out (Hotmail, Yahoo, Google especially) and demanding re-login, only for re-auth to open a blank screen or "page not found" — and then mail won't flow. For some, an update wiped access to every account at once.

product.title: Search got buried in a submenu — and broke
product.minus: Fast search used to sit out in the open; now it's pushed behind the three-dot menu in favor of a chat button — and it either finds nothing, refreshes and overwrites the list, or loses the result the moment you tap it. For people who hunt old work emails daily, it wrecks the workflow.

product.title: Emails won't send and get stuck in the Outbox
product.minus: The most basic function — sending — fails for many: a permanent "sending" status, mail hung in the Outbox, messages that only go out if you babysit them. For an email client that's a foundational failure, and it's exactly what pushes people to Outlook and Thunderbird.

product.title: The spam filter stopped holding the line
product.minus: Bluemail used to be praised specifically for spam filtering, but post-update it collapsed: blocking doesn't work, unblocked senders get re-flagged, and junk that used to be auto-filtered now floods the inbox. Conversely, some users now lose legitimate mail to the spam folder.

product.title: Lag, freezes and crashes after the update
product.minus: A once light, fast app turned slow and bloated after the update: emails that take forever to load their body, the client freezing on a blank screen, and startup crashes up to it not launching at all (especially on Android 16 and new flagships). Often only a reinstall helps.

product.title: Silent or AI-templated support finishes off trust
product.minus: Amid the breakage, people write to support and wait weeks with no reply, or get an automated brush-off asking for details they can't send back — because sending email is exactly what's broken. That turns a one-off bug into a final reason to leave.

product.title: The unified inbox is the reason people stay
product.plus: The core love for the app is keeping every mailbox (often 5-10+) in one place, switching between them instantly, with color-coded accounts. It's why people pick it over Gmail and Outlook, and what keeps even the frustrated ones around.

product.title: Magic Sync moves your setup across devices painlessly
product.plus: Multi-device users prize Magic Sync: set up the Windows client exactly like Android with one "magic number," no manual re-entry of every account. It's a rare feature in email clients and genuinely saves time when migrating.

product.title: Free, ad-free and surprisingly full-featured
product.plus: Many call out that it's free with no intrusive ads, yet matches Outlook on capability — POP/IMAP, folders, built-in PGP, dark mode, powerful filters. For some, "no ads" alone is reason enough to stay.

product.title: When an update lands right, loyalty snaps back just as hard
product.plus: The flip side of the rage: a chunk of users report that recent patches fixed the bugs, restored the old speed, even improved the look and search — and they immediately restore 5 stars. It shows the base is ready to forgive if the dev finishes the job.

product.title: One unified inbox for every account is the reason people stay
product.plus: Over and over, the one thing people praise is having every mailbox in a single place, with no jumping between apps. This is exactly why they leave Gmail, Outlook and Yahoo.

product.title: Emails crawl back from spam and from folders into the inbox
product.minus: The most alarming complaint: emails sorted into folders or marked as spam come back to the inbox on their own, sometimes within seconds. People end up re-filing the same messages several times a day.

product.title: Mail fails to arrive, won't sync, or simply vanishes
product.minus: For some users the inbox just won't update: mail doesn't arrive, doesn't show up even though it's on the server, and sometimes disappears right in front of them as the inbox syncs, not in trash or archive.

product.title: Sending breaks: it says "sent" but the email never goes
product.minus: Sending is its own pain point: the app reports "sent" while the message never actually leaves, and you can't close the app mid-send, especially with attachments over a few megabytes.

product.title: Delivers mail and alerts faster than the native apps
product.plus: When it works, the speed wins people over: notifications arrive almost instantly, where Yahoo lagged by an hour and Gmail and Thunderbird stayed silent.

product.title: Rendering glitches: emails overlap, the screen flickers and skips
product.minus: After updates the rendering itself increasingly breaks: open an email and the screen flickers, skips, message bodies overlap each other, and it becomes impossible to read.

product.title: Beats Outlook: lighter, crash-free, with a unified inbox
product.plus: Many arrive as refugees from Outlook and stock Gmail: it's lighter, doesn't crash on open, and has the unified inbox Microsoft still never figured out.

product.title: Pricey subscription, in-your-face buy button, no refunds
product.minus: Basic things like rules sit behind a pricey subscription, buy-now pop-ups nag constantly, and the purchase button sits conveniently dead-center — one user accidentally subscribed for 100 dollars and got no refund.

product.title: Updates log you out of accounts and wipe your settings
product.minus: Updates are a recurring source of disaster: the app logs you out of accounts and won't let you back in, drops pinned items, and signs some users out without warning so important mail slips past.

product.title: Responsive support that actually sees a problem through
product.plus: One of the warmest positives is support: they reply fast even to free users, dig into the problem (sometimes not even theirs, but Android WebView), and see it through to a fix.

product.title: Fails to connect certain accounts: Office 365, IMAP, Comcast, Xfinity
product.minus: Hooking up some mailboxes turns into a quest: Office 365 demands admin approval, a plain Gmail IMAP box gets stuck on an old message, and Comcast/Xfinity disconnects daily.

product.title: Notifications just stop working — the whole point of the client
product.minus: The paradox: for all the praise of fast push, some users see notifications (both sound and icon) suddenly die, fail to fire from folders other than the inbox, and the "delete" action in the banner not work.

product.title: A clean, simple interface anyone can figure out
product.plus: What holds many people is the look and feel: a clean, clear interface, handy swipes, pinned messages, customisation — an app that feels like desktop email and works for any skill level.

product.title: Spam is praised and cursed at once — the filter is hit or miss
product.minus: Spam is wildly inconsistent: some praise a great blocker, others drown in spam after installing (porn mailers included) and suspect their address was leaked; filtering catches junk only when it feels like it.

product.title: A subscription bolted on after years: a long-free app suddenly locked behind a paywall
product.minus: People used Spike free for years, then access was cut off without warning and payment demanded — by far the loudest, angriest theme in the reviews.

product.title: Can't even test it: payment is demanded before you ever see the app
product.minus: On first launch you hit a paywall or a forced 7-day trial requiring card details — there's no way to evaluate the product before paying.

product.title: The price feels absurd for personal email
product.minus: For light users reading mail from a couple of people, $30, £8 or £15 a month feels pricier than a whole office suite.

product.title: Accounts get blocked and never restored — people lose access to their own email
product.minus: Even paying subscribers report being locked out and blocked with no reason given, unable to sign back in.

product.title: Charged after cancelling: the money keeps coming out
product.minus: Users cancel but charges keep happening, and refunds only come through their bank or Google.

product.title: Login breaks: sign-in bounces to the browser and loops
product.minus: Entering email and password redirects to Chrome or stalls on authentication, and you just can't get in.

product.title: Crashes, won't sync mail, and loses messages
product.minus: The app crashes, stops syncing, and some emails simply never reach the inbox.

product.title: The chat-style email format is what fans love most
product.plus: Turning emails into a messenger-style thread feels fresh and easy to many — they can't go back to a regular client.

product.title: All accounts and conversations in one place — the headline strength
product.plus: Mail is grouped by sender and pulled into one app, which heavy-volume users especially appreciate.

product.title: Read receipts on emails — a feature singled out for praise
product.plus: Seeing whether the recipient opened your email is called out as one of the most useful, distinctive features.

product.title: AI summaries are liked, but the added AI and chat-bot turned many off
product.plus: The AI email summary and priority grouping genuinely help, though the built-in chat-bot reads as a gimmick and the AI pivot itself alienates some longtime users.

product.title: The email-chat angle made it a magnet for scams and phishing
product.minus: Because it can push messages and invites straight to email, scammers exploit it and victims tie large losses to the platform.

product.title: A favorite channel for staying close to loved ones far away, especially military
product.plus: Many keep Spike specifically for private contact with family and partners far away — for some it's the only link to a spouse on deployment.

product.title: The purchased "lifetime" Pro license is no longer honored, and users are forced to subscribe again
product.minus: Dozens of veterans who paid years ago for a one-time Pro license find, after a phone switch or update, that the license is voided and the app demands a costly yearly subscription for what they already bought. It reads not as a business-model change but as a betrayal of loyal customers.

product.title: Full-screen video ads with no close button block reading email for 30 to 120 seconds
product.minus: In the free version, an unskippable video ad plays for several seconds before each email opens, and the close button is sometimes hidden behind the navigation bar. Users call this unique among email clients and reason enough to uninstall.

product.title: The free version is capped at one mailbox — adding a second account immediately demands payment
product.minus: The core reason to use an email client — managing several mailboxes — is locked behind the subscription: only one account works for free. New users call it deceptive marketing and uninstall before finishing setup.

product.title: Unmatched depth of customization — literally every element can be configured
product.plus: This is Aqua Mail's signature strength and the reason veterans keep coming back after every experiment with rivals: colors, fonts, Wi-Fi vs. data behavior, the bottom action dock, per-account settings. For many it is "the most customizable mail client in existence."

product.title: A decade of reliability — a client that "just works" for years across every new phone
product.plus: The most frequent praise: people have used Aqua Mail for 8 to 15 years, carrying it from phone to phone, and never switch away. Stable sync and predictability make it their decade-long favorite for managing multiple mailboxes.

product.title: Responsive support actually fixes problems and flips ratings from 1 to 5 stars
product.plus: Despite the licensing fiasco, a distinct support team (Martin is often named) replies quickly, explains settings, and restores Pro access — after which users raise their rating right inside the review. For many it is the deciding reason to stay.

product.title: Recent updates break Outlook/Microsoft connectivity and force re-authorization
product.minus: After a given update, Outlook and Hotmail mail stops syncing, the app won't accept the password, and it hangs on the login screen. Especially painful for those who discover it while traveling with no time to re-configure every account.

product.title: Frequent SSL/TLS errors and Gmail access blocked by Google's "sensitive info" wall
product.minus: Users repeatedly hit SSL certificate errors and handshake failures that other clients don't produce, while Gmail accounts get blocked by Google over sensitive-data access. Resetting helps for a couple of days, then the error returns.

product.title: Aggressive trackers, a cookie banner with "legitimate interest" on by default, and constant Play Integrity checks
product.minus: On launch it greets users with a huge list of companies with "legitimate interest" pre-ticked, which must be disabled by hand. On top of that the app constantly hits the Play Integrity API even after verifying — privacy-conscious users call it unprofessional and uninstall.

product.title: The subscription is seen as absurdly expensive for an email app, and the one-time option is gone
product.minus: A price of $9.99/month or $29/year for email reads as greed, especially next to free Gmail, Thunderbird, and K-9. Many would happily pay once but flatly refuse a monthly subscription and leave for rivals.

product.title: Broken spam handling: rules aren't remembered and there's no proper junk folder
product.minus: What you mark as spam isn't blocked next time — the filter has to be reapplied by hand daily, and there's no proper rule-based junk folder. For some users this alone drove the switch to eM Client or BlueMail.

product.title: Reverting to first-letter chips instead of sender avatars and icons broke at-a-glance recognition
product.minus: After an update, sender photos and brand icons in the message list were replaced by a colored chip with just the first letter. For users who chose Aqua Mail specifically for avatars, this removed their main reason to use it.

product.title: Smart Folder and a unified message list across all mailboxes — the favorite feature of multi-account users
product.plus: Seeing mail from every account in one list, plus color-coding for read and unread, makes Aqua Mail a convenient hub for people with multiple domains and mailboxes. Many keep the app specifically for the Smart Folder.

product.title: Frequent crashes and sharp slowdowns after updates: opening an email and syncing take 2 minutes
product.minus: After recent updates the app crashes constantly when switching back to it, sync and opening an email stretch to two minutes, and typing lags by 4 to 5 seconds. Clearing cache and resetting don't help — the problem is unique to Aqua Mail.

product.title: Ad-free privacy is the core reason people stay
product.plus: Users prize the encryption, the absence of ads, and the fact that their data isn't sold or fed to advertisers; for many it's a deliberate exit from Google.

product.title: New-mail notifications arrive late or not at all
product.minus: Even after disabling battery optimization, push barely fires — people miss important emails and only see them by opening the app manually.

product.title: Manual account approval is a Kafkaesque sign-up loop
product.minus: A new account goes to manual review for 24 hours, then they ask you to send an explanatory email — which you can't send because the account isn't approved yet.

product.title: Your IP gets banned before you can even sign up
product.minus: Trying to create an account, the app says the IP is temporarily blocked 'to avoid abuse' — on every network, on mobile data, and even through a VPN.

product.title: The app is sluggish and needs constant manual refreshing
product.minus: The inbox loads slowly and there's no refresh button — to see new mail you have to close and reopen the app.

product.title: Free accounts are deleted after six months of inactivity
product.minus: The 'six months active or deactivated' policy hits free users — people lose important addresses and the accounts tied to them simply for logging in rarely.

product.title: Inbox search is locked behind a paid subscription
product.minus: Basic inbox search — something every email has had for decades — is paywalled, and even for paying users it's poor: indexing takes hours and isn't persistent across devices.

product.title: Mail silently lands in spam with no simple 'not spam' button
product.minus: Mail from banks and shops suddenly starts going to spam, and there's no quick way to send a sender back to the inbox without building rules per address — which themselves hit a paywall.

product.title: Mail vanishes after 31 days — and export only works on desktop
product.minus: Old mail is auto-deleted on the free tier, and the only way to save it is the desktop client — out of reach for mobile and Chromebook users.

product.title: Support is slow — and reserved for paying users
product.minus: Free users get only the FAQ, yet even paying ones report days of silence: ticket after ticket asking for authentication, then nothing back.

product.title: When support does respond, the impression flips to praise
product.plus: For some the experience is the opposite: unbanned in under 10 hours, polite and actual solutions — for them the team and its responsiveness are why they chose Tuta.

product.title: Email import is sold on the Legend plan but doesn't work on Android
product.minus: People pay for Legend to import their mail, then discover import only works in the desktop version — false advertising for anyone on a phone, tablet, or Chromebook.

product.title: Clean, minimalist interface — though some call it dated
product.plus: Many love the calm, no-noise interface — simple, intuitive, with a pleasant theme; that 'easy on the eyes' feel is what keeps them.

product.title: Can't log in: 'invalid credentials' even when the password is right
product.minus: People get abruptly signed out and login returns 'invalid credentials' — even the recovery key fails, and access to the mailbox is lost for good.

product.title: Custom domains and a calm, owned inbox — what people happily pay for
product.plus: Custom-domain support, aliases, a built-in calendar, and a sense of owning your inbox — for many it's reason enough to go paid and back the mission.

product.title: Deleted emails reappear in the inbox
product.minus: The most ingrained mechanical breakage: you hit «delete» and the message stays or comes back seconds later. People delete the same email 4-6 times, then exit the app and re-search to confirm it's gone. Emptying trash fails too — items resurface.

product.title: Screen dims and demands an extra tap after every action
product.minus: After deleting, closing, or exiting a message the screen greys out and freezes, forcing a random tap to wake it. It happens on EVERY email, turning inbox triage into a marathon of needless taps.

product.title: Folders vanished — only the inbox is visible
product.minus: The redesign buried or removed folders: they now take several clicks, and many users are left with only the inbox accessible. Worst of all, the per-folder unread count is gone, gutting auto-filters — you can't tell if new mail arrived without opening every folder.

product.title: Login loops with «Something went wrong»
product.minus: After the update sessions drop, accounts «expire», and logging in spins forever or throws «Something went wrong». Reinstalling doesn't help — the same account works on a second phone. Without a paid plan there's no human support.

product.title: Linked mailboxes keep falling out of sync
product.minus: Logging into the main account used to auto-load linked mailboxes. Now secondary accounts light up with an orange exclamation mark, demand re-login every couple of days, and re-authenticating doesn't stick — you have to log out of everything and clear app data. Linking is pointless now.

product.title: Tap one email, a different one opens
product.minus: The list loads slowly, and tapping a message before it finishes opens a different one — whichever loaded last. Swiping between emails gets stuck between two messages and flashes back and forth uncontrollably; the only escape is force-stop.

product.title: Can't select a few emails — it's all or nothing
product.minus: The long-press to select messages from one sender is gone. Now you can bulk-delete or move ALL emails or none — there's no way to pick five. Swipe-to-move into folders is clunky too and often won't show all folders.

product.title: Ads inside the inbox — with «delete» trapped under a banner
product.minus: Ads wedge between emails and masquerade as emails, blocking swipe-delete. A bottom banner covers messages so they can't be selected. The only way to remove ads is a paid tier — and outside the US the ad-free upgrade is often unavailable at all.

product.title: Storage slashed — pay up or lose access
product.minus: A sudden, unannounced storage cut locked out 20-plus-year loyal users and pushes them toward a paid plan. Many read it bluntly as a tactic: break deletion and shove Yahoo+ to squeeze out money.

product.title: Streaks, a planner and AI instead of just reading mail
product.minus: Gamification in an email app infuriates: a daily streak, achievements, an intrusive holiday planner bar at the bottom covering the mail tools, and AI features shoved in where people just want to read and delete. Meanwhile the genuinely useful «remind» feature was removed.

product.title: On tablets half the screen is empty space
product.minus: The new layout was clearly phone-first: on tablets the email squeezes into a narrow column beside a huge empty space or a grey block covering half the screen. The preview pane shows «no email selected», making reading physically hard.

product.title: Lag and freezes scrolling the inbox
product.minus: After the redesign the app turned sluggish even on flagships: the inbox shows unread mail after 10 seconds, scrolling stutters and glitches up and down, and oversensitive swipes accidentally archive and delete messages. Sometimes it just spins and won't open.

product.title: The list won't sort by date and hides emails
product.minus: Yahoo now decides what to show: open the app and month-old emails sit on top, with the latest buried below. New mail «randomly» doesn't load, so you think you cleared the inbox until older ones surface. Search is broken on top of it — it won't find by keyword.

product.title: 20-plus years of loyalty — and first-ever thoughts of leaving for Gmail
product.minus: A through-line: people with mailboxes since the 90s stuck with Yahoo for its simplicity, not love. One update broke that inertia — users are migrating mail to Thunderbird and Gmail and cancelling Pro. The brand's strength is tenure, but that's exactly what makes the betrayal sting.

product.title: The developer talks down to negative reviewers
product.minus: A distinct sore point is the tone of official replies: users find them passive-aggressive and condescending — «get used to the changes». People explicitly say Yahoo's response to the backlash («we're listening» while changing nothing) repels them more than the bugs themselves.

product.title: For its faithful it still «just works»
product.plus: Amid the pile-on there's a quiet core for whom Yahoo Mail stays convenient and familiar: easy setup, years of reliable service, disposable addresses right in the app, and — for many — none of Gmail's painful storage limits. This is the very inertia that held the audience for decades.

product.title: Accurate GPS replaces a rangefinder out of the box
product.plus: The headline reason people love it: yardages match a rangefinder within five yards, and it works for free on any course.

product.title: Every hole greets you with a "buy Premium" pop-up
product.minus: The upsell is baked into play itself: pop-ups, contact-import prompts and an upgrade nag at every turn make the app feel like "one giant ad".

product.title: Android watches are a second-class citizen next to Apple Watch
product.minus: Automatic shot detection and accurate tracking only work on Apple Watch; on Wear OS / Galaxy / Pixel the watch drops the session, won't connect, or gives only basic distances — driving people to Golf Shot.

product.title: "Smart" shot tracking logs phantom swings
product.minus: The new Smart Tracking that replaced the old manual mode invents extra shots on every stop and clusters pins around the green — users beg for the old logic back and can't turn it off.

product.title: The free version is generous and fully usable
product.plus: Many play for years on the free tier alone: GPS, scorecard, score-keeping and a handicap are all available without paying and with minimal ads.

product.title: The subscription auto-charges quietly after the "free" trial
product.minus: The 7-day trial demands a card, the promised pre-charge warning never comes, the annual fee ($99 / £90) is taken without notice, and refunds are refused — even when the app was never used.

product.title: Support goes silent and ignores tickets for years
product.minus: Paying users wait months for a reply: dozens of unanswered tickets, scripted brush-offs, courses never fixed — leaving the impression the app is abandoned.

product.title: The app closes itself between shots
product.minus: A common Android complaint: advancing to the next hole freezes the app or kills it in the background, forcing you to reopen it via "recents" each time just to see yardage.

product.title: The social feed and leagues make the round shared
product.plus: A favourite of regulars: watching friends' rounds in real time, running leagues and skins, following the leaderboard — "the Facebook of golf".

product.title: A dark, dim screen is unreadable in bright sun
product.minus: Grey text on a dark background (apparently to save battery) makes the app nearly unreadable in sunny on-course conditions — especially on Samsung watches.

product.title: A cluttered interface hides the basics
product.minus: It "does everything except the basics": finding a past scorecard is impossible, it jumps between holes on its own, and with no indication of which hole you're on, scores land in the wrong place.

product.title: The AI swing analyzer doesn't work and can't be trusted
product.minus: The paid feature either won't upload a video with no error at all, or returns dubious scores — one user fed it Fred Couples' swing and got an 8 out of 11.

product.title: On Android watches the app falls apart: «start round on phone», crashes, or «loading» instead of yardage
product.minus: The whole reason people install it — glance at distance on the watch without pulling out the phone — barely works on Wear OS / Galaxy / Pixel. The watch hangs on «loading», crashes when starting a round, demands «open on phone» even after the round was started, and stops showing yardage after 5-7 holes. On the phone, meanwhile, it's fine.

product.title: The hole flyover and visual distance map are what keep people for years
product.plus: The warmest thread in the reviews: the flyover view of the hole, distance to the green center and to hazards laid out on one screen, accurate yardage. Many call it «the best golf GPS I've tried», stay subscribed for 10-15 years and recommend it to friends.

product.title: Paid for «lifetime» — now they demand a yearly subscription; many feel cheated
product.minus: Buyers of the old lifetime / Pro licenses flatly call it a scam: the app stopped recognizing their purchase and keeps pushing an upgrade. People who promoted Golfshot for years say they no longer will.

product.title: Trashy game ads on every launch — even for paying subscribers
product.minus: A recent wave: after an update, an unskippable ad for a cheap game shows on launch. It annoys free users, but most of all the paying ones who still see it; some cancel the subscription and delete the account over it.

product.title: The watch logs the shots, then the phone wipes the whole scorecard at round's end
product.minus: A brutal sync bug: a player walks all 18 holes logging on the watch, then the app shows no shots and no score. For people who rarely get a full round in, it stings — the round is gone for good.

product.title: Support adds a new course in hours and actually fixes bugs — a beloved part
product.plus: A sharp contrast to the complaints: when support does respond, the praise is genuine. Email a photo of the scorecard and the course appears the next day; they migrated 400 rounds to a new address; they fixed broken scorecards within a week.

product.title: And when support goes silent, it stays silent for weeks — especially to «free» users
product.minus: The flip side: tickets get closed unresolved, replies are off-topic boilerplate, and some suspect they're ignored for not paying. Cases drag on for months with no reply.

product.title: The watch won't auto-advance the hole — you reach for the phone every shot
product.minus: Auto-advance to the next hole doesn't work on Android: you either pick the hole manually, or the app goes to «sleep» between holes and must be restarted after a loading screen. Starting on the 10th tee often ends the round instead of looping back to hole 1.

product.title: The free tier is generous — distance, scorecard and stats with no payment
product.plus: For many the free version is more than enough: yardage to the green center, scorekeeping, stats and hole flyovers without a subscription. People use the free tier for years and call it a «super bargain».

product.title: The course can't be found — blank outside your home state or country
product.minus: Travel breaks the app: at home every course is there, but in another state or country it «can't find the course», search fails — while a friend in the same group has it. It hits paying users hardest, who counted on coverage while traveling.

product.title: Can't get past login: «account created but login failed» at the door
product.minus: Some users never reach the golf at all: the account is created but login errors out, Facebook sign-in fails, and those without Facebook are locked out entirely. Reinstalls and password resets don't help — they uninstall on the spot.

product.title: Stableford and non-US handicaps miscalculate (UK/AUS/WHS)
product.minus: Outside the US the math breaks: an extra shot on Stableford holes, no way to enter a playing handicap, no link to the WHS/CDH index, and the handicap on the scorecard changing on its own. Paying UK and Australian users flatly say they won't renew.

product.title: The data and analytics are the one thing that keeps people hooked
product.plus: Even in furious reviews the same line recurs: the stats, per-club distances, SG and caddie advice genuinely help — players shave several strokes off their handicap and forgive the system a pile of bugs for it.

product.title: Shot tracking misses strokes, so you play with your nose in the phone
product.minus: The most frequent pain: sensors and Link either miss strokes or invent phantom/other-people's ones and muddle holes. Instead of playing, you check and fix the score after every hole — the very chore the automation was meant to remove.

product.title: Android is a second-class citizen at the same price as iOS
product.minus: They pay the same $200 a year, yet Green Maps, AI features, social features and proper watch tracking are iPhone-only. Support flatly confirms there's no plan for iOS parity.

product.title: Subscription trap: annual-only, cancel by email, charges after you've cancelled
product.minus: The free trial takes card details "for shipping" and quietly enrols you in annual auto-renew; you can't cancel in-app — only by emailing support, and people still get charged hundreds of dollars after cancelling.

product.title: The new UI update broke what worked: editing a round is nearly impossible
product.minus: After the big redesign the app lags, crashes, ends rounds mid-play and lost the tap-and-hold distance measure. And because the missed shots force constant edits, the clunky editor hurts twice as much.

product.title: The WearOS watch went from caddie to bare rangefinder (or just broke)
product.minus: It worked for a year — then an update stripped score, putts and points down to just distance-to-green, and for many the watch shows gibberish or a black screen entirely. For a system meant to keep the phone in your pocket, that's critical.

product.title: The caddie and smart distances feel like magic when they fire
product.plus: When the caddie recommendation works it factors in wind, elevation and your shot history and hands you a club you want to trust — players describe it as "a caddie on your shoulder" and beat personal bests.

product.title: "Ask Caddie" often returns an error and the club tip vanishes after a couple of shots
product.minus: The very feature people pay premium for is hit-or-miss: on Android the club recommendation disappears after a couple of holes and the caddie button throws "caddie error" most times you tap it. Support calls it a known bug.

product.title: Pricing stings and there's no monthly plan — northern players pay for downtime
product.minus: The $150–200 is billed all at once with no monthly option, so people who only play half the year (Canada, northern US, UK) effectively pay double per season. Many say they'd stay for $10–15/month.

product.title: Pairing clubs and creating an account is a struggle before round one
product.minus: Onboarding breaks at the gate: the sign-up form hangs on an error, sensors duplicate or won't pair, and the app refuses to record a round unless 8–10 clubs are paired — even if you only bought a couple of sensors.

product.title: Ad notifications you can't turn off without breaking the app
product.minus: Paying subscribers get weekly marketing pushes that can't be silenced: the app requires notifications enabled to function, so the choice is "tolerate the ads" or "don't use it".

product.title: Drains phone and watch battery, sometimes even with the round closed
product.minus: Constant GPS and a background process drain a 95%-charged phone by the end of 18 holes, and the watch loses battery even without an active round — some don't make it past the 15th hole.

product.title: Outdated satellite course maps and slow support to fix them
product.minus: Home-course maps can be snow-covered, blurry or missing the green overlay, and support takes months to update them — even asking the player to mark the greens and bunkers themselves, which stings at a premium price.

product.title: Support and product win praise once it finally works flawlessly
product.plus: For a chunk of players the system catches 90–95% of shots, the Link or belt clip works almost flawlessly and support resolves issues — and then the review flips to "game changer" and a recommendation to buddies.

product.title: The watch is the core pain: the app freezes, shows no yardage and keeps losing sync with the phone
product.minus: The phone version works well for many, but on smartwatches (Galaxy, Pixel, OnePlus) the app freezes after a couple of holes, shows blank yardage, drops sync or won't launch at all — the very reason people bought Pro.

product.title: Basic score entry on the watch was moved behind a paid subscription — long-time users are furious
product.minus: After an update, watch scoring and yardages — free since the very beginning — got locked behind a ~$60/yr subscription, with patch notes saying only "bug fixes". People who relied on exactly that for years are uninstalling en masse.

product.title: Sign-up is a minefield: "country must be a string" and "general error" block people from even logging in
product.minus: Many can't get past the sign-up screen on Android: creating a username throws "the country must be a string" (with no country field anywhere), or "General Error", or the verification email never arrives.

product.title: Phone GPS is the headline strength: accurate yardage replaces a rangefinder
product.plus: The top reason people love the app is fast, accurate GPS yardage with satellite hole maps: users ditch their rangefinders and praise the graphics and accuracy down to a couple of yards.

product.title: Rounds and scores vanish: a finished round disappears, the back nine gets lost
product.minus: A serious data-loss fear: people finish 18 holes only for the whole round to vanish or fail to upload; the back nine disappears; guest scores get wiped at the end. For an app whose whole point is scorekeeping, that's critical.

product.title: Social features and GHIN linkage are what keep people loyal
product.plus: A strong hook: people follow friends' rounds, run leagues and push scores straight to GHIN for an official USGA handicap without club membership. Many get their whole golf group to install it.

product.title: Crashes after updates: black screen, endless loading, the phone gets bricked
product.minus: After successive updates the app stops opening: a black screen with the logo, endless "Where golf happens" loading, crashes on club selection or starting a round, and for some the phone freezes for a couple of minutes.

product.title: The interface got overloaded: the new UI is too "busy", yardage shrunk into a corner in tiny font
product.minus: The redesign is seen as a step back: the screen is cluttered with shot lines and numbers, distance-to-green was pushed into a corner in a tiny font you can't read without eagle vision. Many preferred the old simplicity.

product.title: Auto-starting at par and being unable to fix a hole break score entry
product.minus: Score entry is annoying by design: the app won't auto-advance and silently logs a par, records a stroke on the wrong hole, and a mistaken score often can't be edited or deleted. The back nine won't open until every front-nine score is entered.

product.title: Stats and game history are a genuine draw: you can see what to work on
product.plus: Enthusiasts praise the detailed stats — putts, GIR, fairway accuracy and round-over-round breakdowns; for them it's a tool to improve their game and a reason they keep years of history.

product.title: The trial charges the full fee, and there's nowhere to cancel
product.minus: Billing behaves aggressively: the trial immediately takes the full annual fee, there's nowhere in the app to cancel a subscription, and refunds get denied — some lost $60 this way.

product.title: Support often comes through and onboards courses, but goes silent on watch bugs for months
product.plus: Support is often a high point: responsive replies, refunds secured, home courses onboarded quickly and bugs confirmed. But on watch breakages the answer is the same for years — "we're working on it" — with no fix.

product.title: A sudden price jump punishes long-time loyal users
product.minus: People who paid $20-25 for years are suddenly asked to renew at $99-170 — a two-, three-, even fourfold hike with no visible reason, and they leave en masse for Hole19, 18Birdies and others.

product.title: After the update you can't enter scores — the card sticks on one hole
product.minus: The headline breakage of the new version: entering a score throws you back to the first player or hole one, won't advance, and back-nine scores often don't save at all.

product.title: Accurate tap-the-screen GPS rangefinder is the main reason to love it
product.plus: Distances to the front, middle and back of the green check out against friends' rangefinders "within a yard or two," and tapping anywhere on the course to get a distance is a favorite feature.

product.title: After the update the app just won't open — endless spinner
product.minus: For many the app stops launching entirely: a spinning circle, an "error" or "gateway timeout"; the only fix is uninstall and reinstall — every single round.

product.title: Relentless email spam you can't unsubscribe from
product.minus: Daily emails, an unsubscribe button that does nothing, support tickets that don't help — users call it a privacy violation and delete the app specifically over the email bombardment.

product.title: Cancelling is hidden or broken — "cancel anytime" is a lie
product.minus: "Manage subscription" leads nowhere or to a Google Play with no control, auto-renew comes back after being turned off, and people find they've been billed for years with no way to cancel from the phone.

product.title: The watch is useless — distance comes from the phone, not the watch
product.minus: People buy in for the watch app, but distance won't update unless the phone is nearby with the app open in the foreground — defeating the entire point of a wearable.

product.title: The update stripped free features and career-long stats
product.minus: Beloved free features — drive direction, putt totals, the detailed scorecard, lifetime stats over hundreds of rounds — got hidden behind a paywall or removed entirely; veterans feel robbed.

product.title: Huge course database and fast fixes on user request
product.plus: The app finds nearly any course worldwide — some have used it 10-15 years — and when a course is missing or scores are off, support often fixes it within a day and ships a new version.

product.title: Ads before a hole crash the app and disrupt score entry
product.minus: On the free tier a pop-up ad before the 9th/18th hole crashes the app, and the slow ad refresh wipes the score you just entered — you can't get back to the hole you're playing.

product.title: GPS, elevation and club recommendations broke after the update
product.minus: Once-accurate distances now drift randomly, elevation shows an absurd −55 yards on every shot, and the "plays like" club recommendation goes wrong — the very thing the app was prized for.

product.title: Aggressive paywall pop-ups and charges with no confirmation
product.minus: A $49 upgrade ad on every tap, choosing "free" ends in a charge, a sneaky $1.95 music add-on, and during upgrade it's easy to buy the wrong tier by accident with no refund.

product.title: Easy, fast interface — "like having a caddie"
product.plus: Simple intuitive scoring, the ability to jump to any hole when you skip one, good satellite course maps, and round tracking with a handicap — many play every round with it for years.

product.title: Heavy battery drain from constantly flickering location
product.minus: Since the update location flickers on and off and drains the phone within a couple of hours — especially on Samsung; some players have to carry a power bank for 18 holes.

product.title: The watch is the core pain: distance freezes, loses sync, falls asleep
product.minus: People buy the app specifically for the watch, yet on Galaxy and Pixel watches it freezes mid-round, stops updating yardage, loses sync with the phone, and forces a watch restart every few holes.

product.title: The watch app won't stay on screen — you must reopen it for every shot
product.minus: The watch screen sleeps or the app minimizes, so you have to reopen it by hand after every shot — awkward with a glove on, and some users end up pulling out the phone on every hole instead.

product.title: Recent updates set the app back — features and stability regressed
product.minus: Long-time users say in unison that recent updates broke what worked: removed Clubhouse Details, Stableford, shot editing, scorecard readability — and added crashes.

product.title: Scoring jumps between holes on its own and loses entered data
product.minus: The app jumps to the wrong hole when you try to enter a score, mismatches the hole number against the displayed data, and sometimes wipes scores you already entered — trust in the scorecard collapses.

product.title: The subscription is pushed, auto-charges, and is nearly impossible to cancel
product.minus: Users report auto-renewals without consent, charges after cancelling, and that cancelling or reaching the company is extremely hard — some were billed without ever signing up for premium.

product.title: Advertised as "free" but premium-priced in reality — and the price keeps rising
product.minus: Sign-up leads straight to payment, the subscription isn't disclosed upfront, and the premium price jumps (£39.99 → £59.99, up to £99/year) and differs from what other users see.

product.title: Support goes silent, while login and registration break
product.minus: Support often goes unanswered for weeks, while login won't accept the password or let you reset it, and registration throws "something went wrong" — locking people out of an app they've used for years.

product.title: Spam emails and intrusive ads on top of the round
product.minus: After install you get a flood of emails you can't unsubscribe from even after a dozen tries, and ads pop up right while you're entering scores.

product.title: Phone GPS yardage is accurate and the free tier is generous
product.plus: On the thing that matters most — distance to the green — the app is praised for accurate front/middle/back yardage, a clear hole map, and a free tier that gives distances and basic scoring on any course, even small ones.

product.title: When the watch works, it's the beloved use case: yardage on the wrist without the phone
product.plus: For those whose watch works, this is the whole point: GPS right on the wrist, no need to pull the phone between shots, battery lasts 18 holes, and the free tier gives smartwatch distances even disconnected from the phone.

product.title: Course coverage is huge, and support fills gaps fast
product.plus: Almost any course is on the app, including small municipal and rural ones; if a course is missing or has changed, a remapping request is often done in under a day — a service users single out for praise.

product.title: Android and the watch stay second-class to iPhone
product.minus: Some premium features — club recommendations, score entry from the watch, slope-corrected distance — are missing or half-baked on Android and the watch, while iPhone gets the full experience.

product.title: Starting a round demands a handicap and extra steps
product.minus: Just to start a round the app demands a handicap and extra setup; the start button stays greyed out, and some can't play at all without a WHS handicap — when all they want is scoring and yardage.

product.title: The phone interface is pleasant but confusing without instructions
product.minus: The look is liked, but navigation isn't obvious: it's unclear how to change holes or record scores, there are no clear instructions — newcomers spend ages figuring it out, and some leave for clearer competitors.

product.title: The watch can't hold GPS — phone's in your pocket but no yardage
product.minus: The single most common pain: on Samsung and Galaxy watches the app endlessly «waits for location» or drops GPS mid-round even when other apps connect fine. People close and reopen the app dozens of times a round just to get a distance, and having the phone in their pocket doesn't help.

product.title: It used to be free — now you pay for it
product.minus: Long-time users are furious: yardages, handicap and watch support that were standard for years got moved behind premium. Many call it greed and say this is their last season with the app.

product.title: As accurate as a laser rangefinder — at a third of the price
product.plus: The core thing people love: distances match a pricey laser rangefinder within a yard or two, all for $30 a year. Many leave their rangefinders at home, treating the app as a full replacement for pennies.

product.title: GPS sometimes lies — 999 yards instead of the real distance
product.minus: Against the general accuracy, a subset see wildly wrong distances: 999 yards to the hole, or a fixed 206 yards regardless of position — and you don't catch it right away, which defeats the whole point of a rangefinder.

product.title: Tags and shot tracking — like a caddy in your pocket
product.plus: Golf Pad Tags and shot tracking break the game down: you see shot dispersion, where you're losing strokes, and club recommendations. Beginners learn their distances, experienced players shave 2-3 strokes a round.

product.title: Phone in your pocket auto-swipes holes and adds phantom strokes
product.minus: Accidental touches through the pocket: the app jumps between holes on its own, logs phantom strokes and adds random clubs, sometimes «finishing» a round while still in the pocket. There's no confirmation before changing holes.

product.title: Support is the real ace: fixes in a day, customizes courses for you
product.plus: Even among critics, many praise support by name (Stacy, Darya, Alexandra): fast replies, custom tournament tees added, course errors fixed in a day or two. For many it's the reason they stay.

product.title: Billing bites: triple charges, a trial trap, no way to cancel
product.minus: Money complaints stand on their own: charges after cancelling, being billed three times for one year, a hidden trial-cancel button, and a card-update error there's no way past. People call it a scam.

product.title: It no longer calculates your handicap — now pay GHIN/USGA on top
product.minus: A painful loss for long-time players: the app stopped calculating handicap from round data, and now you pay GHIN/USGA separately on top of the subscription. Competitors include it in the price.

product.title: Direct score posting to GHIN/USGA — built-in handicap reporting
product.plus: A recent feature praised as one of the best improvements: round scores post straight to your USGA/GHIN account with no manual entry. For many it's what won back their love for the app.

product.title: Best price on the market — cheaper than Arccos, 18 Birdies and Grint
product.plus: Compared to rivals, users are unanimous: $30/year is a bargain. Arccos costs multiples and needs hardware, 18 Birdies drains the watch battery, and Grint charges $60 — Golf Pad gives more for less.

product.title: Maps and hole flyovers save you on unfamiliar courses
product.plus: Satellite imagery and per-hole flyovers help you pick your line and get distances to obstacles on courses you've never played — and maps can be downloaded for playing abroad offline.

product.title: Doesn't auto-advance holes — forget once and your card breaks
product.minus: An annoying gap: the app doesn't advance to the next hole automatically, and if you forget to switch, your score lands on the wrong hole. For some, the back nine shows holes as 1-9 instead of 10-18.

product.title: Every update fixes one thing and breaks another — especially on Galaxy
product.minus: A systemic gripe: updates ship half-baked, breaking previously working functions on Galaxy watches, and you only find out on the course. Strokes gained sits «under construction» for months, maps load slowly.

product.title: An update moved features bought outright behind a paid subscription
product.minus: People who bought premium or a lifetime unlock years ago lost markup, swing comparison and pro models after the update — now it only works under a $59–99 annual subscription, with no way back to the old version.

product.title: Years of saved videos and lessons vanished after the update
product.minus: Coaches and players report en masse that the update wiped all or nearly all of their swings, lessons and comparisons — some lost thousands of recordings built up over a decade.

product.title: On Android the app crashes and freezes constantly
product.minus: The Android build feels abandoned next to iOS: black camera screen, crashes on recording and editing, freezes when comparing, low fps and broken import on Samsung, Pixel and other devices.

product.title: Cancelling the subscription is near-impossible and refunds don't happen
product.minus: They charge during the "free" trial, hide auto-renewal, never show the subscription date, drag cancellation out over days of emails — then refuse refunds citing the terms, even when you cancel within hours.

product.title: An intrusive "upgrade to Pro" screen blocks every action
product.minus: Tap anything — draw a line, import a video, analyze a swing — and the upgrade banner pops up; newcomers can't even see what the app does and uninstall within minutes.

product.title: Account creation and login often fail with errors
product.minus: Sign-up is mandatory but the form throws nameless errors, password reset fails, and after a forced update people are logged out and told their account doesn't exist — even though they paid for it.

product.title: Importing and recording video frequently just fails
product.minus: Imported clips won't open or crash, trimming fails, orientation flips, and importing your own footage is now locked behind paid V1+ — breaking the core swing-analysis workflow.

product.title: Human support rescues the app from almost any hole
product.plus: Don, Lynn, JT and Mathew reply in minutes rather than days, recover lost lessons, fix logins and often refund payments unprompted — it's the human support that keeps loyalty alive.

product.title: As a swing trainer the app genuinely drives improvement
product.plus: Recording, slow-motion, frame-by-frame and markup expose the gap between what a player thinks and actually does — users report real gains in ball-striking and scores.

product.title: The coach link and pro-swing library are the standout value
product.plus: A coach records a lesson and sends it straight into the app, the student replays it endlessly, and comparing your own swing against tour models is motivating and shows exactly what to fix.

product.title: Notification spam and in-app ads bury even paying users
product.minus: Promo notifications flood the inbox with hundreds of messages and cover the lesson screen, and ads pop up even on premium accounts, sometimes with no visible close button.

product.title: The watch won't connect to the phone — the central pain
