product.minus: By far the most common complaint: the Bluetooth link between watch and app works maybe half the time. People spend days and dozens of attempts trying to pair, restarting the phone and reinstalling the app — and without that link the hardware is often useless.

product.title: Rounds fail to sync — and the data is lost for good
product.minus: The round transfer reaches 100% then fails with an error, or the app says "synced" but the round never appears. Worst case the data just vanishes and a played round is gone forever.

product.title: Editing a round crashes the app over and over
product.minus: Because the sensors miss shots, every round needs manual editing afterward — and the app crashes mid-edit, often on hole 17 or 18, wiping all the work. People save after every single hole just to avoid starting over.

product.title: The club sensors miss 10+ shots a round
product.minus: The headline feature — automatic tracking via club tags — works poorly: it catches barely half the shots, worst of all on pitches and chips. You often have to physically touch the club to the watch, which defeats the whole point of hands-free tracking.

product.title: After an update — a white screen and a dead app
product.minus: Time and again a new update breaks what worked for years: the app won't open, shows a blank white screen with "Welcome back", or just force-closes on launch. Hardware you paid for instantly becomes a useless bangle.

product.title: Firmware updates stall at 99% and never finish
product.minus: Firmware updates are their own torture: the process hangs at 0% or freezes at 99%, and the watch won't let you play until it completes. People delete and reinstall, swap phones — no luck, a brand-new tracker can't even get past initial setup.

product.title: The core value — stats and strokes gained, no subscription
product.plus: For those who got it connected, the data is a revelation: strokes gained, average distances per club, the exact weak spots in their game. And it's all free with no annual subscription — exactly why people leave Arccos and Garmin and drop their handicap by 8 strokes.

product.title: When it works — the best GPS+tracker for the money
product.plus: The watch itself draws constant praise: accurate GPS, a clear screen, long battery life, detailed hole mapping. Against pricier rivals, Shot Scope delivers the same GPS-plus-tracking combo for noticeably less — low cost of entry, high payoff.

product.title: Support is responsive and adds course maps fast
product.plus: Support gets warm mentions: course-mapping requests are handled in a day or two, missing courses get added, beginners get help. For many it's this human service that offsets the software glitches and keeps them in the ecosystem.

product.title: The maps glitch: zoom resets, position jumps hundreds of yards
product.minus: The GPS map has a mind of its own: it zooms all the way out, drops the player in Greenland or 400 yards from their real spot, and takes 5-10 seconds to update. On the hole this kills the pace of play and forces constant re-zooming.

product.title: The interface ignores metric — it shows everything in yards
product.minus: Players who use metres are stuck: the app stubbornly shows distances in yards even when the watch and website are set to metric, and the setting reverts entirely in edit mode. For non-US golfers it makes the numbers useless.

product.title: Your local course is missing — and it depends on Google Maps
product.minus: Some users can't find their course at all: it sits in "Being Mapped" status for months or is simply absent, especially outside English-speaking countries. And support explains the mapping depends on Google Maps imagery — the course updates only when Google's images do.

product.title: Basic features moved behind a paywall — and longtime users are leaving
product.minus: By far the most common complaint: things that were free for years — group games, adding players, HCP rounds, basic stats — now require a Gold subscription. People say outright they're switching to competitors.

product.title: GPS rangefinder is paid yet frequently wrong
product.minus: GPS is locked behind payment while rivals give it free, and when it does run it confuses holes, sends you to the wrong tee box, or pins you on a different course. No front/middle/back option.

product.title: Sign-up is broken: «bad request» and you can't decline notifications
product.minus: Many simply can't create an account — declining notifications throws a «bad request» or «something went wrong» error and setup won't continue. The forced mandatory login annoys people on its own.

product.title: The subscription jumps in price and is hard to cancel
product.minus: Prices leap (from £4 to £15/mo, from $25 to $80), people get charged more than promised, and cancellation is buried so deep they delete the account to stop paying. Double-charges and refused refunds too.

product.title: Lag, freezes and crashes on Android
product.minus: It freezes mid-round, crashes on launch and lags through menus — especially on Samsung and Pixel. Often only a reinstall helps, which is maddening on the course.

product.title: A long influencer splash screen slows every action
product.minus: Before every interaction — entering scores, checking distance — a 5+ second loading screen with YouTube golfers appears. Longtime users feel the «influencer» turn has bloated and slowed the app.

product.title: Forced fullscreen mode hides the navigation buttons
product.minus: The app runs in a forced fullscreen mode, so on Samsung its on-screen buttons sit on top of Android's system buttons — some options simply can't be reached.

product.title: Ads even after paying
product.minus: The free version is buried in ads and slow menus, but the real sting is that ads remain even for paying Gold users — and support ignores the complaints.

product.title: No smartwatch support — a recurring request
product.minus: The top feature request: a client for Wear OS, Samsung Galaxy Watch, Garmin and Pixel Watch. Several say they'd subscribe outright if a watch were supported.

product.title: The live group leaderboard is what people love it for
product.plus: The core strength: on tournaments, golf trips and big groups everyone sees each other's scores live and can follow other flights. For group play it's best in class.

product.title: Easy score entry and clear stats to analyze your game
product.plus: Happy users praise the easy score entry instead of a paper card and the clear stats — fairways, GIR, putts, chips — that help spot weak areas and improve.

product.title: Lots of game formats — but people want even more
product.plus: A rich set of formats — Ryder Cup, skins, Stableford, better ball — makes rounds more varied and fun, and the new Ryder Cup mode draws special praise. Still, many ask for yet more formats and individual games.

product.title: The main timer screen won't load — a blank white screen instead of the fast
product.minus: The single most common complaint: on open, the main timer screen simply doesn't render — a white/blank box where the current fast should be. Reinstalling, clearing cache and rebooting the phone don't help.

product.title: You have to open and close the app several times just to start or end a fast
product.minus: To simply start or stop a fast, people have to close and reopen the app 3–20 times and wait for minutes. It defeats the whole point of a real-time timer.

product.title: A simple timer suddenly needs the internet to end a fast
product.minus: The app syncs with its servers for every action, so without a connection you can't even stop a fast to eat. Users rightly point out a timer should work offline.

product.title: The free timer is locked behind a full-screen subscription popup with no close button
product.minus: On launch a plan-selection banner covers the whole screen and reappears after you dismiss it — sometimes with no X to close it. A new user literally can't reach the app without entering a card.

product.title: "Google said it was free" — but inside it asks for $70 a year
product.minus: The app is presented as free, but basic features are locked behind a pricey subscription (~$70/yr, $10/mo). People fill out a personal questionnaire only to learn they can't use it without paying.

product.title: Once-free features were moved behind the paywall one by one
product.minus: Long-time free users describe basic things being gradually taken away: the length of each fast in the calendar, monthly/yearly hour totals. They're left able to "just see hours of a fast."

product.title: The once-clean timer bloated with features you can't turn off
product.minus: Veterans recall a simple "timer plus calendar" app and complain it now pushes food, water, steps and ring-goals with no way to hide them. The bloat slows launch and buries the core view.

product.title: You can't edit or delete a past fast — the "overlaps" bug
product.minus: The edit icon is there but does nothing: you can't fix a time, delete an accidental one-minute fast, or back-date a fast. Changing a time throws an error claiming it overlaps an existing fast.

product.title: Streaks, badges and milestones don't get credited
product.minus: The motivational mechanic — a key draw — is buggy: multi-day streaks reset, badges stick at "1 fast" or repeat, and achievements only return after a full reinstall.

product.title: It "used to work flawlessly" — the classic post-update decay story
product.minus: Dozens of multi-year users tell the same arc: for years it was fast and clean, they gave it 5 stars and recommended it — then recent updates made it slow, buggy and unusable.

product.title: Charges don't match the price shown: $3.99 on screen, $69.99 off the account
product.minus: Several users report surprise charges far above the plan they picked, and being unable to cancel inside the app — they have to unsubscribe via Google, with only an AI bot for support.

product.title: When it works, the best simple fasting tracker — genuinely drives weight loss
product.plus: Despite the bugs, the app has a deeply loyal base: a clean interface, a clear progress wheel, time-passed/time-left toggle and day/month tracking helped people lose dozens of pounds and stay disciplined for years.

product.title: Good support — sometimes fixes bugs within a couple of hours
product.plus: Some users praise the team: emails get quick replies, certain bugs (like a login issue) were fixed by the developers in under two hours, and people bumped their rating from 2 stars back to 5.

product.title: The top feature request — a smartwatch app (Wear OS / Samsung / Garmin)
product.minus: Even happy users dock a star over the missing watch app and the lack of real sync with Fitbit, Garmin, Samsung Health and Health Connect — weight, sleep and step data don't pull in automatically.

product.title: Every action in the free version triggers an ad
product.minus: Start a fast — ad, end a fast — ad, log a single food item — ad. The videos are long, often unskippable or looping, and the only way out is to close and reopen the app. What used to be a simple timer is now unusable unless you pay.

product.title: Marketed as free, but useless without a subscription
product.minus: The ad and the store say "100% free," but inside even basic features are locked behind a subscription. To see the app at all you must add a card and start a 3-day trial. People feel lied to and uninstall on the spot.

product.title: A long onboarding quiz before the paywall is revealed
product.minus: Setup means 10–30 minutes of questions about personal data, goals and habits, and only at the very end do you learn the app is paid. Many just wanted a fasting timer and were marched through a survey straight into a payment screen.

product.title: You can't cancel — the Manage Subscription screen spins forever
product.minus: The most painful complaint: trying to cancel, the management page just spins endlessly. The subscription is missing from Google Play, support stays silent, and money keeps being taken. Users flatly call it a scam.

product.title: Charges after cancelling, double billing and refused refunds
product.minus: People get charged for an annual plan after cancelling, billed twice after an account merge, hit with $29.99 after declining renewal. Refunds don't come, support sends canned replies and goes in circles — some end up disputing the charge with their bank.

product.title: The AI food scanner and food database are often wrong on calories
product.minus: Photo recognition and the database miscount calories: a double Whopper with cheese shows "266 calories for 100g," the same sandwich reads 475 one day and 1079 the next. The database is small, barcodes won't scan, and you fix everything by hand — which defeats the very feature people paid Plus for.

product.title: Used to be a beloved simple tracker — updates bloated it
product.minus: Long-time users (2–3 years, tens of thousands of fasting hours) mourn: it was a clean, easy timer app and is now bloated with AI slop, ads and upsells. The new interface is called chaotic, and people are leaving for Easy Fast, Cronometer, FatSecret.

product.title: Aggressive tracking: hundreds of ad partners, no "deny all" button
product.minus: Data goes to 300+ external partners; there's an "accept all" but no "deny all," so you uncheck boxes by hand for minutes. Declining "legitimate interest" doesn't save, and paid users are told the only way to stop data sharing is to delete the account.

product.title: The fasting tracker with body-stage visuals is what people love most
product.plus: The fasting timer is the reason people stay: it reminds you when to start and end your window, shows what stage your body is in (ketosis, autophagy), and gamifies the process. Even critics admit it beats rivals at its core job.

product.title: Photo calorie counting — when it works, it delights
product.plus: The same AI feature that infuriates when wrong is a favorite for many: snap a photo of your plate and get the macros, no manual entry. Some users call the scanner "amazingly accurate" and stay specifically for it.

product.title: Real weight-loss results — tens of pounds, kept off
product.plus: The warmest reviews are about results: people lose 20, 50, 56 pounds, one user 100 over two years, and keep it off. The app gives structure, motivation and habit, and for many it's the only thing that has ever worked.

product.title: All-in-one: fasting, calories, water, steps, recipes and education
product.plus: For happy users it's not just a timer but one health hub: fasting, calories and macros, water, steps, recipes with a ready shopping list, and an "academy" of lessons on doing IF right. They love that it's all in one place and teaches as you go.

product.title: Three years of asking for an Android fasting widget — still none
product.minus: Even loyal paying users keep asking for one thing: a home-screen fasting-timer widget. There are widgets for steps, water and weight, but none for the app's whole point — and iOS had one.

product.title: Won't sync with fitness trackers or Health Connect
product.minus: A complaint even among paid users: no working sync with Samsung Health, Google Fit/Health Connect, Fitbit, Garmin. Sleep pulls in as 0, weight isn't retrieved, steps must be entered by hand — enough to make some look elsewhere.

product.title: Basic fasting locked behind the paid "coach"
product.minus: People come for a simple timer and find that custom schedules, windows like 18/6 or 23/1, OMAD, and fasts longer than 16 hours are all gated behind a paid "coach" subscription.

product.title: Charges keep coming after a cancellation you can't complete
product.minus: The subscription can't be cancelled through Google Play — cancellation is buried inside the app, and people keep getting charged after they've cancelled and even uninstalled.

product.title: A free tier generous enough to actually use
product.plus: Plenty of people run for years on the free version — window tracking, water reminders, tips and fasting plans are enough to stay on track without ever paying for a coach.

product.title: Knowing exactly what stage your body is in
product.plus: The stage-by-stage explanations of what's happening in your body each hour are a standout feature — people use them to time workouts and to push through the hard final hours.

product.title: Wanting a timer, getting quizzes and a "contract"
product.minus: Just to start you must create an account, wade through endless questions and "sign a contract" — far too much for someone who only wants a countdown to the end of their fast.

product.title: Editing fasting times is a chore, worse since the update
product.minus: Adjusting windows is fiddly — there's no manual start/stop, and a recent update turned the once-instant time change into a slow click-by-click slog for every single day.

product.title: Advertised as free, paywalled from the first step
product.minus: Google lists the app as free, yet after setup it demands payment — and people resent wasting time configuring it only to hit a paywall.

product.title: Water and stage reminders keep people on track
product.plus: The notifications — when to start fasting, when to eat, when to drink water — are the main engine of discipline for many: easy to forget, gently reminded.

product.title: Intrusive ads and upgrade pop-ups, even for payers
product.minus: Loud video ads and constant "upgrade" pop-ups get in the way — and in some reports they keep showing even after the user has paid.

product.title: The paid "coach" is a PDF of generic web tips
product.minus: Those who pay for the "coach" feel shortchanged: instead of a personal mentor they get generic fasting tips findable for free, with no workout guides and no real personalization.

product.title: Simple, clear, and it actually helps people lose weight
product.plus: Many highlight the clear interface and real results — kilos and centimetres drop, and for some, fasting turns from a diet into a lasting lifestyle.

product.title: Skews weight-loss diet, not a neutral fasting tracker
product.minus: For those fasting for health rather than weight loss, the relentless weight-and-BMI focus grates — it pushes even already-lean users to drop more.

product.title: Asking for a widget and a total-hours-fasted counter
product.minus: Even happy users miss a home-screen widget showing the fasting phase, and a count-up of how many hours they've already fasted, not just the time remaining.

product.title: Cancelling is nearly impossible — charges continue even after you opt out
product.minus: The single most common complaint: people spend days, weeks, even months unable to find a cancel button, the links dead-end, and charges keep hitting their card after they've already cancelled.

product.title: Surprise charges: the price jumps and they take more than promised
product.minus: A $1 or $7.99 trial turns into a $44–$129 charge, an annual auto-renewal at a higher price with no warning, and sometimes money is taken for something the person never bought at all.

product.title: The ad promises tai chi or a workout plan — inside it's a fasting app
product.minus: Many arrived via an ad for a "free tai chi walking program" or an exercise plan, and got a fasting-and-food-logging app instead — nothing like what they signed up for.

product.title: The mascot shames you for missing a log instead of supporting you
product.minus: The purple/green creature (Blinky, Pinky, Fuzzball) pulls hurt faces and sends guilt-trip messages when you fail to log a meal — users find it childish and manipulative rather than motivating.

product.title: The AI food tracker logs calories and nutrients wrong
product.minus: The AI doesn't recognise brands or packaging, double-counts ingredients, insists everything is "too high in sodium," and assigns absurd numbers to chicken or spinach — the accuracy can't be trusted.

product.title: The AI coach ignores medical limits and pushes unsuitable plans
product.minus: Despite stated limitations — a wheelchair, back pain, a doctor-prescribed diet — the app sends standing workouts, bike rides, and a fasting schedule that contradicts medical advice.

product.title: Glitchy, freezes, and loses data — especially after updates
product.minus: The app freezes while logging, throws errors, loses entered weight and fasting data, and updates break features that used to work.

product.title: Nagging notifications for things you've already done
product.minus: The app keeps reminding you to log your weight or check in even though you already did and the box is ticked — it's annoying and undermines trust.

product.title: The fasting timer drifts and loses long fasts
product.minus: The fasting schedule works poorly: you have to start it manually, it sets the wrong time, and fasts longer than a day get lost or bleed across days.

product.title: The AI coach and avatar genuinely motivate and keep you accountable
product.plus: For many, the avatar coach (Avo) stands in for a 24/7 personal mentor: it gives non-judgmental support, answers questions, and it's the daily engagement that keeps them on track.

product.title: People actually lose weight and build habits
product.plus: Plenty of reviews report real weight loss — 10, 17, 20, 22, 34 pounds — and credit the app with building healthy habits and a better relationship with food.

product.title: Simple logging and gentle home workouts for any age
product.plus: The interface is praised for its simplicity: easy to log food, water, and weight, and the gentle workouts and tai chi suit seniors and people with limitations — all doable at home.

product.title: Cancelling is a trap: charges keep coming after you've cancelled
product.minus: The single most common complaint: people cancel — in the app, in Google Play, by email — and the money keeps coming out anyway, sometimes for years and into the hundreds of dollars. Cancellation is buried behind their website and a chain of pop-ups with a final hidden 'submit'.

product.title: The price is hidden until the end of the quiz, then they hit you with an expensive plan
product.minus: Users are walked through a detailed survey about themselves and asked for an email — and only then shown the paywall. No free mode, no price up front; many uninstall right after the questionnaire, feeling duped.

product.title: The $1 trial turns into a full quarterly charge
product.minus: People take the $1 week-long trial, cancel in time — and still get hit with a $79 three-month charge. They aren't warned the trial is ending as promised, and the real price of the three-month plan is nowhere to be seen.

product.title: A 14-day refund is promised, but in practice refused or halved
product.minus: The site advertises a 14-day money-back guarantee, but in-window requests are either ignored, met with 'digital goods are non-refundable', or offered back at 25–50%. Some only get their money via a chargeback or PayPal dispute.

product.title: The 'personalized plan' is you picking from a list of things you could've Googled for free
product.minus: The survey sells a 'personalized program', but after payment the user picks their own fasting times, food and exercises from preset options. It's essentially a timer plus articles already freely available online.

product.title: The app freezes on the start/end-fast button and just stops working
product.minus: The core action — marking the start and end of a fast — regularly freezes or throws red 'Resource not found' bars. Reinstalling and clearing cache don't help; people pay for an app they can't even get into.

product.title: The branded smart scale becomes a brick when the app stops pairing
product.minus: People buy the proprietary DoFasting scale for body composition, but the app won't see it because of a never-ending bug — leaving only manual weight. Without the app the scale is useless.

product.title: Food logging is painful: missing items, broken portions, custom meals don't save
product.minus: The calorie tracker is the weak spot: basic foods are missing, serving sizes can't be adjusted, and the barcode scanner won't recognize even common snacks. Custom meals don't save, so you re-enter the same dish from scratch every time.

product.title: Steps and activity only sync with Fitbit or Google — every other watch is left out
product.minus: Activity only pulls from Fitbit or Google, and only steps at that. Owners of Samsung, Garmin, Apple Watch and Polar get no sync, and there's no way to enter a workout (swimming, aerobics) manually at all.

product.title: No female-cycle support, despite ranking for 'Fast Like a Girl'
product.minus: The app markets itself on the popular book about cyclical women's fasting, yet has no way to tie fasts to cycle phases — it's a standard timer. Women feel this is misleading advertising.

product.title: Support answers with a canned '48 hours' and then vanishes
product.minus: The only contact is email or chat, and replies are an autoresponder or a promise to 'get back in 48 hours' followed by silence. There's no phone, emails sometimes bounce — and meanwhile the charges keep coming.

product.title: When it works, the fasting timer and reminders genuinely keep people on track
product.plus: People genuinely like the fasting timer itself: gentle, non-pushy reminders for the start and end of a fast, fat-burning stage markers and a water tracker really help beginners stick to the plan and lose weight.

product.title: Recipes and educational content are what even skeptics praise
product.plus: Many like the recipes and multi-level exercises, the information on what happens at each stage of a fast, and the clean interface. For beginners it's a handy learning package that motivates habit change.

product.title: Past windows can't be edited — forget to tap start and the day is lost
product.minus: The single most common pain: if you forget to start or end a fast on time, you cannot go back and fix the time or date. The entry either won't save or the app crashes when you try to edit it, and long fasts (48 and 70 hours) aren't recorded at all.

product.title: Subscription charges early and without warning — it reeks of a scam
product.minus: Money is taken before the trial ends — sometimes after 3 days instead of the promised 7-14, sometimes twice, even after cancellation. Many call it outright deception and spend months chasing a refund.

product.title: Windows flip on their own — the fast breaks overnight with no input
product.minus: The app opens an eating window in the middle of the night or stops the fast around 2-3 a.m. on its own, even when closed. The timer shows 43 hours instead of 19, and there's no way to fix it.

product.title: Paywall from the very first screen — no card, no progress past start
product.minus: The Start Plan button leads to a payment page, you can't get past setup without card details, and the "free" trial demands them up front. Many uninstall within minutes, never having used the app.

product.title: Upgrade pop-ups every few seconds — the X is hidden in the background
product.minus: Premium ads pop up on practically every tap, two full-screen prompts at once, and the tiny X in a non-contrasting color is nearly invisible. It feels designed to nag you into subscribing.

product.title: Support doesn't reply — or fobs you off with "not a priority"
product.minus: Emails with screenshots are ignored for weeks, the support chat and address don't work, and when they do reply they say they won't take on the issue. For a paid app this kind of support destroys what trust remains.

product.title: Cancelling becomes a loop between the app and Google Play
product.minus: The subscription doesn't show up in the Google Play list, and support points you back to Google — round and round it goes. People keep paying for an app they deleted long ago.

product.title: Data vanishes on reinstall or when you switch phones
product.minus: There's effectively no account, so a reinstall or a new phone wipes the entire history and sometimes the subscription itself. There's also no sync between phone, tablet and web.

product.title: Manual timer and flexible window — the main reason people love it
product.plus: Many praise the manual mode: you can open and close the window intuitively, set a custom long fast, and the app doesn't penalize you for starting or ending early. This simplicity is exactly what keeps loyal users.

product.title: Educational notes and fasting-stage facts genuinely motivate
product.plus: Users love the tips about what happens to the body at each fasting stage, the daily challenges and the journal. It turns the timer into a source of motivation rather than just a counter.

product.title: Clean, simple interface — ideal for beginners to intermittent fasting
product.plus: The clean, modern design that isn't overloaded with info or buried in notifications gets praised especially by beginners. Real weight-loss results reinforce the loyalty.

product.title: Useful features (weight, water, long fasts) are locked behind subscription
product.minus: Only the 12-hour preset and a manual timer are free; anything longer than 16 hours, weight tracking past three entries, and detailed stats require payment. Many find the feature set too thin to justify a subscription.

product.title: When support does respond, refunds come instantly
product.plus: A notable group reports the opposite: when they reached out, the money was refunded straight away, no arguing. For those who got through, the service turned out to be a strength.

product.title: Without subscription it's "just a timer" — many see no value for the price
product.minus: A frequent verdict: for $30 a year the app does no more than a phone alarm or an Excel sheet. The paywall grates precisely because the core function feels trivial.

product.title: Eat/water reminders and notifications often don't fire
product.minus: Even with notifications enabled and re-enabled, the reminders to end a fast or drink water don't fire. For a paid basic feature, this reduces the app to a useless background timer.

product.title: Ads after every entry make the free version unusable
product.minus: Every food entry turns into a ritual: 1-2 full-screen video ads you can't just dismiss (you have to open the advertised app's Play Store page), followed by several screens pushing premium. A 10-second log stretches into minutes, and people leave for competitors.

product.title: Duolingo-style gamification annoys even paying users
product.minus: Streaks, a yeti mascot, chests, diamonds, and an "I'm committed" screen on every launch turned a simple tracker into a clingy game. There's no way to switch it off even with premium, and long-time subscribers leave repeating one thing: "Don't be Duolingo."

product.title: An endless onboarding survey scares people off before they ever reach the app
product.minus: Before the first use you must answer dozens of personal questions (down to "how many kids you have" and "which clothes you'd wear after losing weight"), you can't skip them, and at the end there's a paywall and a discount wheel. Many uninstall mid-signup.

product.title: Animations and meal tips can't be turned off, even with premium
product.minus: After every logged meal there's a screen of slow animations and "meal tips" you have to wait through or click away. Users have begged for a toggle in settings for years — Yazio's answer is that it's "by design."

product.title: AI photo recognition systematically underestimates calories
product.minus: The headline feature — calories from a photo — consistently misses, underestimating by 30-40% versus manual entry and barely knowing non-European cuisines. You can't correct the scan, so people end up entering everything by hand — after paying for the AI.

product.title: The May 2026 update took the app down: "no internet" on a working Wi-Fi
product.minus: After the April-May 2026 update, paying users couldn't log food for whole days: the app demands a constant connection, throws "no internet" on working Wi-Fi plus 502/412 errors, and there's no offline mode or status page.

product.title: Replacing manual entry with an AI chat and the redesign broke the familiar workflow
product.minus: Recent updates removed the "add manually" button in favor of AI text, buried Recently/Frequent/Favorites inside a dropdown, and swapped icons for menus — so a simple action now takes several extra clicks. Long-time users are furious.

product.title: The onboarding survey repeats every time you pause for a few days
product.minus: Skip the app for a few days and on return it drags you back through the same long survey about weight and goals, with no skip option. It happens even to paying users and feels like punishment for using it irregularly.

product.title: The AI "tips" pressure your eating and trigger disorders
product.minus: The mascot and AI critique your food choices after every meal and push you to "swap for something healthier" with no context, which for people with eating disorders feels insulting and drags them back to dark days. Requests for an off toggle are ignored.

product.title: Dark patterns around the subscription: paywall before trial, triple charges, hard cancellation
product.minus: They demand a subscription before letting you try the features, the "free trial" can't be declined, and in-app cancellation fails — money is taken anyway, sometimes triple. The price is double competitors, and the "discount" wheel is hard-coded.

product.title: A huge food database and convenient search — the main reason to stay
product.plus: Even the angriest reviewers admit it: Yazio's food database is huge, you can find almost anything, plus you can create custom meals and scan barcodes. It's the reason people endure the ads and stay, calling the database the best thing about the app.

product.title: A pretty, simple, intuitive interface that genuinely helps people lose weight
product.plus: Under the layer of ads sits a beautifully made, simple, pleasant tracker that people actually lose weight with — 9 to 21 kg in a couple of months, streaks of 150+ days. For many it was a years-long favorite, and they cling to it regardless.

product.title: When you get past the bots, support replies fast and actually solves things
product.plus: Despite a wall of AI chatbot, Yazio's human support exists and works: people flip an angry review to 5 stars after a fast reply, a refund, or a bug fix — often within ten minutes.

product.title: Yazio does listen: a snooze for tips appeared — and ratings climbed back
product.plus: Some criticism doesn't fall on deaf ears: the developers added a "snooze tips for 2 weeks" option and a way to skip the post-scan hints almost entirely — and several users publicly raised their rating, noting logging is enjoyable again.

product.title: Double-counting steps and calories — dangerous for anyone tracking a deficit
product.minus: When syncing with trackers, Yazio counts activity twice (both phone steps and watch data), inflating burned calories by up to ~1000 kcal. For an app people rely on to stay in a deficit, that's a direct risk of overeating.

product.title: The fasting timer decides when to end and won't let you edit the past
product.minus: The very reason people install it — the intermittent-fasting tracker — is half-baked: it's locked to the chosen fasting type and ends your fast for you, with no way to set the real start/end or edit past entries, even on the paid plan.

product.title: Basic analytics and data export are locked away or simply missing
product.minus: Even paying users can't export their data (no API or file export for a doctor), weight history is trimmed, and weekly/monthly nutrient summaries simply don't exist — for a tracker, that reads as a missing core feature.

product.title: Launch ads went from tolerable to app-blocking
product.minus: Short clips used to be fine; now it opens with full-screen ads of two minutes or longer, the close button doesn't respond, and you can't reach the home screen — people set the phone down and walk away, or uninstall.

product.title: The ad 'close' button does nothing — an inescapable loop
product.minus: The ad freezes, the X does nothing, so you have to kill the whole app, after which the same clip replays — users describe it as an endless loop.

product.title: The stage-by-stage body timer is the main reason people love it
product.plus: The app tells you what your body is going through at each stage of the fast, and users call this the key value — it motivates and educates.

product.title: The free version is genuinely useful — rare for the genre
product.plus: Many stress that even without a subscription the timer, widget, water and basic flow fully cover the job — and some pay only afterwards, by choice.

product.title: Simplicity and a clear interface — why people stay for years
product.plus: 'Easy', 'intuitive', 'simple' is the most frequent praise; people come back after breaks and stay for 2–3 years because getting in and out is fast.

product.title: Barcode scanning and food recognition return wrong data
product.minus: The food log is called the worst part: barcodes scan wrong, the database is inaccurate, a photo of a bottle counts as the whole thing drunk, and you can't fix it manually — no units, no decimals, no editing.

product.title: Editing the fast start time came and went between updates
product.minus: Editing the fast start time is critical for people who forget to log on time; some praise it as the best feature, but after updates it vanished for some, and the fasting hours stopped counting.

product.title: A long onboarding with dozens of personal questions repels at the door
product.minus: Before letting you try it, the app runs a long setup and '50 questions', then hits you with a paywall — people call it data-grabbing and uninstall before reaching the product.

product.title: Subscriptions break: paid access vanishes, data is lost
product.minus: People who bought a yearly plan are suddenly asked to subscribe again, can't cancel or switch tiers, and trying to restore access wipes all their data.

product.title: It actually helps people lose weight and stay consistent — the bottom-line outcome
product.plus: Users cite concrete results — 2–5 kg off in weeks, 26 kg in a year, lower blood pressure — and credit the app for keeping them on schedule and motivated.

product.title: No Google Fit / Health Connect link — data has to be entered by hand
product.minus: Google Fit sync is described but doesn't work, there's no export/import to Health Connect, and weight, steps and activity must be entered manually — a frequent ask people would give five stars for.

product.title: A persistent notification timer keeps the fast in view without nagging
product.plus: An icon in the corner and a notification showing the current fast time is a favorite touch: it reminds, prevents forgetting, and doesn't feel intrusive.

product.title: Small gaps in customization: water sizes, custom plans, diet types
product.minus: Loyal users ask for little: 8 oz and 16.9 oz water sizes, custom fasting plans, vegetarian-aware recipes, OMAD, and building your own meals from ingredients — until that's added, the rating caps at 4 stars.

product.title: A long quiz funnels you straight into a paywall, not into the product
product.minus: Users answer 20+ screens of personal questions expecting a "personalized plan," then slam into a subscription wall without seeing a single feature. There's no free tier, and the offer screen often can't even be dismissed.

product.title: Listed as "free," but nothing works without a subscription
product.minus: The store labels the app free, so people download it to "try it," then can't even start the timer without paying. Many call it bait-and-switch.

product.title: Post-trial charges are surprise, inflated, and unannounced
product.minus: A cheap trial silently rolls into a full subscription: instead of the promised £15 people are hit with £38-66, sometimes twice. The amount and auto-renewal are barely disclosed up front.

product.title: Cancelling the subscription is nearly impossible
product.minus: There's no in-app cancel button; the instructions point to Google Play where the subscription simply isn't listed. People end up locking their card or going to the bank to stop the charges.

product.title: Refunds refused — even on double charges or their own error
product.minus: Every refund request is met with "all sales are final" and an offer of a free year instead. A refund is only promised if you spend 14 days proving the fasting didn't work.

product.title: It's essentially a timer: you could do the same on paper or a clock
product.minus: For your subscription you get what any alarm clock replaces: a countdown and water reminders. No calorie database, no barcode scanner, no real personalization.

product.title: No watch sync — steps only count if the phone is in your pocket
product.minus: The app won't connect to Fitbit, Garmin, Samsung Health or any smartwatch, and there's no manual step entry. The "just keep your phone on you all day" advice frustrates people.

product.title: Food logging is clunky: you enter calories yourself, recipes don't fit
product.minus: Calories must be looked up and entered by hand with no food database. Logged meals can't be edited, and the recipes are repetitive, keto-leaning, and ignore allergies and diets.

product.title: It actually helps people lose weight and stay disciplined
product.plus: Many report genuine weight loss — from a couple of pounds in a week to 47 lbs in six months. The app keeps people accountable and lets them feel the results.

product.title: Water reminders and tips genuinely change habits
product.plus: The constant water reminders and daily tips help people build hydration and mindful eating — for many that's the single biggest benefit.

product.title: Explains fasting stages and the science — valuable for beginners
product.plus: The app shows which stages the body goes through while fasting and offers lessons on the benefits — beginners find it easy to start and understand what's happening.

product.title: Rigid input limits: weight caps at 331 lbs, the fast window at 23 hours
product.minus: Starting weight can't be set above 331 lbs (150 kg), shutting out the people who need help most. And the timer won't allow fasts longer than 23 hours, so alternate-day and 36-hour fasts can't be set.

product.title: The "perfect body photos" onboarding reads as body-shaming
product.minus: Onboarding shows photoshopped bodies and asks you to pick "normal" versus "flabby/extra" — people find it insensitive, inaccurate, and shaming, enough to uninstall on the spot.

product.title: Charges keep coming after the subscription is cancelled
product.minus: A wall of reviews describes the same thing: people cancel (often via Google Play), delete the app, and are still billed for months. It reads as a systemic complaint, not a one-off glitch.

product.title: Cancellation is hidden inside the app, not handed to the store
product.minus: Unlike most apps, the subscription can't be cancelled through Google Play; the option is buried inside the app, support instructions dead-end, and people end up calling their bank.

product.title: Double and multiple charges, surprise amounts
product.minus: Users report being billed not once but three to five times in a row, sometimes triple the promised amount and before the trial ends. A hidden charge for 'downloading the guide' finishes off the trust.

product.title: 'Free' on the listing, paywalled at the first real action
product.minus: Google lists the app as free, yet basics — your own plan, OMAD, fasts longer than 16 hours — are locked behind the 'coach'. People feel baited after a long setup.

product.title: Refund refusals and stonewalling support
product.minus: When it comes to refunds, support stalls, quotes policy, or goes silent. The advertised 'refund if unsatisfied in two weeks' doesn't hold up in practice.

product.title: Changing the fasting schedule is painfully clunky
product.minus: Manually editing start/end times is the core UI pain: you can't set arbitrary hours (18/6, 20/4, 23/1), you must rebuild the plan every week, and the 'time period change' update made it worse.

product.title: A simple timer turned into a 'coach' and a contract
product.minus: People just want a fasting timer, but get funnelled through quizzes, a mandatory account, 'signing a contract', BMI, and forced weight-loss framing. The flow feels like joining an expensive cult.

product.title: Ads and pop-ups make the app unbearable
product.minus: The free tier is flooded with loud video ads and upgrade pop-ups — to the point it's embarrassing to open near others. Some report ads even after paying.

product.title: The paid 'coach' turns out to be a generic PDF
product.minus: Those who paid for the coach are uniformly let down: instead of a personal mentor they get generic tips and a PDF you could google for free, with no workouts or real personalization.

product.title: A genuinely generous free tier covers the basics
product.plus: Despite the pop-ups, many use the free tier for years: a fasting tracker, water reminders, clear plans, and stage-of-fasting info — and find it enough on its own.

product.title: Stage explanations and reminders keep people on track
product.plus: The mechanic loyal users love: the app shows which fasting stage your body is in, nudges you to drink water, and feeds tips — motivating, and handy for timing workouts.

product.title: When the format clicks, people lose weight and stick around
product.plus: For those it suits, the app becomes a lifestyle: users cite concrete results — kilos and centimetres off, more energy — and return years later.

product.title: No widget and no count-up timer — fans' top requests
product.minus: Even happy users hit the same gaps: no home/lock-screen widget showing current fasting status, and no count-up of hours elapsed alongside the countdown.

product.title: Subscription ads hit the people who already paid for maps
product.minus: You buy the World Pack or offline maps as a one-time payment and still get full-screen "go Premium" popups on every launch and screen switch. There's no way to turn it off, and it's the number-one reason long-time fans are leaving.

product.title: Lifetime licences and the World Pack suddenly turn into a pumpkin
product.minus: People paid for a "lifetime" licence or world pack and now hit a paywall as if they'd just installed the app. A region promised "free for life" demands payment, and restoring the purchase or getting a refund is impossible.

product.title: Route discovery is what keeps people around
product.plus: The standout strength: it surfaces quiet, safe trails and bike routes even in unfamiliar areas, steers you away from highways and traffic, and leans on its community. For hiking, gravel and MTB it's often called the best mapping out there.

product.title: Post-update the map lags and drops a pin on every tap
product.minus: Recent updates turned a smooth map into a mess: scrolling stutters, every tap drops a stray pin, and planning a route becomes impossible. Many say outright the app became "unusable" right after an update.

product.title: Drains the battery faster than any other map
product.minus: Power draw is its own pain: the phone or watch dies within 1.5–3 hours of a ride, the screen won't sleep despite the settings, and there are reports of wakelocks held even when the app isn't in use. For multi-day or long hikes that's a dealbreaker.

product.title: Navigation sends you the wrong way — onto highways, into rivers, into dead ends
product.minus: Turn-by-turn navigation lets you down: it routes onto dangerous main roads instead of local cycleways, through rivers and private property, instructions arrive late, and dead-end U-turns are routine. Several say the app literally "insisted I walk off a cliff".

product.title: One-time map purchase instead of a subscription — that's the love
product.plus: A historically loved feature: you can buy a region or world pack once and use it with no monthly subscription, unlike Strava and AllTrails. This is the model people paid for and recommended the app over.

product.title: Cancelling a subscription and deleting an account are built like a trap
product.minus: You can't unsubscribe in-app — you're pushed to a browser; the delete-account button doesn't work and loops you through endless auth screens ending in an error. The trial charges immediately, and cancellation is "hidden so well it's close to a scam".

product.title: The Bending Spoons takeover feels like the start of enshittification
product.minus: Long-time users tie the decline directly to the sale to Bending Spoons: the dev team was laid off, ads and AI support replies appeared, and useful features get cut or paywalled. The word "enshittification" comes up again and again.

product.title: The elevation profile now goes full-screen and breaks navigation
product.minus: A specific regression that infuriates many: the elevation profile used to open in a small window you could scroll and measure distances on. After the update a tap expands it full-screen, hiding the map, with no interaction — a loss of a key feature for mountain hikes.

product.title: You can't just follow a route — it forces you to record and save the trip
product.minus: The basic "plot A→B, ride it, leave" flow is broken: navigation only works coupled with activity recording, and at the end the app forces you through 8 save screens. Want to just ride without tracking and social features — you have to fight the UI.

product.title: Garmin, Wahoo and watch sync — when it works, it's brilliant
product.plus: A prized combo for serious riders: routes push to Garmin Edge, Wahoo and smartwatches, with turn-by-turn on the wrist saving phone battery. Many stay with the app specifically for this integration.

product.title: You can't shut up the voice prompts
product.minus: An annoying detail with no off switch: the voice keeps shouting about lost GPS signal or "Let's go!", cutting into your music, with no way to disable it. For some that alone makes the app unusable.

product.title: Mandatory Google/Facebook login often breaks
product.minus: You can't do anything without an account, and the login itself fails: Google and Facebook sign-in errors out, sometimes loops endlessly, and trying to register without internet is pointless. A barrier before you even reach your first route.

product.title: Once-free features moved behind the paywall — a bait-and-switch feeling
product.minus: Long-time users are furious: features they relied on for free for years now require a subscription. Maps, search, activity breakdowns, sharing — they all migrated into Premium one by one, and without paying the app «won't let you do anything».

product.title: Subscription popups on every tap make the app nearly unusable
product.minus: The loudest complaint: you can't press a single button without a «buy Premium» popup. Two popups just for finishing an activity, ads blocking the record button — users call the UX «desperate» and «pathetic».

product.title: Recording cuts out mid-activity and loses the whole route
product.minus: The core technical failure: the app silently stops recording, then greets you at the end with «Strava recovered from a problem» — with nothing actually saved. People lose half-marathons and long rides, and it has gone on for years.

product.title: GPS «bounces» and miscounts distance — stats come out wrong
product.minus: Distance is systematically off: a 30-mile ride logged as 16, a 21-mile ride as 0.11. GPS throws you into the next street from inside a stadium, and in the mountains or among skyscrapers the track falls apart entirely.

product.title: Charges without consent after a «free trial» — money meant for school and food
product.minus: A whole stream of identical stories, especially from the Philippines: 1500–2999 pesos pulled from GCash/bank accounts without confirmation, often money set aside for school. The «free trial» quietly becomes a yearly plan, and refunds get delayed or denied.

product.title: One-time-code login breaks and locks you out of your account
product.minus: Removing Facebook login and switching to 6-digit email codes left people locked out — including paying subscribers. Codes «aren't accepted», an endless «try again with a new code» loop, and support tickets sit unanswered for weeks.

product.title: Support goes silent, and accounts get banned with no explanation
product.minus: Tickets sit for weeks with zero reply, and some users get banned «for logging workouts» with no reason given. Support is described as «non-existent» — not afraid to take your money, but unwilling to help.

product.title: Screenshot interception forces «share» and gets in the way of saving ride data
product.minus: Take a screenshot of your own data and a window pops up saying «just share it through us», with no way to turn it off. It breaks scrolling screenshots and annoys people whose actual share function doesn't show what they want.

product.title: Poor syncing with watches and third-party services
product.minus: Galaxy Watch and Samsung Health, Whoop, Oura, Huawei Health, Shimano E-Tube — integrations either won't connect or import garbage (a 21-minute swim becomes 1h 34min). People end up running two apps at once.

product.title: Forced AI and bloated updates crowd out what used to work
product.minus: Long-time subscribers beg them to «not go down this AI nonsense»: AI insights and AI workouts are useless, the «muscle map» is constantly wrong and can't be disabled, new animations lag. The app gets «worse every update».

product.title: The gold standard for accurate tracking and analytics — when it works
product.plus: For its happy users this is the best tracker out there: accurate GPS, clean breakdowns of distance, pace and segments, clear progress over time. Many call it the «gold standard» for runners and cyclists and praise the low battery drain.

product.title: A social network for athletes that motivates and hasn't drowned in ads or toxicity
product.plus: Its strongest side is the community: kudos, segment leaderboards, challenges and following friends genuinely motivate people to train on days they'd rather not. It's one of the rare social networks people call «good for you».

product.title: Minimize the app and the workout pauses
product.minus: After recent updates, recording stops the moment the screen locks or you switch apps: a nagging "resume" button appeared, and workouts come back fragmented or reset entirely.

product.title: Recorded workouts vanish without a trace
product.minus: The app says "saving" but the history stays empty; it crashes mid-ride and loses the whole result, sometimes hours of it. For people who use it precisely to log workouts, that defeats the entire point.

product.title: You pay for the trainer, then pay again to control it
product.minus: After buying expensive hardware, basic functions — erg mode, resistance control, routes — got locked behind an $18–25/month subscription. Users see it as blatant double-dipping.

product.title: An update yanked heart rate and cadence off the workout screen
product.minus: The "simplified" interface stripped heart rate, cadence, power and calories from the live screen — sometimes leaving just a clock. Those readings were the whole reason people used Wahoo.

product.title: Health Connect sync was suddenly cut
product.minus: The autumn 2024 update removed Google Health Connect / Google Fit sync that many had built their routine around; some manually rolled back to an old version. At times the sync even corrupted other step data.

product.title: Simply pairing a sensor or trainer became a lottery
product.minus: The app fails to find or connect its own Wahoo gear — Bolt, Roam, Kickr — even when it shows up in system Bluetooth. Connections drop mid-ride, and some models are flatly declared "not supported".

product.title: Demands location permission just for a Bluetooth sensor
product.minus: To connect a trainer or heart-rate monitor over Bluetooth, the app insists on precise location access; users read this as data harvesting and refuse, losing the ability to use it.

product.title: The home screen is clogged with junk widgets and social features
product.minus: Once-simple, the app bloated: a home screen littered with suggestions, extra taps before starting, AI "mental fitness" check-ins, constant browser pop-outs. Setting resistance now means navigating a maze of menus.

product.title: Endless prompts to rate the app, even mid-ride
product.minus: The app aggressively begs for a rating and won't let you skip surveys, interrupting the workout. After hundreds of dollars on hardware, that pestering stings.

product.title: Deleting your account is nearly impossible
product.minus: Just to request account deletion you must hand over extra personal info, and the account still isn't deleted. Users suspect the app's main purpose is harvesting data for marketing.

product.title: Pairs any third-party sensor straight to your phone, for free
product.plus: For those it works for, this is the draw: it freely connects heart-rate, cadence and power sensors of any brand — Garmin, Polar, Coros, Scosche — directly to the phone, no separate bike computer needed.

product.title: A serious free alternative to paid subscriptions
product.plus: For many it's a full fitness hub with no subscription or ads: customizable screens and HR zones, support for many activity types, .FIT export — it even replaces Zwift and dodges Strava's data "tax".

product.title: Custom HR zones and profiles for every sport
product.plus: A real strength for zone-based training: custom zones, voice cues, separate profiles for cycling, running, strength, even a wheelchair, plus big readable numbers and zones that light up in real time.

product.title: Seamless auto-upload of workouts to Strava
product.plus: Many keep the app for reliable auto-export to Strava (plus Garmin Connect and Fitbit) — especially those on a stationary bike that Strava can't track on its own.

product.title: A long-hauler that just works for years
product.plus: A substantial group of loyal users have kept it 5–10 years without major issues; some even note responsive support that genuinely resolves things over email.

product.title: Long-free core features got moved behind a paywall
product.minus: What enrages users most isn't the subscription itself but that it walls off things that were free for years: route comparison, maps, progress, audio cues. Many would pay a one-off fee but not a monthly one for what used to be included.

product.title: Tracking dies mid-workout and loses the route
product.minus: The most common failure: recording just stops mid-run or walk, leaving half the distance or nothing at all. It's often blamed on power saving, but people disable everything they can and nothing helps.

product.title: Constant 'always' location demands feel like surveillance
product.minus: The app demands location access even when not in use and spams pop-ups at every screen unlock. People check and see it really pings GPS in the background for no reason — hurting battery and trust.

product.title: Forces a login every single time you open it
product.minus: A recent update stopped remembering the login: the app demands sign-in on every open, which means it's unusable without internet. For tracking in the mountains or woods off-grid this is a flat-out dealbreaker.

product.title: Locking audio feedback behind premium stings the most
product.minus: Audio cues for distance and pace were free since the very first version, and their move to premium is named more than any other loss. For runners it was the key 'don't look at your phone' feature, and removing it feels like a slap to loyal users.

product.title: Distance and route come out inaccurate
product.minus: The GPS either undercounts distance many times over or draws straight lines and 'flights' over buildings. Ran 7km, got 1.2; walked the same trail two days running and got different numbers. For an app whose one job is measuring distance, that's fatal.

product.title: Crashes on screen lock and newer Android
product.minus: After a screen lock or incoming call the workout is often lost for good, and on Android 16 and Pixel the GPS only connects intermittently. Crashes that lose half the route and login errors (1014, 1414) finish off an already fragile stability.

product.title: The UI redesign turned manual entry into torture
product.minus: After the 2026 update manual workout entry broke: dates shift by a day, a roller instead of a keyboard, zeros instead of blank fields, edits won't save. Long-time users for whom the app 'suited really well' are stunned by the regression.

product.title: No way to edit or trim a recorded route
product.minus: If you forget to stop recording and get in a car or train, the route gets ruined by a 70mph 'flight', and you can't fix the start/end — only delete the whole workout. A simple track edit has topped the wishlist for years and still isn't there.

product.title: Won't play with third-party HR sensors and watches
product.minus: Many popular chest straps — Polar H10, Wahoo Tickr X — won't pair, and some data is even hidden behind an ad for Suunto's own belt. There's no WearOS or Samsung-watch app, cutting off a whole audience.

product.title: When it works, the best private tracker earning 10+ years of loyalty
product.plus: The core love is alive: people have logged activities with this app since the Nokia days, for 10–14 years, prizing its simplicity, accuracy and privacy-by-default. Zoomable graphs, the workout calendar, photos pinned to the route map — many call it better than Strava.

product.title: Support is silent and the app feels abandoned
product.minus: Emails and bug reports go unanswered for years, at best an AI template replies. Refunds for non-working premium drag on for months, and the lack of new features amid rising prices suggests the app is quietly dying like Endomondo.

product.title: Core actions are locked behind a subscription — you can't even save or navigate a route without paying
product.minus: Users complain over and over: you can map a route, but the moment you save it or hit navigate a paywall window pops up. The gate blocks what other maps give for free, and it pushes many of them straight to uninstall.

product.title: The price feels like a rip-off, and it's annual-only — no one-time purchase, no monthly option
product.minus: Many would pay once but flatly refuse a yearly subscription at $60–90. The lack of a monthly plan stings most: you can't ride in winter, yet you're forced to pay for the whole year.

product.title: Ride recording randomly pauses and loses miles in the middle of a ride
product.minus: The most painful technical complaint: the app stops recording mid-ride, cuts trips short and under-counts distance. Turning off autopause doesn't help, and support just blames your battery settings.

product.title: Distance and time figures are wrong — the track cuts corners and under-measures mileage
product.minus: When GPS doesn't refresh with the screen off, the app reports distance off by 25% or more, mangles moving time and cuts corners off the track. For a paid account that stings even harder.

product.title: Routing sends you onto dangerous roads and ignores bike paths
product.minus: A cycling app oddly drags you onto shoulderless highways, steep climbs and main roads to save a tenth of a mile, while ignoring parallel bike paths. A cyclist wants the easiest, safest miles, not the shortest.

product.title: Forced sign-up: you can't map a route without an account
product.minus: Some users just want to map a route, not join a "community," but the app demands an account and nags you to register. For them that's reason enough to bail right away.

product.title: Free trial and cancellation turn into surprise charges
product.minus: The trial tries to charge you at the start, promised reminders never arrive, and you can't cancel from inside the app — you have to go to a website. Several people got hit with unwanted yearly charges.

product.title: The interface is unintuitive and the planner lags, especially after updates
product.minus: Many admit the app is powerful but call the interface convoluted and awkward on a phone, with a laggy route builder. Recent updates, they feel, only make route planning worse.

product.title: Best-in-class route planner with outstanding accuracy
product.plus: For loyal users it's the gold standard for planning: import KML/GPX, combine routes, see grades and elevation gain, export to Garmin. The most powerful and accurate route-building engine they've tried.

product.title: The free, ad-free tier covers what the everyday cyclist needs
product.plus: Despite the paywall complaints, many on the free tier are happy: it records rides, keeps stats, has no ads, and that's enough. Some plan to buy a subscription just to support the ad-free model.

product.title: Offline navigation and Garmin/Strava integration shine for bikepacking and long trips
product.plus: A warm use case: touring a foreign country on offline maps with seamless syncing to Garmin, Wahoo and Strava. Turn-by-turn with offline maps lets you just enjoy the ride and not stress about navigation.

product.title: Responsive support and hassle-free refunds
product.plus: Where the company gets praise, it's usually for support: quick replies, instant fixes for offline-map issues, refunds for accidental renewals without a fight. It noticeably softens the subscription frustration.

product.title: Public-by-default privacy and aggressive data collection alarm users
product.minus: Routes and profiles are public by default, you can't disable data collection without an account, and logs show thousands of tracking attempts per hour. Users call it a privacy violation and a gift to stalkers.

product.title: You can't turn on navigation without paying
product.minus: The single biggest sore point: for free you only get to look at the map and plan a route, while the 'start trip' button and turn-by-turn navigation are locked behind a paid subscription. Users feel baited — the app is marketed as free, yet without premium they can do 'literally anything'.

product.title: Routing sends you down nonexistent and dangerous roads
product.minus: The router constantly plots paths through roads that don't exist, through woods, rivers, fences, ravines and even a mine field. People hit dead ends and impassable terrain — for a navigation app this is a safety issue, not a convenience one.

product.title: Turn-by-turn lags, doesn't recenter or reroute
product.minus: Even for paying users, voice guidance calls turns too early, too late, or not at all. The map won't recenter after a missed turn and there's no rerouting — leaving people to restart the app mid-ride.

product.title: Ignores bike paths that are visible on its own map
product.minus: The very paradox people install it to avoid: it routes you onto busy car streets while skipping dedicated bike lanes — even ones its own map displays. The bike-specific routing ends up worse than Google Maps.

product.title: Address and place search simply doesn't work
product.minus: A core function fails at step one: search returns nothing, can't find even nearby well-known places, or offers a same-named address thousands of kilometres away. It's especially broken outside Europe/US — Japan, Australia, Korea and India addresses go unrecognised.

product.title: Won't let you set a start point — only routes from here
product.minus: The app insists on starting from your current location and won't let you pick an arbitrary start point. You can't plan an A-to-B ride the way Google Maps does when A isn't 'home', and you can't set a route's end point.

product.title: Ride recording drops out mid-ride
product.minus: GPS recording is unreliable: the track cuts out, logs only a few points across miles, draws straight lines, or invents wild elevation gain. Worse, the app logs people out on its own and the ride isn't saved at all.

product.title: Demands card before trial, then traps the subscription
product.minus: Just to try it you must hand over card details up front with no way to look first. Then come payment errors, charges without consent, an inability to cancel, and refusals to refund. People call it a predatory scheme and a scam.

product.title: Laggy, crash-prone and a battery hog
product.minus: The interface is slow and unstable: it freezes, crashes several times an hour, and 'back' closes the whole app instead of undoing an action. On top of that it drains the battery fast — up to 40% in an hour, several times more than comparable apps.

product.title: Placing waypoints is painful — the map keeps zooming out
product.minus: Route-building is clumsy: entering waypoints has to be repeated until the app finally accepts them, and after each one the map zooms back out, forcing you to zoom in again. You can't drag points or edit the route line the way the web app allows.

product.title: Huge route library and bike-trail visibility are the real draw
product.plus: Despite everything, what keeps people is the rich worldwide library of user routes and the fact that it surfaces bike paths and trails invisible to Google Maps — colour-coded and named. For discovering new routes and exploring an unfamiliar city, people call it a 'must'.

product.title: When it works, it logs rides well and routes you safely
product.plus: For happy users it all comes together: the app reliably records the track, distance, elevation and average speed, supports pause/resume and export to Google Fit. Routes run longer than Google Maps but safer and prettier — through parks and away from traffic.

product.title: Offline map downloads stall and fail
product.minus: Offline maps are a paid feature, yet even it breaks: downloads are slow, stick at 64–70% and abort, and when they do finish the maps come out pixelated and unreadable. For some premium users downloading stopped working entirely after an update.

product.title: Relentless 'buy Premium' nagging on every tap
product.minus: The free version buries users in upgrade banners — the premium prompt pops up on virtually every action and every launch. For many it backfires: instead of wanting to pay, they want to uninstall.

product.title: Mid-ride crashes and freezes wipe the whole workout
product.minus: The most common complaint by far: the picture freezes or the app crashes a few km in or near the end of a long ride, nothing is saved, and you start over — even on downloaded routes with strong hardware and a stable connection.

product.title: Real video instead of a cartoon world — the main reason people leave Zwift
product.plus: What they love: real footage of real roads from around the world feels far more immersive than Zwift's drawn universe; dozens switched from Zwift just for this and don't regret it — «doesn't feel like a game».

product.title: A huge worldwide route selection that motivates you to get on the bike
product.plus: Hundreds of routes across dozens of countries — flat and fast to brutal climbs; the variety keeps it interesting and gets people pedalling for hours where 45 minutes used to be a struggle.

product.title: Routes take 5–10 minutes to load even on gigabit internet
product.minus: The app is painfully slow: a route can take 7–10 minutes to load on fibre at minimum video quality, search lags, the UI hangs — warm-up eats more of your limited ride window than the ride itself.

product.title: Every update breaks what worked, and you can't skip it
product.minus: Forced updates land constantly, weigh over 500 MB, and routinely break things that worked — the app won't open, sound disappears, virtual shifting dies; there's no way back to the old version, and without updating you can't use the app at all.

product.title: Can't even log in: the email field won't activate, especially on Chromebook
product.minus: Many are stopped at the login screen itself: the email box won't activate, the keyboard isn't recognised, splitting login and password across pages breaks Google's password manager; on Chromebook the app installs but lets no one log in.

product.title: You must hand over a card and sign up on the website just to look around
product.minus: The cold start drives people away: you can't create an account in the app — it sends you to the website, demands card details before the trial even starts, and won't show routes or features until you subscribe.

product.title: Cancellation is hidden, money is taken after you cancel, and refunds are denied
product.minus: Dark patterns around the subscription: you can't cancel in-app, cancellation is buried across many pages, after the trial it silently charges a full year with no warning, keeps charging after you cancel, and refunds are refused or hit with a 15 € fee.

product.title: Support replies with AI boilerplate and then goes silent for weeks
product.minus: When something breaks there's no help: the chatbot is useless, emails get slow copy-paste «ride on downloaded routes» replies, and after a positive word about a refund they ghost you — though a minority did get problems solved quickly by support.

product.title: Virtual shifting and trainer connection keep dropping out
product.minus: Hardware connects unreliably: virtual shifting was promised for months and never fixed, the Wahoo Kickr drops over Bluetooth, sensors and heart-rate straps disconnect after updates — all while the same gear works fine in Zwift.

product.title: When it works, the ride is genuinely immersive and gets results
product.plus: Long-time users say the app has improved markedly across updates, the global routes are addictive, drafting and Strava segments keep adding up, and it brings back the joy of cycling — some have had zero crashes over years.

product.title: Avatars and UI lag behind: no dark skin tones, tiny stats, forced landscape
product.minus: The presentation grates: the default avatar is a white man even when you set female, there's no dark skin tone to pick, on a phone the app is locked to landscape, the buttons are tiny and unreadable, and there's simply no in-app sound.

product.title: Set-and-forget: auto-pause and voice splits make tracking effortless
product.plus: What users love most: auto-pause when you stop and auto-resume when you ride, plus voice mile announcements — strap the phone in and just go.

product.title: Does one thing and nails it: nothing bloated
product.plus: Users prize that it doesn't try to be everything — it gives map, distance, time, speed and calories, and stops there.

product.title: The free tier is genuinely enough — and it doesn't beg for money
product.plus: Many ride on the free version for years and stay happy: the basics cover their needs, ads are minimal, and the upsell doesn't nag.

product.title: Perfect for beginners and seniors: clear from the first try
product.plus: Brand-new cyclists and older users specifically note they got it right away — the app motivates them and doesn't intimidate with complexity.

product.title: Multi-sport: one tracker for cycling, walking, horses and kayaking
product.plus: People use it well beyond cycling — for walking, running, motorcycling, horse riding and kayaking — valuing one home for all their activity.

product.title: Years-long reliability: runs for years without failing
product.plus: A large group of long-timers report using it for 3, 5, even more years, several times a week, and it has never let them down.

product.title: The forced sign-up before you can start frustrates even fans
product.minus: The app demands a login and acceptance of terms before it lets you ride — people want to just start and sort it out later, and login/password failures lock them out entirely.

product.title: Hidden subscription and hard cancellation wreck trust
product.minus: Some users are furious that the subscription and its price aren't disclosed up front, that the app takes your card and won't let you cancel before charging, and that email opt-out doesn't work.

product.title: Updates break what worked: saving, consent screens, crashes
product.minus: After updates, workouts stop saving, the terms and privacy screens become impassable, and the app crashes — taking other apps down with it.

product.title: Nagging about disabled notifications, and settings that change themselves
product.minus: Users deliberately turn notifications off, yet the app still tells them on every launch that they're off — and sometimes rewrites its own settings.

product.title: GPS is accurate, then draws straight lines and shorts your miles
product.minus: Many praise the accuracy, but for some the track comes out as a straight line, jumps between points, shorts the mileage, or fails to align over repeated laps.

product.title: Battery drain and no power-save mode for long rides
product.minus: On long rides the app noticeably drains the battery, won't run in power-save mode, and lacks a lightweight large-readout speedometer mode.

product.title: Missing route planning, sensors, and auto-finish
product.minus: Power users miss planning a ride in advance, connecting speed and cadence sensors, and auto-finish — a forgotten ride keeps recording in a car at highway speed.

product.title: Connection to trainer and sensors drops mid-ride
product.minus: The single most common pain: the app loses its link to the trainer, heart-rate monitor or controllers mid-ride and the workout is gone. Users say swapping phone, Wi-Fi or device makes no difference, and many leave for competitors over it.

product.title: Endless mandatory updates before every ride
product.minus: Almost every time before a ride there's another update to wait through — sometimes 3GB, sometimes ten minutes. You're ready to pedal and instead you sit and wait; for many this has become the defining annoyance.

product.title: The sharply raised subscription feels like a rip-off
product.minus: The price jumped 40-50% (to £17.99 / $20 a month), and users find it out of proportion to what they get, especially given the bugs. Many name free rival MyWhoosh as the reason they're leaving.

product.title: Crashes and freezes mid-workout that wipe your progress
product.minus: The app crashes every few minutes, gets stuck loading, or 'stops responding,' forcing you to start the workout over. Android is especially unstable, and reinstalling or rebooting doesn't fix it.

product.title: The screen flips itself upside down
product.minus: A known Android-tablet bug: auto-rotate misfires and the picture keeps flipping, especially from the shake of hard pedaling. Support tells people to install third-party apps — hardly a fix for a screen you can't read.

product.title: Graphics look dated, especially on Android
product.minus: Many find the visuals primitive — '90s,' 'Atari.' The sting is that Android graphics are visibly worse than on iPad/Mac/Windows, even on high-end devices with flagship specs.

product.title: Huge size and updates devour storage
product.minus: A 1.5-3GB download, updates that demand even more, and on weaker devices it hits 'out of storage' — failing to open or freezing on 'unzipping files.' People are begging for a lite version.

product.title: Forced sign-up and data collection before you can even ride
product.minus: You can't even check trainer compatibility without creating an account loaded with personal details and a card on file. The pushy location permission, the missing account-delete option, and post-signup spam all grate.

product.title: Payment and cancellation are a broken mess
