product.minus: Billing bypasses Google Play: people keep getting charged after cancelling, the sign-up flow simply doesn't work, foreign cards are refused, and refunds are near-impossible. Support is no help here.

product.title: Turns dull indoor training into an addictive game
product.plus: The core reason for the love: people who hated training indoors now look forward to it. The virtual worlds, riding with real people, and gamification make time fly and keep them hooked.

product.title: Genuinely motivates you to train and keeps you fit year-round
product.plus: Through winter, rain and snow, the app gives people a reason to get on the bike every day. They report real progress: weight lost, power and speed up, better sleep and mood.

product.title: Structured workouts and training plans are praised for quality
product.plus: Beyond the game, users value the well-designed workouts, plans and FTP tests: the app coaches you through the session, gives tips, and helps with cadence and power. For many it's a full-blown coach.

product.title: The mobile UI is a squeezed-down desktop, awkward on a phone
product.minus: On a phone the fonts are tiny and unreadable, lists snap back to the top, buttons are small, and sound won't mute. Many ask for a dedicated mobile app instead of the PC version crammed onto a small screen.

product.title: Cycling and running only — rowers and other machines left out
product.minus: People buy a rowing machine advertised as Zwift-compatible, only to find the app supports just cycling and running. Requests for rowing and other activities recur but go unanswered.

product.title: Running is effectively free — a standout reason to love it
product.plus: Runners point out that Zwift is free for running, turning a dreary treadmill into a competition. With a speed pod and a Garmin watch it sets up easily, and the motivation to run climbs.

product.title: The watch keeps disconnecting and demands re-pairing several times a day
product.minus: The single most common pain: after an update the app stops holding the link to the watch, sync breaks, and people have to re-pair from scratch — sometimes several times a day, across different models and phones. It turns the watch into a useless brick.

product.title: The sheer depth of training and health analytics is the main reason people love it
product.plus: For those whose setup just works, the volume of data is the draw: sleep, stress, HRV, body battery, recovery, training load, per-activity stats. Many say Garmin gives more information than they could ever ask for, and it motivates them more than Fitbit or Apple ever did.

product.title: The Connect+ subscription and paywalling features that came with the watch they bought
product.minus: Loyal long-term fans are furious about the new subscription: they paid $1500 for a watch and now Garmin charges a recurring fee and locks basic features, AI, challenges and route sending behind a paywall. It reads as greed and a betrayal of the people who built the brand.

product.title: A cluttered, unintuitive interface — software from a hardware-first company
product.minus: A recurring theme: data is scattered illogically, there are too many tabs, the graphs are hard to read, and settings are buried so deep you have to Google or hit Reddit. People say outright that Garmin is great at hardware and that this is the worst app of any wearable they've owned.

product.title: Every update breaks something: the calendar, sync, notifications
product.minus: Updates here are a source of risk, not improvement. After updates, calendar events break with wrong time zones, breathwork stops working, notifications vanish, and sleep and stress stop syncing. The refrain is 'worked for years, and now it doesn't'.

product.title: The app barely loads: 30 seconds, minutes, sometimes won't open at all
product.minus: Performance is its own pain: the app is slow, laggy, gets stuck on the 'connect' splash screen, takes 30 to 170 seconds to open instead of two, and for some it simply stops opening at all even after a reinstall.

product.title: Useless without internet — an outdoors company with no offline access to your data
product.minus: A paradox for a brand built on hiking and the backcountry: with no connection, the app won't work. You can't view your watch data over Bluetooth in the mountains, the woods, on a boat or at sea — exactly where Garmin is supposed to shine.

product.title: The 'share your data' prompt keeps popping up over and over
product.minus: A distinct irritant: every time you open the main page, a 'help us keep improving' / share-your-data prompt appears, and tapping 'no' is never remembered. Combined with half-screen ads for a free trial, it drives people to rage.

product.title: A thin exercise database and an unforgiving search for strength training
product.minus: For strength training the exercise database is thin: basic gym machines are missing, you can't add a custom exercise, and search won't find 'pull-ups' or 'situp' unless you type the exact name. People hold up Hevy as how it should be done.

product.title: Drains phone battery with background sync you can't turn off
product.minus: The app sits in the background and drains the phone battery — especially on Samsung, where the OS diagnostics explicitly flag its high CPU usage. There's no way to stop it running in the background, and some have to restart or uninstall just to get their data.

product.title: Garmin Pay and integrations that exist on paper but don't work in practice
product.minus: Garmin Pay works for no bank across dozens of cards worldwide for many users, units won't switch to miles/kg, there's no in-app language separate from the system one, and MyFitnessPal sync suddenly sits behind a paywall. A lot of what's advertised simply doesn't work.

product.title: When it works, a reliable companion for years — the best for serious athletes
product.plus: Beneath all the complaints sits a solid core of happy users who've run Garmin for 7 to 20 years, value the backward compatibility with old watches, the LiveTrack feature for solo runs, and the fact that the app keeps getting friendlier year over year and closing the gap on rivals.

product.title: Escaping a sinking Fitbit: Garmin became the refuge for users Google abandoned
product.plus: A noticeable wave of newcomers arrived after Google 'ruined' Fitbit, and they're delighted: more data, MyFitnessPal sync that works out of the box, no AI junk or paywalls (in their experience), and top-notch food logging. To them, Garmin is what Fitbit should have become.

product.title: Impossible to uninstall — locked out even with the password
product.minus: The single most common complaint: the app blocks its own removal. Even parents who know the login and password get stuck — it becomes a device admin and won't let go, driving people to threaten lawsuits, do a factory reset, or buy a new phone.

product.title: Blocks things the parents never blocked
product.minus: The app blocks allowed apps and sites of its own accord — Google, Gmail, settings, the bank app, school resources, even the clock. Parents see "nothing blocked" in their panel, yet on the kid's phone everything is still locked.

product.title: Glitches, lags, and bricks the phone
product.minus: Relentless bugs: the phone lags, restarts, freezes for 5-15 minutes, and the block overlay demands a restart. Picture-in-picture and split-screen are hit hardest — open one and the screen goes into a spasm you can't break out of.

product.title: Kids bypass it in minutes — the protection is for show
product.minus: Kids openly brag how easy the controls are to defeat: safe mode and hard reset, pulling accessibility during an update, Samsung's Secure Folder, deactivating straight from the Play Store. Parents pay and keep losing control to a tech-savvy child.

product.title: Teens feel surveilled and trust destroyed
product.minus: The most emotional reviews come from the kids themselves: the app reads their messages and search history, strips their privacy, and in their words wrecks the relationship with their parents. It's described as "jail," "spyware," "ruined my social life."

product.title: Kills basic phone features with no toggle
product.minus: Split-screen, pop-up window, edge panel, other browsers, voice search, AI assistants — all blocked with no way to turn it off. Users keep asking for toggles so they don't lose ordinary phone capabilities.

product.title: The timer lies — it cuts screen time early
product.minus: Time tracking is inaccurate: it locks early, closes all tabs 10 minutes before the limit, kicks you out of apps and calls, and the phone won't turn back on at 7 AM as set. There's often no "2 more minutes" button to save your work.

product.title: Breaks Google and the browser — can't do schoolwork
product.minus: Google and image search get flagged "unsafe" and refuse to work, the browser reloads endlessly. Kids can't look up info for a project, open a school site, or sit an exam — schoolwork takes a direct hit.

product.title: Nagging shortcut bubble and a flood of notifications
product.minus: A permanent floating bubble clings to the screen edge, gets in the way, and won't go; meanwhile the app spams blank notifications and "update" / "grant permissions" demands — sometimes every five minutes, mid-game.

product.title: Drains the battery and eats mobile data
product.minus: The background activity hammers battery life — a Samsung that lasted 2-3 days dies in 3 hours. On top of that the app devours gigabytes of mobile data overnight, and you can't turn it off.

product.title: Expensive and you can't cancel the subscription
product.minus: You pay $30-50 a year for what many call money down the drain, and the app won't let you cancel. Parents feel they're simply being milked while the core features barely work.

product.title: For anxious parents it still works as a tool
product.plus: A minority of parents (and a couple of honest teens) admit it helps: you can set schedules, per-app limits, cap screen time, and cover both phone and laptop. Several reviews point out the low rating is upset kids, not a broken product.

product.title: Monitoring constantly disconnects from the kids' devices
product.minus: The number-one pain point: the app loses contact with the child's phone daily and has to be reconnected by hand, with the device in your possession. iPhone and Android alike; for a paid service it turns the parent into unpaid tech support.

product.title: Location freezes for hours and updates with huge delays
product.minus: The map shows the child at school hours after they've left, or simply "no activity in 24 hours." For people who bought it for safety this defeats the whole purpose: the one time you actually need a location, it isn't there.

product.title: The AI flags utterly harmless things as threats
product.minus: The system tags jokes, slang and song lyrics as bullying or sexual content — down to a statue of Helen Keller and a photo of a frog. The flood of false positives is so big that parents stop reading alerts and miss the things that actually matter.

product.title: Misses the genuinely dangerous — porn and threats slip through
product.minus: The flip side of the hypersensitivity: while Bark screams about nonsense, the truly alarming stuff — porn sites, disturbing content — gets through. Parents end up finding it themselves by checking the phone by hand, which nullifies the value of paid monitoring.

product.title: Kids easily bypass the protection, and the whole point collapses
product.minus: Teens turn the app off, delete it, share internet via another device's hotspot, or log in through the parent's saved password. Blocked apps get downloaded and run anyway. Protection that can be switched off stops being protection.

product.title: Support is an AI bot; reaching a human is near impossible
product.minus: When something breaks, the parent meets only an AI chatbot with canned advice like "uninstall and reinstall." No phone number, promised callbacks and emails never come. Against the high price, this is what enrages people most.

product.title: Endless manual updates on the child's phone
product.minus: The app demands updates several times a week, and each time you must physically get hold of the child's phone and redo the permissions setup (especially accessibility). There's no push update — it kills any stealth and steals your time.

product.title: Cluttered, unintuitive interface — especially after the redesign
product.minus: The app behaves like a clunky website: the back gesture closes it entirely, settings are impossible to find, simple actions take ten steps. The recent redesign only made navigation worse and removed some of the old features.

product.title: Drains the battery and slows the child's phone down
product.minus: Bark eats up device resources: the phone lags, the battery dies by midday, the VPN breaks the internet and stops other apps working. Kids feel it most — the phone turns into a brick.

product.title: Pricing is steep, and cancelling the subscription is a trap
product.minus: Around $14 a month or ~$200 a year for a service that works half the time. Cancelling is hard: "cancel anytime" turns out to be a non-refundable year prepaid, prices quietly rise, and the app locks you out of subscription management.

product.title: For the kids themselves it's total surveillance that kills trust
product.minus: Teens describe Bark as a prison: every word goes to the parents, you can't change a password or add a friend without a code, and it breeds anxiety and a constant sense of being watched. Many write that the app destroyed their relationship with their parents.

product.title: When it works, it gives parents genuine peace of mind
product.plus: A chunk of parents genuinely love Bark: alerts about bullying, peer pressure and sexual content open up important conversations, and being able to see location and block content gives a feeling of safety without having to hover over the child.

product.title: Text monitoring is the thing that keeps people in and brings them back
product.plus: Despite every complaint, many admit Bark does message monitoring better than anyone. People who try alternatives come back, because no one else surfaces glimpses of the actual texts and alarming photos the way it does.

product.title: Limits and locks silently stop working
product.minus: The core complaint: the kid uses a blocked app for hours while the parent thinks everything is fine. Downtime fails, limits never apply on the device, the phone won't lock — and the app shows no error at all. The whole point of the product evaporates.

product.title: Bonus-time bug: the phone never re-locks
product.minus: The sharpest failure mechanism: a parent grants 'bonus minutes', they expire — and the device stays wide open for hours. Worse, the app itself hands the kid 12-20 hours or unlimited time with no parent action. The re-lock command between Google's servers and the phone just gets lost.

product.title: Kids easily bypass the controls
product.minus: Teens routinely strip supervision themselves: revoke the permission in app settings, delete the account, slip through in-app browsers in Viber, flip on Do Not Disturb or the hotspot. After 13 a kid can officially stop supervision with no password. The protection only exists on paper.

product.title: Changes take forever to apply
product.minus: The sync problem also hits speed: after an unlock command the phone opens 5-30 minutes later while the kid whines the whole time. Any limit edit just hangs, the app lags and freezes. The real-time control it's installed for simply isn't there.

product.title: Teens hate it and feel imprisoned
product.minus: A huge slice of reviews comes from the kids themselves: a sense of a cage, being cut off from friends, mental-health damage to the point of crying themselves to sleep. Their shared thesis: strict control breeds sneaky, distrusting kids and wrecks the parent relationship rather than protecting anyone.

product.title: Location is inaccurate and lags
product.minus: The very thing many install it for — tracking the child — works badly: coordinates lie (kid is home, app says not), the map loads forever, arrival/departure alerts come 30-60 minutes or hours late. Next to Life360 it's night and day.

product.title: Impossible to remove or unlink — you get trapped
product.minus: A nightmare of its own is getting out. Removing the app demands deleting the child's Gmail account; restrictions stay on the phone even after the app or account is gone; the parent can't sign in on the child's device and lands in an endless loop. Old devices won't unlink.

product.title: No flexibility for teens or multiple devices
product.minus: A blunt tool: the same settings hit phone, tablet and Chromebook at once, with no per-device limits. There are no age presets — a 15-year-old is treated like a five-year-old, every app needs manual approval. After 13 there's almost nothing left for the parent.

product.title: Confusing UI and zero support
product.minus: After updates the settings scatter: menu items for the parent code or locking vanish, instructions don't match reality. There's no live support, the help-section steps don't work, 'Something went wrong' errors persist for years. People leave for Bark and Qustodio.

product.title: When it works it gives parents peace of mind
product.plus: A loyal core of parents values the essentials: screen-time control, 18+ blocking, app and location monitoring — all of it free. Many say they tried paid Bark and Life360 and came back here: simpler and nicer to use. For younger kids it's a genuinely working tool.

product.title: Some kids admit the discipline helped them
product.plus: An unexpected but real strand: some teens who first hated the app admit the limits worked — grades up, new hobbies, a healthier body, calmer before exams. A rare self-admission of the product's value from the very people it's used on.

product.title: Missing message monitoring and finer features
product.minus: Engaged parents ask for what isn't there: reading messages and photos, controlling device brightness and volume, separate availability schedules instead of one all-day 'downtime', blocking the kid from turning off mobile data or airplane mode. The volume of feature requests makes the product feel unfinished.

product.title: Blocks the very things the parent allowed
product.minus: The single most common complaint: you whitelist a site or app, and Mobicip blocks it anyway. Approving the child's request does nothing, school and educational sites get cut off, YouTube stays blocked even when allowed — while the stuff you actually wanted blocked slips through.

product.title: Impossible to uninstall or deactivate
product.minus: The uninstall protection turns into a trap: the app won't come off via password, settings, Play Store, or the parent device. People resort to a factory reset to get rid of it — "worse than a virus."

product.title: The VPN filter breaks the internet in allowed apps
product.minus: To filter traffic Mobicip runs a VPN — and that VPN is the problem: Instagram won't load images, Snapchat and TikTok die with "no connection," pages hang on certificate errors. Disable the VPN and the apps work instantly, which pins the blame squarely on it.

product.title: Glitches and crashes, especially after updates
product.minus: Constant instability: the app crashes, lags, throws errors, slows the phone and even chews up 70% CPU. Each update routinely breaks what used to work — after an update everything suddenly gets blocked for no reason.

product.title: The parent app shows no activity or location
product.minus: The whole point — monitoring — fails: history comes up empty, videos are labelled "untitled," the dashboard is blank, the digest reports "no activity" while the kid was on the phone all day. Location shows the parent's spot instead of the child's, or finds nothing.

product.title: Kids easily get around it
product.minus: The limits are trivially bypassed: restart the phone, toggle the screen off and on, change the date forward, put the app to sleep in battery settings, or sideload browsers from Chrome. One kid "killed" the protection in two days — the filter turns out to be decorative.

product.title: Locks down basic apps and bricks the device itself
product.minus: When it overreaches, it blocks the calculator, contacts, phone, maps — or the whole screen, refusing to let the device out of the Mobicip app until the battery dies. Sometimes it even locks the parent out, turning the tablet into a paperweight.

product.title: Screen-time limits don't actually shut the device off
product.minus: Sleep schedules and daily caps often don't fire: the kid is on the phone at night past the limit, while the tracker absurdly logs 45 minutes for a full day of heavy use. Changes to the limit take up to an hour to reach the device.

product.title: Paid, and you can only unsubscribe by email
product.minus: The "free" framing is dishonest: they take your card the moment the trial starts, charge a year upfront, and there's no cancel button — the only way out is emailing support, which may never reply. Some users call it a scam and block their bank card.

product.title: Support: some delighted, others wait months
product.plus: Many praise support as a genuine strength: real people reply within a day, polite and on-point, sometimes crafting a custom fix and even calling. For some users the service alone is the reason they stay.

product.title: Support vanishes for days and months
product.minus: The flip side: no phone line, replies take 24–72 hours, or silence for weeks. People email for months with no response, can't cancel a subscription or unlock a child's locked device — and end up disputing the charge through their bank.

product.title: The only one that truly spans every platform at once
product.plus: The core reason fans love it: one profile per child applies across Android, iPhone, Chromebook and laptop alike — where Google Family Link and Microsoft Family stay locked inside their own ecosystem. For mixed-device families it's often the only option that works.

product.title: When it works, you run everything from the parent's phone
product.plus: A real strength for those it works for: remotely from your phone you can block apps, grant extra time, set a sleep schedule, locate the child — all without touching their device. A handy dashboard and clear reports deliver peace of mind.

product.title: A "time bank" and chores teach kids responsibility
product.plus: A surprisingly beloved mechanic: the child earns extra screen time by doing chores, and unused minutes "roll over" into a personal time bank. Parents value that it teaches both self-regulation and saving, rather than just forbidding.

product.title: Long-term peace of mind — works for years for some families
product.plus: A substantial share of happy users: families keep Mobicip for 4–5 years or more, the content filtering genuinely shields kids from harmful material, and keyword-search blocking works. For them it's a dependable tool they recommend to others.

product.title: Kids bypass the blocks: VPN, airplane mode, factory reset, or just deleting the app
product.minus: Over and over, parents say a child defeats the controls within minutes — via VPN, airplane mode on Wi-Fi, a factory reset, or removing the profile, even with uninstall protection on. The protection sold as tamper-proof lasts exactly until the first search for «how to get around OurPact».

product.title: Setup needs a PC and a USB cable — a wall in the 2020s, and many simply don't own a computer
product.minus: To pair the child's phone you need a Mac or PC and a USB cable, especially for Android↔iOS pairs. People are stunned: no web option, no Chromebook support, and many simply don't own a computer — so onboarding dies right there.

product.title: Glitchy, laggy, overheats the phone and drains the battery — sometimes literally bricks the device
product.minus: The most common gripe after bypassing: the app lags the child's phone, heats it up, and burns the battery in a couple of hours. Some say the device got bricked outright or needed a factory reset, and the glitchiness feels virus-like.

product.title: Location is unreliable: shows the kid in the wrong place, not in real time, and broke after an update
product.minus: For many, tracking is the whole reason they pay — and it's what fails. Location won't update, shows yesterday instead of now, and places the kid miles off. One mom's app «showed me my child was 10 miles in the desert».

product.title: Support sends the same link, then goes silent — and won't answer email, only review replies
product.minus: When something breaks, support keeps sending the same help page, then stops replying after you push back. No phone line, email only, and people note the bitter irony: the developer replies to a review but not to an email.

product.title: Billing trap: charged for a year with no trial reminder, and refunds refused
product.minus: The promised trial-ending notice never arrives — the card gets hit for nearly $100, sometimes twice, and there's no unsubscribing or refund even after cancelling before the renewal date. Several call it an outright scam.

product.title: Schedules and blocks don't fire on their own — the block only kicks in if the kid opens the app
product.minus: The core mechanic breaks: schedules drop, blocks don't apply in real time, and the status flips itself to «access granted until I say so». Worse, the block often only triggers when the child opens the app on their own phone.

product.title: No per-app time limits and no usage reports — only on/off and a single time allowance
product.minus: Parents want to cap a specific app by minutes per day and see where screen time goes — but get only a blanket «allowance» and a block-everything toggle. With no reports and no per-app limit, it feels narrower than Apple Screen Time.

product.title: The start/stop design: the kid has to start and stop their own time — a baffling UX choice
product.minus: To do anything, the child must open the app and manually press «start», then «stop» on their allowance. Parents are baffled: why not just measure the time and block when it runs out? This mechanic makes the control a fiction.

product.title: Android is the stepchild: can't block Play Store, individual apps aren't visible, the UI is cut off
product.minus: On iOS the app is «phenomenal», but on Android it's gutted: you can't block Google Play, new apps aren't auto-blocked, individual apps don't fit on screen, and some controls are only visible from an iPhone.

product.title: Scrambles icons and folders, breaks layout and widgets, sometimes wipes notes on the child's device
product.minus: Installing and blocking scatter the child's carefully arranged folders and home screen, break widgets, and for some it deleted saved notes and data. You're left rebuilding everything by hand — a painful side effect.

product.title: Teens hate the surveillance: a red «RECORDING» banner, a sense of total control and resentment
product.minus: A huge chunk of reviews come from the kids themselves: the control suffocates, parents «treat me like a toddler», and the red «RECORDING IN PROGRESS» banner blows the cover on the screenshots. Some say it damaged family relationships.

product.title: Screenshots of the child's screen — the killer feature that keeps people despite the rest
product.plus: Many loyal users stick around precisely for the screenshots of the child's screen: you can see what the kid is actually doing. For parents it's the one capability free rivals lack, and it outweighs the bugs.

product.title: The one cross-platform control that actually works: an Android parent managing a child's iPhone
product.plus: The standout win over rivals: the «I have Android, my kid has an iPhone» combo actually works here, which is nearly impossible to find elsewhere. Long-time subscribers call it the best option for managing kids' iOS devices.

product.title: When it works it brings peace of mind: kids sleep on time, grades rise, screen habits under control
product.plus: For some families it genuinely changes life: the kid sleeps on time, behavior and grades improve, and the parent gets peace of mind. Some kids later thank their parents for removing the temptation — years-long loyal users back this up.

product.title: The free tier is hollow: everything useful is behind a ~$10/mo paywall, no way to test it first
product.minus: The free version offers almost nothing — just bedtime — while everything useful costs $9.99/mo or $99.99/yr. People resent that they can't even test the promised features before paying, and point to the free Google Family Link.

product.title: Adware behavior: self-installs via the browser, reinstalls and won't uninstall — people call it a virus
product.minus: A distinct group is angry not about the controls but about how the app reached them: it self-downloaded from an ad or via Chrome, reinstalls, and resists removal. To them this is straight-up malware behavior.

product.title: Limits and blocks silently fall off — the control is fake
product.minus: Parents set downtime and limits, and the kid's phone stays wide open: restrictions remove themselves, blocked apps become accessible again, and the parent only finds out once the child has already been on Snapchat for hours.

product.title: The «bonus time» bug: the phone never re-locks
product.minus: The single most cited concrete defect: after granted bonus minutes the device fails to re-lock. The app itself hands the kid 12–20 hours of unlimited access, while the parent app shows everything as fine.

product.title: Kids easily bypass the controls and remove supervision themselves
product.minus: The kid disables control via app permissions, the embedded browser inside Viber, quick-settings hotspot — or, once they turn 13, simply removes supervision themselves with no password. Protection a teen can switch off in a minute.

product.title: Location is inaccurate and arrives badly delayed
product.minus: Arrival and departure alerts lag by tens of minutes or hours, the map pin is wrong about whether the kid is home, and sometimes tracking just drops out — for an app selling safety, that's a gap in its most important job.

product.title: Teens feel imprisoned — the app destroys trust
product.minus: The loudest emotion in the reviews: kids aged 13–18 say they feel like prisoners, cut off from friends and social media. Many state outright that strict control wrecks the parent-child relationship and brings them to tears.

product.title: After updates the settings become impossible to find and change
product.minus: Changing limits means flipping them back and forth manually every day, you can't set a limit on a group of apps, and after each update the buttons you need (lock, bedtime) just vanish from the menu. The interface only gets worse.

product.title: «Something went wrong»: changes won't save, for years
product.minus: Lock and unlock commands never reach the device, every action returns «Something went wrong. Try again in a few minutes», and saved times jump to something else. The sync between the servers and the kid's phone simply gets lost.

product.title: The screen-time counter is wrong
product.minus: The app burns time the kid never used: it says «time's up» at zero minutes, counts unlimited apps, and doesn't match the real per-app usage. The result is fights between kids and parents.

product.title: You can't lift the controls or uninstall the app
product.minus: The control stays on the kid's phone even after the app or Google account is deleted; there's no way to unlock without the password, and the phone stays locked with no option to open it. Even adults can't wipe the imposed app.

product.title: When it works — it brings peace of mind and really changes the kid's habits
product.plus: A chunk of parents, and even some kids, admit it: the limits helped cut phone addiction, raise grades, and pull the kid back to studying and hobbies. Remote control of screen time and location gives a real sense of safety.

product.title: No fine-grained settings for the teen's age
product.minus: Past 13 the control nearly ends, and before that it's all equally harsh: you can't give a 15-year-old more freedom than a seven-year-old, can't split settings per device, and every download has to be approved by hand.

product.title: Downtime blocks calls — no way to reach the kid in an emergency
product.minus: The whole phone locks down, including the basic phone function: the kid can't call or text during downtime, and the parent can't reach them if something happens away from home. A safety app cuts off the very means of communication.

product.title: Kids bypass and uninstall it within minutes
product.minus: The core failure: kids uninstall it, disable device-admin through settings, add a second user, or just google "how to disable FamiSafe" — and the whole point of control evaporates, especially on iOS where a child can simply remove it with no code.

product.title: Works for a few days, then stops
product.minus: A recurring pattern: great for the first days, then limits stop limiting, sync hangs, and you constantly have to "repair"/reinstall the app and re-grant permissions. No stability even on a paid plan.

product.title: Screen-time limits and app blocking don't hold
product.minus: Blocked apps still open via split-screen or a floating window, limits reset or show different times day to day, there's no real-time instant block, and you can't grant bonus time without fiddling app-by-app.

product.title: Updates stripped out core features
product.minus: Loyal users are furious: the "Fammy"/"Fammy Plus" update (late 2025) removed the per-app time breakdown, the remaining-time view, bonus time, and YouTube Kids / Messenger Kids monitoring, and the new UI is called worse than before.

product.title: Cross-platform with iOS is its own nightmare
product.minus: The Android-parent / iPhone-child pairing barely works: setup only via a PC (which many don't have), apps vanish, social media and photos aren't tracked, and a couple of times setup hard-locked the child's iPhone until a factory reset.

product.title: Screenshots and audio listening exist on paper only
product.minus: Screenshots come back blank or never load (especially when the app flags one as inappropriate but you can't see it), the interval isn't honored, and the one-way audio either won't connect or only works while the child is actively using the phone.

product.title: Billing and refunds: price jumps, charges stick, no refund
product.minus: The store shows one price (e.g. ₹395 or ₹1950) but charges several times more at checkout; money is taken after cancellation or without OTP, refunds are nearly impossible, and Google purchases sometimes land on a "guest account" you can't access.

product.title: Support is a bot and canned replies, no human reachable
product.minus: On hard problems support is useless: only AI bots and canned replies, no phone line, the website link is broken, people are told to wait weeks for "analysis" and end up with "no resolution" — dozens of emails with nothing to show.

product.title: Impossible to uninstall — and sometimes bricks the device
product.minus: An ugly tail end: it refuses to uninstall, blacks out the screen when you try, leaves the phone "supervised by famisafe" even after deletion, and some users are forced into a factory reset and lose everything.

product.title: Location tracking gives parents real peace of mind
product.plus: The most-praised feature: location and geofences are accurate enough to check on a child without constant calls; many keep the subscription for years just for this — more precise than maps, real reassurance when kids travel or come home late.

product.title: Balanced control without a total lockdown is why people pick it
product.plus: Parents of older kids are won over by the middle ground: you can cut social media and endless scrolling while keeping calls, school, and needed contact; alerts come when something's off rather than constantly — which reduces fights, since it's "the app" enforcing rules, not the parent.

product.title: Recent updates and stability won some skeptics back
product.plus: Not all downside: some users see bugs fixed, the child-usage notifications finally arriving, new features added (WhatsApp), and the app holding stable for weeks — a few raised their rating from 1 to 5 stars after the improvements.

product.title: Kids escape the locked mode — the lock just doesn't hold
product.minus: The one job fails: spam the home or recents button, catch a pop-up, or just poke around and the child lands on the full phone with every app. Many say it's all set up correctly (pin, home locked) and it still leaks.

product.title: Ads invaded the free version — and killed it
product.minus: After going ad-supported, long-time users say the app "went downhill": a video before kids mode starts, an ad on every pin press in the parent screen, adult ads inside an app built for kids. Many uninstalled over exactly this.

product.title: In-app ads are a back door to the Play Store and YouTube
product.minus: Even with the Play Store blocked, the child taps an ad inside an allowed game and lands in the store, YouTube or a browser and downloads anything. The whitelist is bypassed not by a "hack" but by the app's own ads.

product.title: Glitches, launches itself, freezes for days
product.minus: Stability is shaky: it auto-launches at random, "bounces" on screen, freezes on the timer and won't open until reinstalled. The painful part is that when it crashes the protection drops and the phone is wide open.

product.title: A simple lock with no hidden catch — that's why they love it
product.plus: When it works it does exactly what it promises: the phone becomes a kiosk of allowed apps, the kid can't call, delete, buy or change settings. Many have used it for years on old phones and tablets and trust the free version specifically.

product.title: Hidden paywall: "free" turns out to be a subscription
product.minus: It's not the price but the timing: they walk you through the whole setup, then hit you with "$5 a month." The subscription is described as mandatory, with no warning up front, and it feels like a trap.

product.title: Once-free features got moved behind the paywall
product.minus: Users are angry that basics — adding/removing apps, locking the notification bar, icon size, wallpaper — used to be free and now need premium. Those who once bought a "lifetime" license feel cheated.

product.title: You can lock yourself out: pin rejected, phone bricked
product.minus: The same stickiness that traps the kid turns on the parent: forget the pin or it stops being accepted and you can't get out, the phone bricks, only a factory reset saves it. Several people lost access to their device this way.

product.title: Responsive support rescues the hard cases
product.plus: A clear strength for paying and long-time users is live support: quick replies, help configuring for a specific device, refunds on wrong charges. Several raised their rating specifically after the developer reached out.

product.title: Purchases don't activate, cancelling is hell
product.minus: A separate cluster of money pain: you pay for premium but the app still shows the free version, with no restore-purchase button; cancelling is near impossible, charges keep coming, refunds are refused. It erodes trust even among people who like the product.

product.title: Confusing setup: apps don't show, nothing is intuitive
product.minus: Some parents simply can't finish setup: after launching kids mode the app list is empty, it's unclear how to add a game to a category, remote control is browser-only, and the scheduler is "terribly laid out." A powerful feature set drowns in a clunky interface.

product.title: Saves the parent's own phone from a toddler
product.plus: The warmest use case: hand your phone to a toddler without fear. Users value that the child won't make random calls, wipe photos, text contacts or buy things in the store — exactly why many install it on every device.

product.title: Mic eavesdropping reads as surveillance, not safety
product.minus: The single most frequent and most visceral complaint: the ability to listen to the child's surroundings through the mic. Kids describe being recorded in bathrooms and showers, fear over bullying, and being unable to talk to friends. Even neutral reviewers call the feature excessive.

product.title: Total visibility kills any sense of privacy
product.minus: Kids repeat that parents see literally everything: what they google, what they watch, what they text friends. The feeling of "this is mom's phone, not mine" and "I'm being watched 24/7" runs through dozens of reviews.

product.title: The app corrodes the parent-child relationship
product.minus: Not background noise but the headline social effect: kids say they now hide from parents like strangers, argue every day after school, and feel like a "pet" or a "prisoner." Several reviews are direct pleas to parents to delete the app.

product.title: App-blocking takes away schoolwork, downtime and friends
product.minus: Kids complain that parents block the whole phone for hours or months — mid-game, during a school event, when they need to message about homework. The blocks come across as unpredictable with no way to negotiate.

product.title: Can't be removed — a trapped feeling
product.minus: A distinct pain: you can't uninstall it yourself. That frightens not only teens but an adult whose abusive ex installed Pingo — with support offering no way to delete the account. People explicitly call the missing delete option dangerous for victims.

product.title: Drains battery and slows the phone
product.minus: A concrete technical complaint backed by numbers: phones drop from 47 hours of battery to less than half, idle drain jumps from 1.1%/h to 16%/h. Several blame the constant background operation and hardware wear.

product.title: Location is regularly wrong and sparks fights
product.minus: Even supporters admit the tracking is inaccurate. The GPS pin drifts a couple of blocks off, shows the child "in a river" during school hours, draws routes in odd zigzags. For parents it directly causes arguments.

product.title: Connection and tracking break, even after paying
product.minus: Paying parents lose exactly what they paid for: after a yearly subscription notifications stop, the child "never leaves home," the tracker goes silent after six months with no way to restart it. Support is unreachable on top of that.

product.title: Pricing stings next to free alternatives
product.minus: Cost surfaces as its own irritant: $70 for a "deal" when Life360 and others exist, the sense of having paid "for something useless and BAD." With features failing, the price feels especially unfair.

product.title: For parents — peace of mind and a real find when someone's lost
product.plus: Those it helps value the peace of mind specifically: knowing where the child is on the way to school, finding a lost phone, raising an alarm. One user recounts locating a mother with dementia within 50 feet multiple times.

product.title: SOS and the ring feature help in real danger
product.plus: Beyond tracking, users praise the SOS feature that shows the map and the ability to make the child's phone ring when they won't pick up. Even one teen noted the app helped reach parents in a dangerous moment.

product.title: The penguin's menacing look scares kids
product.minus: An unexpected but recurring detail: the penguin icon looks angry and frightening. Kids describe it as a "demon" staring at them, and a parent of an autistic daughter writes she feels sad thinking the penguin is mad at her.

product.title: Protection silently switches itself off — and the kid is back to no limits
product.minus: The Accessibility permission turns itself off on its own — sometimes from battery saver — and the app stops enforcing anything. Parents only find out when they manually check, because there's no alert that a device has stopped checking in.

product.title: Kids bypass the block easily — and say so themselves
product.minus: A blocked app reopens from recents, a blocked site comes back with the 'go back' button, the time-out is dodged by a specific way of starting a video. Teens brag in the reviews that they get around it 'so easily', and support replies 'yes, some kids can break the security'.

product.title: Granular per-app control is the real selling point
product.plus: You can set a limit per individual app, and mark the ones you want — music, school apps, messengers — as 'always allowed' or 'encouraged' so they don't eat into the overall screen-time budget. This granularity is what keeps parents renewing for years.

product.title: Doesn't show texts, calls or message content — the thing people paid for
product.minus: Message and call logs are either empty or never show up at all, and test curse-words don't get flagged. People buy the paid version specifically to monitor texting — and get a feature that simply doesn't function.

product.title: Time-out and extend-time spin forever and never register
product.minus: You tap 'extend' or 'time-out', the circle just keeps spinning, and nothing changes on the child's device until the phone is restarted. It defeats the whole point of the very buttons people keep the app for.

product.title: The limit fires out of nowhere — 'time's up' when the phone wasn't even touched
product.minus: The app claims the daily allowance is used up while the stats show zero usage, or 30 minutes counted as six hours. One user was billed nine hours of Spotify during a window when they were asleep.

product.title: Location lags by hours or fails to deliver at all
product.minus: Location refreshes an hour or more behind, throws 'can't deliver command', and there's no location history. For a parent who bought the app to know where their kid is, it breaks the core reason for buying.

product.title: Drains battery and RAM, slows the device, and hijacks the whole phone
product.minus: It constantly eats RAM and battery even on high-end phones, pops up over other screens asking for permissions it already has, and renders the device nearly unusable. On cheap tablets it bogs things down to the point of uselessness.

product.title: Cheap, and works where Family Link gave up
product.plus: At a low yearly price, it's often the one thing that actually held when a kid hacked or bypassed Google Family Link. For many, the mix of price and uninstall-proof protection outweighs all the rough edges.

product.title: Support sends a canned reply or doesn't answer at all
product.minus: A chunk of users email repeatedly and get back a copy-paste of the same steps they already tried, or silence; there's no live line. It sharply contrasts with others who got a reply within a day and a real fix.

product.title: Google flags the app as harmful and disables it
product.minus: On install, Play Protect warns of a 'harmful app' and periodically disables or even uninstalls Boomerang on its own — and loyal users blame Google and its competing Family Link for it, not the developer. Either way it raises the barrier to entry.

product.title: Kids hate it and see it as surveillance that breaks trust
product.minus: Teens themselves pile on one-star reviews, calling it spyware, an invasion of privacy, and the cause of a broken relationship with their parents. One review describes the block cutting off access to suicide hotlines during a crisis — a genuine safety issue, not just a tantrum.

product.title: An update logged people out and wiped years of workout history
product.minus: After updating, the app abruptly drops users to a login screen, and on signing back in the account is empty: hundreds of workouts, templates, PRs and analytics built over years simply vanish, often with no way to get them back.

product.title: Google/email sign-in just doesn't work, and the reset email never arrives
product.minus: Google login spins forever or throws an error, registration complains the email is "already in use", and the password-reset email never arrives — leaving people locked out even of accounts they've paid for.

product.title: The core strength is a no-frills, ad-free "digital notebook"
product.plus: People love it precisely for its simplicity: no ads, no pop-ups, no pushy AI — you just pick an exercise, punch in weight and reps, and tick it off. It's the notebook-style tracker many had been hunting for years.

product.title: The new inline rest timers cluttered the UI and no longer auto-start
product.minus: The update turned rest timers into a separate line between every set, bloating the list and cluttering the screen; on top of that they no longer auto-start when you mark a set complete, and you have to manually delete them from every exercise when building a template.

product.title: The free plan is capped at 3 (now 2) templates — not enough for a weekly program
product.minus: The free version only lets you save three (and after the update, for some, two) custom templates, which isn't enough for a push/pull/legs split or a week-long program — and you only find out about the limit after a long onboarding.

product.title: The standout feature is auto-filled previous results and PR tracking right in the set
product.plus: During a workout it shows what you did last time (reps and weight), tallies total weight moved and volume per exercise, and flags a PR the moment you beat it — exactly what makes it a reliable progressive-overload tool.

product.title: No watch app for Wear OS / Samsung, even though Apple Watch is supported
product.minus: Many want to control sets and the timer from their wrist without grabbing the phone between sets, but there's no Wear OS or Samsung-watch companion (while rival Hevy has one); on top of that, Garmin notifications stopped arriving after an update.

product.title: One of the few trackers with a genuinely generous free tier
product.plus: Despite the template cap, many use the free version for years and say it covers 90% of their needs with no ads — a rarity next to rivals that lock basic features behind a subscription.

product.title: A one-time lifetime license is a big trust-builder
product.plus: Unlike endless subscriptions, you can pay ~$100 once and own Pro forever; many cite this as the main reason they bought in and call it well worth it after a year on the free tier.

product.title: Missing exercises, and custom ones can't get a form photo/video
product.minus: The library lacks several popular movements (kettlebells, farmer's walk, many bodyweight exercises), and you can only add a custom exercise without a form image or video — which makes manual adding far less useful for beginners.

product.title: The update broke input: numbers land in the wrong box, workouts won't finish
product.minus: After the update, fast input drops weight and reps into the wrong box or into previous sets, and the "completed" mark doesn't register, so the workout can't be finished — forcing an app restart mid-session.

product.title: Replacing an exercise and PR/volume math are buggy
product.minus: When you replace an exercise, the previous session's history doesn't pull through and set/weight data fails to carry over; on top of that the app counts weaker lifts as records and shows different volume on the workout screen versus the overview.

product.title: The paywall appears only at the end, after you've entered everything
product.minus: The app lets you finish the entire onboarding — height, weight, age, email, equipment, goal — generates a first workout, and only then springs a mandatory subscription with no free option. Users call it a bait-and-switch and a waste of their time.

product.title: The free tier was removed with no warning — long-time users got locked out
product.minus: People relied on the free version for years for plans and logging, then one day launch greets them with a mandatory subscription. It reads as betrayal — "enshittification," "greed," a tool they leaned on for years gone with no announcement.

product.title: Your own logged workout history is locked behind the paywall too
product.minus: The sharpest cut: users with years of logged data can't even view their past workouts or progress without paying. They usually discover it right before a session — pay or lose your data.

product.title: The trial auto-rolls into an annual plan — surprise big charges, refunds refused
product.minus: After the "free" week the app charges not a month but a full year — sums of $95–$170. Cancelling is hard to find (browser only, or inside the app you can't enter without paying), and support and Google both refuse refunds.

product.title: It removes all the mental work: open it and just train
product.plus: Users' biggest love: no deciding what to train. The app serves up a ready workout of the day, gives beginners and returners the structure they lacked, and takes the planning out of going to the gym.

product.title: Workouts are built around the equipment you actually have — home, gym, travel
product.plus: A favourite feature: you list what you have and the plan uses only that. You can keep multiple gym profiles, and for missing machines the app swaps in a replacement that hits the same muscle.

product.title: …but the equipment you set is often ignored anyway
product.minus: The flip side of that same feature: even with all available gear selected, the app keeps suggesting exercises for machines the user doesn't own and recommending weights they don't have. Getting machine-only workouts proves impossible.

product.title: Demo videos and how-tos teach you proper form
product.plus: A decisive plus for beginners: every movement has a video with a real person plus how-to descriptions. Users learn technique, avoid injury and pick up new movements without YouTube.

product.title: It visualises your progress and which muscles you've worked
product.plus: A strong motivator: the app maps which muscles you hit, totals your pounds lifted and shows week-to-week strength gains. Users credit it with weight lost and muscle gained.

product.title: Android, Wear OS and Samsung are the cut-down, lagging version vs iOS
product.minus: Samsung and Android users get less: no muscle-based exercise picking, no HIIT generation, no changing weight/reps on the watch and no rest timer there. Workouts don't sync to Samsung Health / Health Connect. The same people rated 5★ on iPhone.

product.title: The algorithm sticks at one weight and churns out repetitive workouts
product.minus: Experienced users knock the AI's logic: without entering RiR/RIR it stalls you at the same weight without telling you what to enter to progress; pushes high reps instead of adding load; serves the same workouts in a new order. Several say they actually lost strength.

product.title: Rest timers are unreliable, and cooldowns have none at all
product.minus: A core tracking feature works badly: the timer won't fire if you switch apps or the screen sleeps, reportedly broken since February 2025 and still unfixed. Cooldown moves that say "30 seconds" have no timer at all.

product.title: The price stings — pricier than a gym membership, with no regional pricing
product.minus: Even people who like the features find the subscription overpriced: $15–$22/month or $75–$96/year, more than the gym membership itself. Users in India and Indonesia call it unaffordable. Many would pay once but not subscribe.

product.title: You can't tick a set as done — the checkbox refuses to register
product.minus: The most frequent and most painful issue: mid-workout, the "set done" checkbox simply stops responding. People tap ten times, back out and re-enter the workout, and still spend minutes logging a single set — the exact thing the app exists to do.

product.title: Crashes and freezes right in the middle of a workout
product.minus: The app crashes for no reason during a session, breaks the rest timers, and for some it goes as far as freezing or force-restarting the phone itself. Especially galling for long-time, paying users.

product.title: Every update breaks something new
product.minus: A recurring complaint: a fresh update reintroduces old bugs or breaks workout upload, forcing a manual force-stop and restart. The sense of instability stacks up release after release.

product.title: The paid "coach" hands out impossible, bad routines
product.minus: The Pro auto-coach disappoints: routines are either physically impossible or just bad. It stings more because this is the very feature you're being asked to pay for.

product.title: Older data and history are locked behind a paywall
product.minus: The free plan holds measurement and workout history older than three months "hostage", limits import/export of your own data, and caps you at four routines. People resent paying just to see their own progress.

product.title: Sometimes loses your set-up routines and history
product.minus: Some people set up routines only to find half gone next time, and lost their workouts when moving to a new phone. For a progress tracker, losing data is the most trust-destroying failure of all.

product.title: A generous, ad-free free tier is the number-one reason people love it
product.plus: Over and over, people are amazed that something this capable is free: no ads, no pushy upsell, and the base tier is more than enough for full workout and progress tracking.

product.title: Makes progressive overload visible — shows you last time's weights
product.plus: The core working value: the app shows the weight and reps you used last time, so you don't have to remember or look it up. It directly motivates adding weight and keeping the progression going.

product.title: Simple, intuitive UI — fast to log right there in the gym
product.plus: People are won over by the clean, clear interface: building a routine, jotting weights between sets, swapping to a different day — it all happens fast and fuss-free, even for beginners.

product.title: Huge exercise library, plus you can add your own
product.plus: A vast library of exercises and equipment with how-to videos covers almost everything; if something's missing, you add a custom exercise. It serves both beginners and advanced lifters.

product.title: Library still has gaps — you settle for the nearest match
product.minus: Even fans keep asking for one thing: add more exercises. When the move you need is missing, you either build a custom one (which looks messy) or track "the closest similar one".

product.title: The lifting social network: motivation for some, unwanted scrolling and NSFW for others
product.minus: The social layer splits people. Some get community and motivation, but others see a forced "yet another feed": workouts default to "EVERYONE" visibility, blocking doesn't hide unpleasant content, and the point is to keep you in the app instead of training.

product.title: Rest timer and post-workout summaries keep you on track
product.plus: The beloved small touches: a built-in rest timer with an alert, an end-of-workout summary with total weight lifted, PR badges, and highlighted muscle groups. These details turn logging into a sense of accomplishment.

product.title: Sync with watches and third-party services is hit-or-miss
product.minus: Pairing with Wear OS and Apple Watch for heart rate delights people, but syncing with Samsung Health, Google Fit, and Garmin is plainly weak or missing — a frequent request to fix.

product.title: AI auto-progression silently rewrites already-logged weights and reps
product.minus: The defining wound of the update: the «adaptive» AI changes weights and reps in saved workouts on its own — sometimes to absurd numbers — breaking the entire point of a workout log. For many the settings toggle simply does nothing.

product.title: Intrusive AI insights and pop-ups fire on every single set
product.minus: The app interrogates you after every set about why you didn't follow its suggested weight and throws «insights» at the start, middle and end of a workout, knocking you out of your flow. You can't turn it off, and it annoys even paying subscribers.

product.title: Even basic logging is now locked behind a «start free» paywall
product.minus: Marketed as the best free app, but after a long questionnaire everything — from your own plans to plain weight tracking — hits an unclosable pay screen. Many call it a bait-and-switch.

product.title: After updates the app hangs on screens like «accumulation» and won't open
product.minus: Recent updates freeze the app on intermediate screens — «accumulation», «intensification», «on ramp», «adapting» — that you can't swipe past. Clearing cache, reinstalling and restarting don't help.

product.title: Updates wipe years of data: notes, plans, workout history
product.minus: Users with 10+ years of history report updates zeroing out saved sessions, per-exercise notes and past records — every lift suddenly a «new PB». For long-timers it's the loss of a journal built over years.

product.title: A huge exercise library with videos is the core that keeps people
product.plus: The most extensive exercise database around: form videos, filters by muscle group and equipment, plus the ability to add your own movements and machines. It's the thing even unhappy users still praise.

product.title: The free tier is genuinely enough — a rarity in the category
product.plus: Long-time users say the free version covers nearly everything you need, with no nagging ads (at least historically). Some pay for Elite not for features but out of sheer affection for the app.

product.title: The go-to long-term progress tracker — across years and decades
product.plus: The anchor strength: people keep 10-15 years of history, value the volume/set/rep tracking, calendar, muscle-group breakdown and the playful volume comparisons (elephants, bridges). It's the «I always come back to it».

product.title: Switching dumbbells to «per dumbbell» broke totals and 1RM
product.minus: The new «per dumbbell» logic mangles total volume and one-rep-max math: with 30kg in each hand it counts only one side, or reports a 1RM of 30kg. Old records logged as total weight get scrambled too.

product.title: Relentless subscription upselling wears down even paying users
product.minus: The «Elite» promo invades the logging screen, pop-ups and notifications — even for people who already subscribed or earned upgrade points they can't spend. The constant «buy» actually makes people want to use it less.

product.title: The interface has bloated: ending a workout drags on for minutes
product.minus: Once simple, the app turned clunky: opening and saving a workout can take up to two minutes, navigation is confusing, and it checks the connection constantly. Cache-clearing and reinstalling don't fix it.

product.title: Integrations (Strava, watch, Fitbit) are promised but half-broken
product.minus: Strava sync works only half the time and doesn't push data back, the watch app got paywalled and shows mismatched weight totals, and Fitbit integration has been requested for ten years with no reply.

product.title: A password leak and spam with no notice erode trust
product.minus: Users report a leaked password surfacing in identity-protection services with no notification, and a flood of spam to the address they gave only to Jefit. Trust in the developer is sliding.

product.title: "Lifetime" access turned out not to be lifetime
product.minus: Hundreds of people paid years ago for a "lifetime" Power Pack — only to find one day that the access was revoked and a subscription demanded instead. Users read it as outright deception and a betrayal of trust.

product.title: Paid-for features were taken away and locked behind a subscription
product.minus: Warmup sets, the plate calculator, history — the very things people paid a one-time fee for — suddenly stopped working with no notice. Users aren't asking for Pro, they just want back exactly what they already paid for.

product.title: Your own workout history held for ransom
product.minus: The most painful part: people lost access to years of their own data — sometimes 10-15 years and thousands of workouts. Just to see your own numbers you now have to take out a subscription.

product.title: Subscription pitched as high-value, though the app is a timer and a spreadsheet
product.minus: For an app that logs numbers and counts plates, a ~$60/year subscription feels absurd. Many say the same thing is easily replicated with a spreadsheet, ChatGPT, or pen and paper.

product.title: You can't even try it without a paid trial sign-up
product.minus: New users are made to go through setup and enter their details, only to hit a mandatory 7-day trial that auto-rolls into a yearly subscription. There's no free version anymore, and it feels like a bait-and-switch.

product.title: The "free" trial charges immediately, and refunds are impossible
product.minus: Several users report that accepting the "one-week free trial" charged them the full yearly amount ($80) on the spot, and Google and the developer point fingers at each other while no refund happens.

product.title: Constant pop-ups and subscription ads get in the way of working out
product.minus: Even before the full lockout, the app nagged with Pro ads on every action — even for those who already owned the Power Pack. Pop-ups blocked working features like warmup sets.

product.title: The simple 5×5 program genuinely gets beginners results
product.plus: For those not driven off by the subscription, the program wins with sheer simplicity: no math, no overthinking — just do it. People describe weight lost, muscle gained, and seeing real strength progress for the first time.

product.title: Automatic weight progression takes all the mental load off the lifter
product.plus: The app manages weight progression, alternates workouts and times rest — users love not having to guess what or how much to lift. For many that's the whole point of value.

product.title: Flexible plan editing and a large exercise library with videos
product.plus: Power users praise the plan editor, rest timers, set variety (regular/drop/pyramid), custom exercises, and form videos. For them it's the best workout tracker around.

product.title: Mehdi's emails and the community are a value of their own beyond the app
product.plus: Loyal users trusted founder Mehdi's advice for years: daily emails, spreadsheets and a mentoring tone gave them knowledge and motivation. It's exactly that trust that makes the subscription turn sting so much.

product.title: Bugs: crashes on launch, resetting workouts, data loss when switching phones
product.minus: Beyond monetization, there are technical complaints: the app crashes on launch even for paid users, workouts reset on their own, and weeks of progress are lost when moving to a new phone.

product.title: The migration to the new app wiped out years of workout history
product.minus: Dozens of users with 10-15 years of history lost everything when moving from BodySpace — workouts, progress photos, stats — nothing carried over and there was no export option.

product.title: The app constantly crashes and freezes mid-workout
product.minus: Crashes on launch, freezes when opening the calendar, and network errors — people spend more time relaunching the app than actually working out.

product.title: Finished workouts don't save and get stuck on the "You crushed it" screen
product.minus: After hitting "end workout" the "You crushed it" animation appears and the app freezes on it — the workout never closes and program progress stays stuck at 0%.

product.title: One accidental tap of "back" wipes out all your logged progress
product.minus: No resume button and no autosave: one wrong swipe or tap sends you back a screen and erases all the weights and reps you entered — you have to start the whole workout over.

product.title: The once-free BodySpace became a $10-15/month paid subscription
product.minus: Free user-made programs were locked behind a paywall and the price was hiked to $15 a month — for a version almost everyone considers worse than the free original.

product.title: A paid subscription isn't recognized — the app demands you pay again
product.minus: People who bought an annual subscription get told to pay again or start a free trial when they try to open a workout, and support replies only with AI templates or stays silent.

product.title: Workout logs don't save and history gets randomized with junk data
product.minus: Weights and reps don't log, history either disappears or fills with random values — tracking real progress through a program becomes impossible.

product.title: A workout tracker was turned into an intrusive social network
product.minus: Instead of easy program browsing there's an Instagram-style feed, people's faces popping up in the menu, and influencer videos at the start that can't be turned off.

product.title: Stripped-down customization: no custom programs and no multiple programs at once
product.minus: Old BodySpace let you build custom workouts and run several programs — now it's one at a time, with no custom exercises, supersets, drop sets, or equipment filters.

product.title: A bloated, unintuitive interface with side-scrolling and too many extra clicks
product.minus: Reaching simple things takes too many clicks, the screen is crowded, side-scrolling is awkward, history is buried in the calendar, and the layout doesn't adapt to foldable screens.

product.title: The programs and coaches themselves are still good — it's all that keeps the app afloat
product.plus: Even amid scathing reviews people admit the content is strong — great programs, coaches like Hannah Eden and Kris Gethin, a useful exercise library. The problem is the engineering, not the material.

product.title: A year of negative reviews and not a single fix: the developers seem to ignore everyone
product.minus: People come back a year later hoping for fixes and find the same bugs; the common refrain is lost progress, crashes, broken history — with no response from the company, only a prompt to buy.

product.title: The sheer variety of programs and coaches is why people stay for years
product.plus: A huge library of workouts for every level, goal and equipment — from bodyweight to gym — with new programs added regularly, so users don't get bored even after 5 years.

product.title: Not just workouts — a holistic bundle of food, meditation and recovery
product.plus: Users value that everything lives in one app: programs, recipes, meditations, sleep and mobility — it feels like complete wellness, not just a set of exercises.

product.title: The coaches motivate you — it feels like training with a friend, not a script
product.plus: Clear exercise delivery, banter and coach encouragement keep people coming back: videos show proper form and the coaches feel like real people guiding you.

product.title: Real results — and a replacement for an expensive personal trainer
product.plus: Users cite concrete numbers — kilos lost, shape gained — and compare a year's subscription to a £200/month personal trainer, deciding the app wins.

product.title: Constant logouts that wipe saved progress
product.minus: The app logs you out on every launch, forces a password reset and erases all recorded progress and saved recipes — for months, with no fix from support.

product.title: A recent update kills music from other apps during a workout
product.minus: After an update you can't play Spotify and keep the workout beeps at once: starting the session kills your music and starting music pauses the session — a choice between no music or no music.

product.title: "Sorry we dropped a dumbbell" — the error that breaks login and workouts
product.minus: The branded error message greets users at sign-up, login and program start; reinstalling doesn't help, and even the cancel-subscription button serves up the same dumbbell excuse.

product.title: Subscription charges even after cancellation — and you can't unsubscribe
product.minus: Annual charges of $80–$153 hit months after cancellation and even after deleting the app; there's no unsubscribe button in-app, and the website loops you back to the app.

product.title: The paywall is hidden until the end of onboarding — "free" in name only
product.minus: Users aren't told the app is paid until they've finished onboarding and handed over personal data; the promised "3 free months" with equipment turn into a 7-day trial demanding a credit card.

product.title: Workouts can't be customized — you take what's forced on you
product.minus: No exercise swaps, no building your own workout or adapting for knees/beginners, no logging weights in guided sessions — the app rigidly dictates what to do with no alternatives.

product.title: Videos and timers freeze right in the middle of a workout
product.minus: The demo freezes, the video won't "play", rest timers stop counting and the beeps vanish — forcing you to skip an exercise or restart the workout; unfixed for months.

product.title: The app "went downhill" after the company was sold — nostalgia for old Centr
product.minus: Long-time subscribers mourn that after the ownership change the Australian feel and community faded, programs grew repetitive with a HYROX bias, and each update makes the app worse.

product.title: Bought Centr-branded equipment — but the app has no workouts for it
product.minus: People buy Centr cable machines, multi-gyms and resistance bands, yet the app offers no programs for that equipment and isn't even compatible with the Inspire gear they bought — money on hardware effectively wasted.

product.title: The library of programs from real coaches is the main reason to stay
product.plus: Again and again, even in angry reviews users concede the program selection is fantastic. Ready-made plans like 5/3/1, Reddit PPL, GZCLP from real coaches and content creators, with auto-progression, technique videos and animations. It is the thing people put up with the app for.

product.title: Sluggish, laggy, and burns seconds on every tap
product.minus: The most frequent complaint: a fundamentally simple app behaves as if it's grinding something heavy in the background. 5+ second startup, a delay on every button press, lag when entering weight and reps. People literally compare it to an Excel spreadsheet — and Excel wins.

product.title: Crashes on launch, stuck on the 'checking for updates' screen
product.minus: For a whole tier of users the app never even reaches the home screen: it shows 'checking for updates' and immediately shuts down with a bug message. Clearing cache, Wi-Fi, reinstalling — nothing helps. For them the product is simply unusable.

product.title: A long onboarding questionnaire that dead-ends at a paywall
product.minus: Advertised as free, the app walks you through a long 'we're tailoring your workout' questionnaire, harvests your data — and only at the end tells you a subscription is required to use it. Many call the questionnaire itself a disguised ad rather than real personalization.

product.title: Swapping an exercise and the rest timer moved behind the paywall — and that stings most
product.minus: The most painful pattern: features that were free for years (swapping an exercise, the rest timer, dark mode, the plate calculator) got steadily locked into Pro. Longtime users read it as a betrayal and drop their rating specifically for it.

product.title: Two full-screen subscription prompts on every single open
product.minus: The redesign brought an aggressive upsell: every launch greets you with one or two full-screen Pro prompts you must dismiss by hand, even mid-workout. People pointedly note these two screens work flawlessly — unlike everything else.

product.title: Loses data on save: you hit 'done' and the day wipes itself
product.minus: The core of the product — the workout log — breaks: after hitting 'save' the day clears, weights don't save on the first try, history gets erased. For a tracker this is fatal, and paying users are especially furious to lose the very thing they paid for.

product.title: Restarts itself the moment you leave the app during rest
product.minus: Switch away to change a song and the app reloads from scratch, eating 15–20 seconds, resetting the rest timer and sometimes kicking you out of the current workout. Against the real gym scenario it turns every set into a fight with the app.

product.title: The new UI broke what was already perfect
product.minus: The redesign is near-unanimously seen as a step back: text overlapping text, everything too big and 'still in beta', programs now hard to find. Many just ask for the old UI back or an option to revert.

product.title: A genuinely generous free tier — that's what wins people over
product.plus: Those who get lucky on performance are delighted: genuinely free programs, progress tracking, technique videos and a PR indicator — all of it ad-free. For many it's the rare case where the free version is so complete it makes them want to pay out of gratitude.

product.title: The subscription feels overpriced — people want a one-time buy, not a rental
product.minus: Even loyal users balk at the price: ~€17 or $20 a month for what amounts to 'automated spreadsheets' feels absurd next to Spotify and Netflix. The recurring ask is a one-time purchase instead of a subscription — many would pay that, but not subscribe.

product.title: 'Home, no equipment' programs still hand you a barbell and parallel bars
product.minus: Equipment-based personalization doesn't work: pick 'home' or 'only bands and a pull-up bar' and you still get barbell bench, dumbbells and parallel-bar raises. People literally suggest scrapping the feature since it fails at its one job.

product.title: The program builder won't reliably save your work
product.minus: The standout feature — building your own program — is in practice unreliable: a created plan drops back to a draft after a day or two, only week one saves, custom workouts get deleted. The rigid UI on top of that won't even let you enter a rep range like '4-6'.

product.title: The rest timer gets fixed, then broken again
product.minus: The rest timer — for many the key reason to buy Pro — has been unreliable for months: doesn't ring, doesn't count, stops when you switch apps. One update fixes it, the next breaks it. For paying users that especially stings.

product.title: Support is barely there — a single co-founder handles tickets
product.minus: Paying users wait weeks for a reply: the in-app 'report issues' link is broken, emails go unanswered, and tickets — by users' accounts — are handled by the co-founder himself. Against the backdrop of subscription charges, the silence pushes people to bank chargebacks.

product.title: The team actually ships fixes and features people ask for
product.plus: The bright side of that same active development: users note requested features (notes, a timer) were actually added, the background timer got fixed, the data-draining issue and the intrusive popups were resolved — and they bump their rating back up to five stars for it.

product.title: A hard «3 workouts then pay» wall hits with no warning
product.minus: By far the most common complaint: the app is presented as free, but after 3 workouts (or ~3 days) it locks you out and demands a subscription. People are furious less about the price than about not being told up front — you only find out when you hit the wall.

product.title: Clear instructions and animations teach proper form
